Alia deinde ex eadem posteriore trunci sede, sed sub secundum, V. da prodit, quae descendens, & ligamentum transuersum transiens, per pedis dorsum excurrit, in digitos abducentes musculos diffusa. Reliquum trunci per tibiae posteriora, deorsum fertur, & circa malleolum internum pedi furculum offert, qui pollicum adit, & pedis dorsum perreptat. Ipse autem truncus inter tendines musculorum digitorum pedis latens, in duos ramos diffecatur, quorum interior pollici duos, duos indici, vnum medio: exterior vero duos minimo, duos huic proximis digitis, inferiore fedelargitur. Ceterum, etsi arteriarum progressus magna ex parte talis fit, qualem descripsimus, quod tamen supra de Venis diximus, non solum pro indiuiduorum diuersitate, sed etiam laterum in eodem homine, ipsorum distributionem plurimum variare, id etiam de arteriis tenendum est, quae aliis hominibus alio modo se habent.

# CAPVT VI.

*Vena arterialis, & Arteriae venalis historiam complectitur.*

<margin>Vena arterialis. Arteria venalis.</margin>
<margin>Ortus.</margin>

<margin>Distribuitio.</margin>

VT perfecta omnibusque suis numeris absoluta sit haec de Venis & Arteriis tractatio, colophonis loco historiam tertiae Venae & secundae arteriae nobis apponere libuit. Vocatur Vena, arterialis, & Vena quidem ab officio, quod Veteres sanguinem deferre ex dextro cordis ventriculo credidissent: at arterialis a tunica, arteriarum membranae simili, cum simplex non sit, vt Venarum, sed gemina. Arteria contra, venalis dicitur, & arteria quidem, quod aerem deuehere, attractum per pulmones Antiqui statuerint: Venalis autem, quod substantia corpori venarum respondeat, cum simplex sit tunica, nec admodum crassa. Reiecimus autem vtriusque tractationem in hunc praecipue locum, vt vtraque simul ageremus, cum & ex eodem viscere nascantur, & in idem inferantur, praeterea que eadem distributione gaudeant. Enascuntur enim ex Corde, & Vena quidem ex editiore sede dextri ventriculi: Arteria autem ex sinistri. Implantatur autem & exhauritur vtraque; in Pulmonum substantiam, & Vena quidem per dextrum asperae arteriae latus porrigitur, Arteria autem per sinistrum. Mox in duos vtraque secatur ramos, quorum alter ad dextram, alter ad sinistram pulmonum partem abit, vtroque iterum bifariam secto, atque his in ramos alios, donec in minutissimos furculos dispergantur. Rami autem maiores sese inuicem comitantur, vt vena cum arteria perpetuo incedat, multis anastomobibus iunctae, in quarum medio asperae arteriae rami excurrunt. Insignia autem vasa sunt, maioraque longe, quam pulmonum magnitudo requirere videtur, cum partes illae, vt diximus libro superiore, quae plurimum dissipant alimenti, venas ampliores requirunt, nulla autem fit, quae pulmonibus ob perpetuum

<meta>continues from previous page: ...The trunk of the great artery, when it arrives at the last vertebra of the loins, along with the entire duct we have described, follows a path below the vena cava to the left, so that it might ascend the vein, lest it be worn away by the hardness of the sacral bone during that continuous movement. It is divided, however, not unlike the Cava itself, into two notable branches, which those skilled in anatomy call the Iliac arteries because of their position, and carried obliquely downward to the thigh, they express the inverted Y of the Greeks. These themselves also, before they are brought into the thigh, provide many branches, just like the iliac veins, to which they respond exactly in every way.</meta>

<margin>Sacral.</margin>
From the lower seat of the artery, before the Iliacs are divided, the <term>Sacral</term> [arteries] emerge, which are notable and, carried downward resting upon the sacral bone, they enter its foramina, and run out to its marrow and the posterior parts of the sacral bone. And through these, too, is a path for the matter causing colicky pain, so that it may effect paralysis of the legs. Hence, a little below the division of the trunk, the Iliacs are subdivided into two branches, of which one is inner and smaller: the other outer and larger.

<margin>Propagations of the Iliac arteries. Of the inner, or smaller. 1. Muscular. 2. Hypogastric.</margin>
The smaller, or inner Iliac, leads out two propagations, one from the outer, the other from the inner seat. The <term>Outer</term>, commonly called the Muscular, [is called] by us by the stricter name, <term>Gluteal</term>, because it descends with the vein of the same name between the sacrum and the hip bone, where they depart from each other, and it extends several shoots into the muscles overlying the ilium bone, called the Gluteals because they are the authors of the buttocks. The <term>Inner</term> is called the <term>Hypogastric</term>, which is quite notable and ample, and carried straight downward to the lower seat of the sacral bone, it bestows certain shoots in men upon the fundus and neck of the bladder, and then also upon the rectum, which can also be called the hemorrhoidal arteries. In women, however, for whom this branch is slightly larger, besides the said parts, it distributes a numerous propagation also into the lower region of the fundus of the uterus, and likewise into its neck. Hence, one may seek the reason why, if the uterus proceeds to the middle of the hip, convulsions occur, as Hippocrates testifies in his book, *On the Nature of Women*. Likewise, if the uterus has settled toward the hip, why menses are suppressed, and pain occurs in the lower belly and in the softness of the sides. For the blood, which is driven by Nature to the uterus, when the arteries are compressed by the settling, cannot be deposited in the uterus, whence necessarily regurgitating, it fills the neighboring veins and arteries, which, swelling, cause these pains. We have often seen in dissections that these veins were so turgid that they were seven times larger than themselves. From this also, the reason can be given for that aphorism, which is the thirty-second of the fifth section, in the same Hippocrates, where he testifies that in a woman vomiting blood, relief occurs upon the eruption of the menses. Which, indeed, happens by the consent of all through revulsion, and truly cannot occur through the benefit of the veins, because the veins of the stomach arise from the portal vein, but those of the uterus from the cava; no other consensus is to be sought than that which occurs through the arteries, especially since the hypogastric artery is not far distant from the coeliac. From these, similarly, the reason will be rendered for the aphorism following this one, where, when menses are deficient, he deems a nosebleed to be salutary.

<margin>Umbilical artery.</margin>
The remaining part of the smaller Iliac descends and brings out the <term>Umbilical artery</term>, which is carried along the length of the great artery and is connected by strong membranes to the sides of the urinary bladder. It loses its cavity in those who have emerged into these pleasant breaths of life, which, how it is done, we shall show later in the ninth book at greater length.

<summary>This page describes the division of the Iliac arteries into the sacral, gluteal, hypogastric, and umbilical branches, detailing their anatomical paths and functions in the lower torso.</summary>

In Mulieribus vero, quibus paulo amplior hic ramus est, præter dictas partes, etiam in inferiorem vteri fundi regionem, & pariter in illius ceruicem numerosam propaginem distribuit. Hinc rationem licet petere, ob quam si Vteri ad medium coxendicis processerint, conuulsiones fiant, vt testatur Hippocrates, lib. de natura muliebri. Item, si Vterus ad coxam decubuerit, cur menses supprimantur, & dolor fiat in imo ventre, & in laterum mollitudine. Sanguis enim, qui ad Vterum à Natura pellitur, arteriis compressis à decubitu, in vterum deponi non potest, vnde necessario regurgitans, vicinas Venas & Arterias replet, quæ intumescentes dolores hos efficiunt. Vidimus enim sæpenumero in dissectionibus sic turgidas fuisse has venas, vt septuplo sese ampliores fuerint. Hinc etiam ratio reddi potest aphorismi illius, qui est trigesimus secundus quintæ sectionis, apud eundem Hippocratem, vbi Mulieri sanguinem vomenti erumpentibus mensibus solutionem fieri testatur. Quod sane, cum omnium consensu fiat per reuulsionem, & vero Venarum beneficio contingere nequeat, quod Venæ Ventriculi à Portæ vena, at Vteri, à Caua oriantur, non alius consensus quærendus est, quam ille, qui fit per Arterias, maxime cum nec arteria hypogastrica procul à Cœliaca distet. Ex his similiter ratio reddetur sequentis hunc aphorismi, vbi mensibus deficientibus hæmorrhagiam narium salutarem censet. 

<margin>Arteria Vmbilicalis.</margin>
Reliqua pars Iliacæ minoris descendit, & t arteriam Vmbilicalem educit, t, η.η. quæ iuxta longitudinem arteriæ magnæ defertur, validisque membranis Vesicæ vrinariæ lateribus connectitur. Cauitatem autem amittit in iis, qui in has iucundas vitæ auras prodiere, quod quomodo fiat, postmodum libro nono pluribus ostensuri sumus.

Harum usum omnes fere, qui hactenus in Anatomicis aliquid scripserunt, unanimi consensu prodiderunt esse, vt Vena quidem pulmonibus alimentum afferat, Arteria autem à pulmonibus haustum aerem ad Cor deducat. Quae opinio absurdissimo fundamento nititur, sanguinem scilicet nulla ratione in hac arteria contineri, in quo confutando prolixiores ellemus, nisi anatomicam inspectionem, & experientiam satis superque falsitatem demonstrare sciremus. Quare ab iis potius standum existimo, qui à dextro cordis ventriculo ad pulmones per Venam arterialem sanguinem transmitti credunt, & hinc in Arteriam venalem per anastomoses deduci, à qua postea ad Cor transportatur, vbi magis elaboratur sanguis ille dextri ventriculi, & fit spirituosus, sicque per Arteriam magnam in vniuersum corpus, pro vita singularum partium, pellitur. Nec verum est aerem in Arteriam venalem rapi, cum foramina ibi nulla sint, sed aer qui per Laryngem in asperam pulmonum arteriam raptus est, bronchia omnia refrigerat, quod frigus cum adiacentibus vasis communicetur (diximus enim vbique bronchia ferri in medio Venae arteriosae & Arteriae venosae) refrigerat simul sanguinem in ipsis contentum, qui Cor ingrediens calorem illum nimium attemperat, vt propterea opus non sit aerem in substantia ad Cor transferri.

Temperare mihi non possum, quo minus de quaestione vexatissima nonnulla suggeram: an et Tragoediae Senecam Philosophum Autorem agnoscant? Notum enim est, quomodo communiter tres Senecae nomine insignes recenseantur: M. Annaeus Rhetor, L. Annaeus Seneca Philosophus, et tandem Seneca Tragoedus. Legi de hoc possunt Bailleti jugemens des Sçauans sur les principaux ouvrages des Auteurs Tomo IV. Parte II. pagina 363. et Autores sub finem citati. Sane diversa eruditi de Tragoediis sentiunt. Non unius esse autoris, modo dicta judicia afferunt; asserit etiam Clarissimus Fabricius loco citato dum Herculem furentem M. Annaeo Senecae, Patri, Hippolytum Senecae Philosopho, et ita reliquas, alias aliis Autoribus vindicat. Those who concern themselves with the philosopher <term>Lucius Annaeus Seneca</term> customarily weigh his name, lineage, credibility, writings, the sharpness of his style, and his dogmas in the balance, and examine each part diligently. Indeed, from the fact that he is called Lucius Annaeus Seneca, some authors—and among them Stadius—confuse Lucius Annaeus Seneca with the historian <term>Lucius Annaeus Florus</term>; this is quite absurd and was rightly noted by Salmasius in his notes and corrections to Florus. For the monuments of history and the verses in which Florus and the Emperor Hadrian vied with each other—"I do not wish to be Caesar, and so forth," "I do not wish to be Florus, and so forth"—abundantly prove how Florus was a contemporary of Trajan and Hadrian. Consult the most elegant program LXIV of the most illustrious Marcus Rosenb. on Florus. Conversely, Lucius Annaeus Seneca lived in the time of Nero, in the first century after the birth of Christ, as Suetonius in *Nero*, chapter 35, Dio Cassius, and others teach. Even if Vossius, a great ornament to the world of letters, concedes that Florus originated from the family of Seneca because his poetic diction savors of a poetic house, I add: the name Annaeus, which is the family name and belongs to Florus as well, testifies that he traced his origin to the same Annaean family. 

To approach more closely the noble lineage of Seneca: there was Marcus Annaeus Seneca the Rhetor, a most learned man of the Equestrian order, who in Corduba in Baetican Spain took to wife Elvia, also a Spaniard and a woman of great talent, and had three sons: Lucius Annaeus Seneca the philosopher, just mentioned; Annaeus Novatus; and Annaeus Mella, the father of Annaeus Lucanus, the author of the *Pharsalia*, that is, the history of the civil war between Caesar and Pompey, which ended on the Pharsalian plains. Lipsius gave us this pedigree of the Annaean family in *Electiones*, Book I, chapter 1, page 463 of his *Opera Critica*, as well as in the preface prefixed to the 1649 Leiden edition of the works of Seneca. Indeed, for one who has at hand those who have recorded the life of Seneca—among whom we count Jannutius Mannettus of Florence and Lipsius himself, who wrote a singular book on the life of Seneca—there is no reason to doubt that one might have accurate information regarding the condition of his life, his death, and other matters. 

The illustrious Lord von Ziegler presented the life of Seneca to the learned world in the vernacular tongue, using Tacitus, Suetonius, Dio, and others, in the *täglichen Schau-Platz der Zeit* [Daily Theater of the Times], April 30, pages 482, 483, 484. Regarding the Christian faith of Seneca, and whether he professed the same, not only did Lord Strauch, a professor at Wittenberg, deal with it in a peculiar dissertation in 1668, but also the blessed Kortholt—first at Rostock, later a truly Christian Professor of Theology at the illustrious <term>CHRISTIAN-ALBRECHT-UNIVERSITY</term> <gloss>Kiel</gloss> (as Lord Lindemann names him in the memorial of Christian Kortholt)—wished to address it in 1667 in his dissertation on the Christianity of Philip the Arab, Alexander Mammaea, Pliny the Younger, and Annaeus Seneca. "A law-expert and near-Christian Heathen," he is called by Lord Doctor Pfeiffer in *Anti-Mel*, Book I, page 19; add the epitaph to be found in Lord Ziegler at the cited location: "A Christian regarding the heathens," etc. These things are not in the least proven by the mutual letters of Paul and Seneca; they are ridiculous, inept, barbaric, and unworthy of Seneca and Paul, the fabrication of a rather unlearned monk. These are the words of Horn in his *History of Philosophy*, Book IV, where he discusses at greater length the religion of Seneca, by which he is said to have been a Christian, and refutes the arguments. One and the same craftsman composed the letters of Paul and Seneca, according to the judgment of the most Reverend Lord colleague, Lucius Ittig.

**XXVII.** Through the rarefaction of the parts of the body, the pores are enlarged; once these are enlarged, space is left for the generation of a part larger than what was lost, without which no increment of a living being could occur.

**XXVIII.** Augmentation occurs by reason of form, and not of matter, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> teaches in the first book of *On Generation* <note>De Generatione et Corruptione</note>.

**XXIX.** However, by the name of "form," one should not understand instrumental parts, nor parts generated from radical moisture, nor any others of such magnitude and virtue that they can generate parts like themselves, nor the pores, nor the form that constitutes the nature of the thing, which, in the growth of no living being except man, persists identical in number to the very end.

At which words the raging man was stirred and struck the most holy man with a slap. Then Blessed Benno, inspired by a divine spirit, said: "God Almighty will avenge this great injury at this same time of the following year." Then he received the Eucharist, that divine food, with great piety, and when he had offered prayers to God, the best and greatest, he departed from life. And this, indeed, in the fortieth year of his pontificate, after Christ was born, one thousand one hundred and sixteen. Thus far concerning those things which, in his life, the divine man accomplished not by human counsel but divinely. We have decided to recite some of the things which happened with the greatest admiration after his death. But not everything that is viciously done lacks the effect of law, which appears in a prodigal donation, etc." Grotius therefore thinks that a promise of an illicit thing or act is invalid, but that a promise on account of an illicit thing and act does not lack a legal effect or obligation. But in truth, a vow made on account of a morally impossible thing produces no obligation in the one vowing, for the obligation resulting from a vow on account of a morally impossible thing is shameful, and there is no obligation given for a shameful thing. That obligation, I say, is shameful. For the cause of which is shameful, that very thing is shameful, since the good, according to the rule of Dionysius, is born from a whole cause, and evil from any defect whatsoever. But the cause of an obligation made on account of a shameful thing is shameful, for the cause of that obligation which arises from a vow is the vow itself, and now the cause of a vow made on account of a shameful thing is shameful; for this reason it is said to be a vow made on account of a shameful cause. A shameful cause of a cause (just as, for example, the homicide to be performed by Caius is the cause of the vow made by Titius) will therefore also be the cause of the shameful effect, namely the shameful obligation. *Which was to be demonstrated.* But the Scholastics wrongly demand of the object of a vow that it not be a thing that is by its own nature intermediate and indifferent. For a *Vow* is a promise made to *God*: and just as we can promise an indifferent thing to men, so nothing prevents us from being able to promise a thing indifferent in its nature to *God* in a vow on account of an honorable circumstance, for example if someone vows a field, a house, or animals to *God*, he is held bound to *God* no less than one vowing morally good things, and indeed, by not fulfilling these vows he sins and wounds his own conscience: for a promise must be kept. seed: as it is now proclaimed, it would be a wonder that Luke in the Acts of the Apostles, Eusebius, Nicephorus in history, Augustine in his City of God, and other ancient ecclesiastical writers had passed over so great a matter. Certainly, Christ is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, leaving no Vicar successor, other than His own holy Spirit, who will be present with His own always. Wherefore in the Melchizedekian priesthood of the New Testament (as was done once in the Old Aaronic one until the Messiah) we know of no pontifical succession. But we also know the succession of the Roman pontiffs, through various schisms and frequent antipopes, to have been foully interrupted in many ways and brutally contaminated: raging against one another with the most invidious and at the same time most atrocious censures. By what spirit they are led, their deeds prove, histories testify, poets sing, libraries speak, and the pious and learned lament. Bernard to Eugenius: What shall I say of the people? he says. They are the Roman people, and I could not open more briefly or more expressively what I feel about your parishioners. What is so well known to the age as the impudence and pride of the Romans? A people unaccustomed to peace, accustomed to tumult: a people harsh and intractable, up to now knowing not how to submit, unless it is unable to resist. The same Bernard: Woe, he says, to this generation from the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy, if it should even be called hypocrisy, which now cannot hide due to its abundance, and does not seek to due to its impudence. A rotten corruption creeps today through the whole body of the church, and the further it goes, the more desperate it is: and the more dangerous, the more internal. All are friends, and all are enemies: all are neighbors, and all are adversaries: all are kinsmen, and all seek their own: they are ministers of Christ, and serve the antichrist. # THEOREMA II.

*Αυτοφονία Spontanea, quaecunque tandem illa sit, nisi expressa et speciali nitatur jussione divina, simpliciter culpanda et damnanda est.*

Consequens ergo jam est proximum, ut quid de variis αὐτοχείρων generibus sentiendum sit aperiamus, id quod commodissime fiet, si spontaneos et plena deliberataque voluntate agentes sui occisores ab Ignorantibus sejungamus, quorum illos, quocunque nomine veniant, cujuscunque sint ordinis, quacunque de causa peccent, culpandos et damnandos simpliciter existimamus.

1. Assertionis fundamenta sint sequentia: 1. *Fortitudinis natura et officium*, quod est, ut hominem in periculis necessariis honeste subeundis fortiterque perferendis disponat, seu, ut *Philosofhus* loquitur *lib. 3. Nicom. cap. 10*, ut homo secundum eam fugere et perferre possit αἰδεῖ, καὶ οὗ ἕνεκα, καὶ ὡς δεῖ, καὶ ὅτε; quorum nihil faciunt hi animarum proditores.

3. Non enim pericula fugiunt vel perferunt ea quae oportet. Fugiunt enim dolores et cruciatus corporis; At horum tolerantiam cum honestate Fortitudo maxime docet, quae taurum milies Phalaridis tolerandum, quam δειλίᾳ turpissima stationem esse relinquendam officioque abdicandum praecipit, hortatur, urget, ita ut is demum κυρίως ἂν ἀνδρεῖος λέγοιτο, ὁ περὶ τὸν καλὸν θάνατον ἀδεὴς. *l. d. c. 9.*

4. Fugiunt amoris illusi et elusi vulnus; At quale? quod vitasse, quam accepisse jam omnes sanum magis et honestum existimant. Quod enim heic lucrum aut emolumentum? subdole blanditur amor, abs re consulit, blandiloquentulus, harpago, mendax, cupes, avarus, elegans, despoliator, latebricolarum hominum corruptor, blandus, inops, amara dat satis, in quem qui se praecipitavit, peius perit, quam si saxo saliat. *ut ait Comicus in Trinummo*; cujus inconstantia tanta, ut non status sed circuitus ejus sit, in quo nihil ne momento quidem stabile est, *Scal. lib. 3. de re Poet. cap. 23.* Quis ergo tam leviusculi, noxii et inconstantis boni gratia sibi semet eripiat? Besides these three sources of cowardice, a fourth still occurs, which is ignominy and disgrace, by which men, struck down, are not only afflicted by sorrow, so that the entire habit of the body is also changed (just as *Scaliger* in *Exercitationes 312* relates the history of someone who, kept in a tower for questioning or punishment due to suspicion of conspiracy, suddenly became entirely gray in one night; and elsewhere, many dissected bodies have shown the heart like a scorched pear), but they also intend evil against themselves.

11. *Cleopatra* provided an example of this, who, when *Antony* was dead and she saw no help remaining for her afflicted affairs, offered her arm to be bitten by an asp, so that she would not be led as a captive in a triumph, and was thus extinguished by this poison. Thus also *Saul*, so that he would not be mocked by the uncircumcised *Philistines*, having seized a sword, rushed upon it, 1 Sam. 31:4. And *Razias* in 2 Maccabees 14:41, when the army of *Nicanor* was attempting to rush into the house, break down the door, and set fire to it, when he was already being seized, he attacked himself with a sword; and when through haste he had not dealt the blow with a certain stroke, running back boldly to the wall, he threw himself manfully into the crowds.

12. By these means, therefore, those become <term>autophonoi</term> <gloss>self-slayers</gloss>, who seem to sin not indeed by malice, but mostly by cowardice. The other rank seems to lack both malice and cowardice, and it includes two orders in turn, the first of which intends the avoidance of sin or crime, and consequently exerts the hand of the desperate person upon himself. In this group are those sacred virgins whom *Augustine* makes mention of, who, fleeing the tyranny of *Sardanapalus* and when the bloodthirsty soldiers were clinging at their backs, with *Christ* devoutly invoked, by a pitiful spectacle all rushed together into the jaws of *Neptune* (the sea), lest they provide the use of their bodies to the enemies. This utility, if it must be declared at greater length, redounds to both the Prince and the subjects; that he should show himself clement or good toward his subjects, and be uniquely intent upon the highest political good and the happiness of the Republic, that certainly is done by intuition of piety, the account of which is applied to him, since otherwise, that being neglected, he would take care of himself, not the people, would make no conscience of it, would oppress the citizens, would deprive them of their faculties, would expose justice itself for sale, or, to condense the matter, would give himself up to tyranny and decline into atheism, expecting the rebellion of subjects and his own resulting destruction, according to that:

§. 54. They think, however, that some provide nutritious juice to the nerves, others receive their waste, and reduce it through the lymphatic vessels into the veins, and others export their excrement outward, whence *Glisson* calls the first *nutritive*, the second *reductive*, and the third *excretory*. Those which are said to secrete the nutritious juice are the *mesenteric glands* and the *lumbar glands of Bartholin*: these glands are said to secrete *nutritious juice* from the chyle passing through the mesentery, which is then assumed by the nerves and carried to the brain: they call those *excretory* which emit their liquid outside the body or deposit it into a cavity, such as the *breasts, testicles*, and other glands: they call those *reductive* which take up the superfluous alible juice and reduce it again toward the veins; to which they refer, albeit incorrectly, the *parotids* and *jugulars*.

§. 55. But we do not approve this opinion either, for it rests upon that false hypothesis that the nerves carry nutritious juice, of which matter we must treat in a special exercise *on nutritive glands*; for I do not deny that some secrete nutritious juice, but I deny likewise that the mesaraic glands do so, as I argue where I deal with the *mesaraic glands*. Reductive glands are nothing other than excretory, for, as they themselves admit, they secrete lymph; that some lymph, however, is reduced into the blood mass, due to various uses, that does not properly pertain to the glands, whose unique and principal duty is to secrete something, whatever use that secreted liquid may be put to.

§. 56. If we correctly assess the nature and actions of glands, then we see that they all act to secrete something from the blood, whether you call it lymph, or humors, or by some other peculiar name, it will be the same to me, provided I obtain this, that that *secreted liquid* is not of the same nature, and that all is secreted from the blood.

Etiam hoc addo: Ubi nos cum diversæ religionis hominibus in eadem provincia aut civitate conjunxit divina vocatio, quæ est magistratus summi permissio, ibi salva conscientia perdurare possumus, modo liceat nostram religionem nobis ritè & tuto colere. Tum enim pios solatur illa Dei promissio, quâ pollicetur, se unicuique in vocatione & vijs suis affore Psalmi 91. 11. 15. id quod in Abrahamo, Isaaco, Jacobo in Ægyptum jussu ejus descendentibus, in Daniele, ejusque socijs captivis in Babylonia degentis videre est. & huc traho illud, quod tanto opere Jurisconsulti & Politici quidam urgent, posse diversas tolerari religiones. concedo, sed à nobis, qui sumus subditi, quando magistratus superior concessit. Num vero de novo in libera Republica admitti debeat religio minus Orthodoxa, qui ex scriptura probaret, hactenus vidi neminem.

Denique (ut omittam alias plures objectionculas, quæ ex jam dictis facilè dissolvi possunt) immane quantum discrepent à præsenti quæstione exempla Abrahæ Genesis 14. & 21. & Isaaci Genesis 26. ferientium fœdera. Primùm enim non desunt (inter quos etiam Lutherus noster) qui negant, eos confœderatos fuisse impios, profanos, aut à religione Patriarcharum alienos, id quod ipsi aliquot ex textu petitis argumentis conantur probare. Ego hoc satis disertè ex locis allegatis evinci posse ajo, non fuisse hæc fœdera Ecclesiastica & mixta, sed tantum politica, de rebus civilibus: & hoc non tam defendendo, quàm de non offendendo, utrumque vero tùm contractum à Patriarchis, quando non admodum ipsi horum ope indigebant, imò, quando hoc petebat ab ipsis Abimelech. In a hidden valley, from the deepest roots 
Of a grassy Hill, a fountain perennially leaps with a twin

Mouth. Which, because rumor had affirmed that the 
Wonder-working tides of the immense sea play in a tiny 
Wave, it seemed (however much Phoebus was hastening) to tarry

Water, and to be witnesses of the rumor. 
The tremulous wave which boils up with glassy waters, the 
Larger of the two, and more splendid, and demanding to be seen alone, 
Is received by a well, not to be compared to built ones, 
But which is more ornate than any accidental birth. 
Thence it flows released, except what is held at the bottom 
Two cubits wide, three long, and one deep. 
I say one when, content with its liquid, it 
Subsides, but two when it is raised by the visiting 
Wave. A stone line of the reclining bank marked the 
Lips, which the swelling waters themselves made, 
Found at times to have ebbed on the blackish rocks.

§. XIV. It is also not to be approved that boys and girls should be trained for this art of walking on a rope. Indeed, it is the duty of parents to take care that their children are instructed in arts that are useful for social and civil life. Our most blessed Lord Boeclerus excellently says in *Political Institutions*, book 3, page 45: "He warns parents to undertake the care of education seriously and constantly, sparing no labor, no expense, if indeed they love and revere the honest succession of their family, the utility of the State and the Fatherland—to which we must present not only ourselves but our own—and above all the authority of God, stimulated by the instincts implanted by nature and the holy laws toward the duties of parents." Parents have no regard for this duty of theirs who even teach their children the rope-dancing art themselves, and allow them to be instructed in it. Such are rightly said to sacrifice their dearest pledges to <term>Moloch</term> <gloss>a Canaanite deity associated with child sacrifice</gloss>, as far as in them lies. Long ago, the Blessed Cyprian, 1st Epistle, 10, very heavily resented that there were those among Christians who did not blush to teach the theatrical art: "I think," he says, "it is appropriate neither to the Divine Majesty nor to evangelical discipline that the modesty and honor of the Church be defiled by such a base and infamous contagion"; how much more heavily we believe he would have taken it that parents themselves instruct their children in such arts, which are unworthy of Christian piety and gravity.

§. XV. Furthermore, since the rope-dancing art ought not to be approved by Christians, the question arises whether it can be tolerated in a Christian State? Certainly the Fathers of the Church—Tertullian, Clement of Alexandria, Cyprian, Arnobius, Lactantius, Isidore, Augustine, Chrysostom, Salvianus (with whom the most learned Rittershusius's annotation on page 190 should be joined)—judge that they should be expelled from their Christian Republic, if we consider those things which they gravely warned about concerning spectacles. # In the year from the birth of Christ 1511

A certain booklet, written in our Germanic or common (if one prefers) tongue, titled Johannes Reuchlin's *Ocular Mirror*, appeared in the light—alas—partly through the printing press. His Imperial Majesty, who is to be celebrated by the letters and tongues of all, not undeservedly prohibited it by his open letters throughout his entire empire—as it was dangerous to all and inclined more than was just toward the favor of Jewish perfidy—from being sold, bought, kept, or publicly disseminated, and he forbade it, led primarily by justice. Now this command of our most serene Emperor, being so holy and salutary, was executed with the utmost equity by the most reverend lords in Christ, the Archbishops of the dioceses of Mainz and Cologne, and also by the most sacred prelates of the churches of Worms and Würzburg. As a result, in Frankfurt, that most noble emporium of all Germany, and in the public fairs there, many of these dangerous booklets were intercepted and held by public decree and most holy law, lest they be disseminated more widely and cause greater scandal to the unrefined populace. ¶ Then, in the year 1513, around April, when the same author, inflated by I know not what spirit, had brought to light for the defense of his booklet another—but a most biting and (if I may say so) most injurious—pamphlet, the sacred Imperial Majesty, out of zeal for the faith, committed by public edict to the most sacred Archbishops of Mainz, Cologne, and Trier, as well as the Inquisitors of heretical depravity, the task of exterminating the scandals from the simple Christian faithful (as has been said above), insofar as they would strive with their strength for the worthy suppression of the recent booklets of the aforementioned Johannes Reuchlin and labor completely and entirely. The *Preservative* is occupied with the prohibition of a new influx, and how the remaining morbific causes can be suffocated as if in the herb, by eliminating that which can harm by quantity, and altering that which can harm by quality.

The *Vital* regards the strength of both the whole and the affected parts, and commands one to preserve what remains of health through good nourishment, to correct the parts that send [the humor] through appropriate medicines, and to corroborate and fortify those that receive [it] through both suitable foods and medicines.

**The material of the remedy is to be sought from three customary sources.**

From the **SURGICAL** first is *Venesection* <gloss>bloodletting</gloss>. Since the source and cause of the evil lies in the blood mass, and this, being abundant in the body and vessels, is stirred up with vicious motion and as it were boils, and the pain attracts the matter more and more to the affected parts so that arthritis is increased or fever succeeds, it will not be ill-advised, provided the strength, age, and concomitant symptoms permit, to open the vein opposite the affected part in the beginning; naturally, if the pain persists in the right arm, [open] the vein of the left, and conversely; but if the foot or hip suffers, [open] the one placed directly, namely in the same side of the elbow or even the ham or the ankle, called the Sciatic, sometimes, according to *Plater*, to cut [it] in the healthy leg, and to extract a just, not excessive, quantity of blood, and always in this operation to look to a good configuration of the heavens.

I am furthermore excluded by the narrowness of time, which scarcely allows it to be granted to add a few things about his disease and its last act, his blessed, I say, passing. Concerning his illness, I think you should recognize the words of the Doctor of Medicine.

Regarding the illness, I would not incorrectly call it hepatic <note>affecting the liver</note>. For as the blessed Lord Rector had a constitution of the whole body that was too hot and dry, so also I observed his liver to be of the same temperament, a fertile mother of bilious humors. There was a close relationship of this to Scurvy. The humors burgeoning from such a constitution attacked the liver above all, the seat of its dominion, obstructing a good part of it. At the beginning, the patient felt a pain of a certain kind weighing down in this organ, and soon his appetite was prostrated, and at the same time his nightly rest failed. It was time to look around for remedies and to expel the snake hiding in the first grass. However, such was the ardor for study in the excellent Master, such was his care for his students, that he took greater account of them than of himself.

With the humors impacted in the liver, time and opportunity were left for it to strengthen its dominion; hence, little by little, everything began to turn for the worse. Nearly months, not weeks, had passed since his body, never accustomed to illness, had felt the first movements of the lurking enemy. The matter in the liver had already visibly turned into fermentation: the mass of the blood, at the same time, with the contamination of rot communicated, while the Blessed one allowed medicine to be made for himself. He committed the business of his care to his kinsman and physician, Lord Johann Köcker. He omitted nothing that he could do for the preservation of the Eximite Man, his most dear friend.

Cicero praises *Brutus*, *Octavius*, and others for having taken up the public cause by private counsel. That deed, indeed, was done with no one opposing: that is, with silent consent. *Zevecotius in his Notes on Florus* thinks that Cicero was carried away by the zeal of faction, and by hatred toward *Antony*. Certainly, it has been a constant law that the right of waging war resides with the public authority: and it has endured to these times. The Romans were always most observant of this, taking notice of anyone who acted otherwise. To such an extent that they even ordered, through ambassadors, that it be asked whether war had been brought upon them by others by public counsel, so that a private undertaking would not be punished by a public penalty and war against the whole nation. *Livy, Book 21.* In our Roman-German Empire, this right resides with the Emperor and the Estates of the Empire. See the Capitulation of the MOST AUGUST LEOPOLD, § 13. And for a war to be so just, it is necessary that it be waged by Majesty. Majesty, however, is supreme power without law. A rough monarch rules and is not held accountable. *He is a king, using his own right, beholden to no one. Aeschylus.*

X. I come to the causes of war. Among *Xenophon*, there is a twofold cause for justly undertaking a war: if someone has either been afflicted by an injury, or attempts to avert it from friends and allies. *It is necessary for those who have suffered injury to take up arms for themselves or to assist relatives, benefactors, and allies who have been afflicted by injury. Aristotle, Rhetoric to Alexander.* However, by allies I understand those joined by a singular treaty or all humans by natural kinship. For it is fair to help all who are unjustly oppressed. *To be afflicted by injury is to suffer unjust things from those who act of their own accord. Aristotle, Rhetoric, Book 1, Chapter 13.* Therefore, to avert it from oneself and one’s own is a most fair cause. Nature teaches us to defend ourselves and ward off injuries. To reclaim what is one’s own is granted by every law.

All those who truly profess to be lovers of political science, and who rightly apply their effort to examining and investigating the laws of nature, judge gravely that for the blessed life of citizens, it is required not only that the state be endowed with great glory, rich in resources, and firm in wealth, but also that it be honorable through virtue. For although those to whom, having abandoned virtue, nothing is lacking for the convenience of all things, seem to some to live well and securely enough, yet it is so far from the case that this, separated from the honesty of morals, should be called true happiness, that on the contrary, we do not hesitate to say it possesses an empty and most deceitful appearance of mutable things and insidious enticements. They have therefore erred vehemently, as many among the ancients as maintained that there is no natural law; that all laws should either be proposed, or changed, or rejected, according to the utility of each person; that it is fitting for every mortal, with nature showing the way, to consider only that which is useful; that justice is to be valued at nothing; and that it is the height of stupidity to propose rewards and honors for good deeds, and punishments and ignominy for evil deeds; for this, they claim, is to afflict oneself with damages while producing profit for others; and that even the most powerful peoples, masters of the whole world, must perish if they return all things to others and employ justice and equity in all their dealings.

### 20.

Secundò vovent Monachi *Paupertatem*. Cùm enim ingrediuntur Monasteria, abdicant omnia, sua bona & in usum communem suorum Ordinum transferunt. Quàm callidè autem hoc faciant, quivis maturi judicii advertere potest. Vovent enim non *Paupertatem*, sed *Otium*. Nec renunciant suis opibus, nisi curis eorum. (3): I reply: The Father ridiculously feigns that Anna had presided over them—for how could she have gone out into public?—and that the Blessed Virgin had been educated among them, who was betrothed to Joseph, *Matthew 1, verse 15*, which is by no means permitted to nuns among the Papists, and is strictly forbidden.

->17.<-

He proceeds, however, and insists thus: *Because Votive virgins have a great reward for their virginity, Revelation 14, verse 4.* I reply: Here, votive virgins or Nuns are not understood; but the pious and elect, who abstained from spiritual fornication with the great harlot and the worship of Idols, and who did not pollute themselves with the lie of heresy and idolatry, and who remain constant professors of the truth, following the lamb. And this periphrastic description of the pious fits the married no less than the celibate, since the inscription of the name of Christ upon their foreheads fits all the pious, *Revelation 3, verse 12; chapter 7, verse 3*. And it behooves all to follow Christ with the denial of self and the bearing of the cross, *Luke 14, verses 26, 27*.

->18.<-

He adds: *Christ praises Eunuchs, who castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of Heaven, Matthew 19, verse 12.* I reply: Neither is votive celibacy nor physical castration understood here, but mystical and moral, such as is also the cutting off of a foot, a hand, or the plucking out of an eye, *Matthew 5, verse 30; chapter 18, verse 8*. Hence, the pious *Job, chapter 31, verses 1, 9, 10*, protests that he had made a covenant with his eyes, so that they would not look upon a virgin. This mystical castration, however, can be understood of all the pious, even the married, who are *girded at the loins of their minds, 1 Peter 1, verse 13*, and mortify their members, *Colossians 3, verse 5*. Finally, Christ is dealing here with the gift of continence, as is evident from what follows: *he who can be capable of this thing, let him take it.*

# Master PETER HENDEL,

### GEORG Steinhagen.

You see, I believe, what I am doing, most distinguished of men. I, a mere stranger, rise to the dignity of your status. See, however, how I justify to myself the logic of this duty. You, when I was hoping for no such thing and had earned nothing, willed that I, a stranger, should be among the number of your own; and should I not honor you, no longer a stranger, but known to me through the greatest benevolence? Seneca rightly says: That favor is pleasant and will live in the mind, which comes of its own accord. How dearly, then, must you think you are held in my mind, you who have laid claim to me of your own volition through the testimony of your highest regard? When I consider this, I see what I owe; when I think how I might conveniently repay it, I find no way. Unless you accept a good intention and deem him to have satisfied his debt who confesses that he owes it. Behold, therefore, these papers as a sponsor for this debt, and I ask that you accept them with an equitable mind. Truly, I would not offend the public good by calling you to read these trifles; but another, in turn, shall not command my mind, so that I might honor anyone other than You, with whom alone it is now permitted for me to confer honor.

### GEORGIUS Steinhagen.

Vides, credo, quid agam, Virorum Amplissime. peregrini soli civis dignitatis tuae fascibus assurgo. Vide verò quàm et officii hujus ratio mihi constet. Tu nihil me tale sperantem, nihil meritum, peregrinum, tuorum numero prior esse voluisti: ego verò te, non jam alienum, sed summâ benevolentiâ mihi cognitum non observem ? Sapienter Seneca; Illud beneficium jucundum, victurumque in animo est, quod obviam venit. Quàm tu ergò eximiè charum animo te meo esse putes, qui summi studii testificatione ultro me occupasti ? Hoc cum reputo, quid debeam, video: cum, quo pacto commodus exsolvam, cogito, non invenio. Nisi bonam mentem accipis, et satisfecisse illum existimas, qui debere se fatetur. Ejus verò sponsorem tenues ecce has chartas, quas aequo animo ut admittas, rogo. Equidem in publica commoda non peccem, ut te ad has legendas ineptias vocem ; sed alius vicissim animo meo non imperet, ut quemvis alium, quam Te, quo uno mihi nunc licet, honore prosequar.

### <term>Protrepticus</term> <gloss>Exhortation</gloss> of Eobanus Hessus for servants

Hidden in servitude, to show yourself a faithful servant,
You who wish for this, read through whatever is here with you.
The first law commands the faith of a servant to be kept,
Beware of trusting words to things.
A good man abstains from the master's things, be diligent,
And do not carry your body at a tortoise's pace.
Wanton impudence has made many fall from grace,
You can be praised for learned simplicity.
Let him avoid gamblers. Let him not be a boaster. And everyone
Who flees the one who has become like an abyss, he is wise.
He will carry out commands quickly: let him not murmur against them: let there be absent
From the servant laughter and immoderate jests.
Hear much: do not speak much unless asked.
He whom you see to be dear to the master, cultivate.
Let you not seem a biting critic of anyone's infamy: but be devoid
Of envy. Flee lawsuits and discord.
Let frequent care make you teachable, lest soft
Leisure make you hard: accustom yourself to be pressed by labor.
Whoever is an adulator is not held faithful to the master,
The law also forbids drunken wine to servants.
It is not right for you to know the secret things of your master,
If you note any by chance: pretend you do not know.

### §. IX.

Furthermore, public scribes formerly obtained various names from the magistrates by whom they were either chosen or to whom they were attached, as Reinefius testifies in *Epist. XXXI to Rupert*, p. 168 (cf. Sigonius, loc. cit.). For Pontiffs, Dukes, Emperors, Consuls, Proconsuls, Aediles, Quaestors, and most other magistrates appointed their own specific scribes for themselves, who managed their business with writings and presided over the balancing of accounts, which were offered to the Republic when their magistracy was finished. Whence they were later called <term>Scribae Pontificum</term> <gloss>Scribes of the Pontiffs</gloss>, <term>Ducales</term>, <term>Imperatorii</term>, <term>Consulum</term>, <term>Proconsulum</term>, <term>Aedilium</term>, <term>Quaestorum</term>, and so forth; indeed, they were even called <term>Juris peritorum et Advocatorum</term> <gloss>Scribes of the Jurists and Advocates</gloss>. C. Barthius collected these names accurately in his *Adversaria*, book LX, which book contains a commentary on Augustine's *City of God*. However, the <term>Scriba Praetorius</term> <gloss>Praetorian Scribe</gloss> does not appear among them, perhaps because the authors of the index of inscriptions collected by Gruter denied that this type of scribe could be found? But the most accurate Reinefius, in the place cited a little earlier, testifies that he found an inscription on a Ladestan stone in Liburnia in which mention of <term>Praetoriani Scribae</term> occurs:

->C. MODIVS. SCR. PR. VERONA. ANN. XX.<-

He adds later: <term>And since there were scribes of the aediles, quaestors, and tribunes, so called either because they were chosen by these magistrates or because they attended them, why would there be none for the praetors? There were perhaps more necessary to this magistracy, and more numerous than for the others.</term>

ERMINOLD departs to inhabit the eternal seats. Therefore, hail thrice blessed, crowned with the wreath of martyrdom, hail, golden torch of the upper seat, hail again, most desired hope of the Bavarian land. Not because you are taken from us do you cease to be a help; a great part of you, your venerable body, a vessel without blemish sacred to GOD, offers remedies. For at your tomb various diseases are forced to depart; the plague, suddenly defeated, releases its foul scales and spots, and the elephantiasis <note>leprosy</note> introduced into the limbs stops the ulcers flowing with shedding pus. Now tongues that were bound, now the use of sight is restored; now suddenly those who were lame extend their steps with strengthened knees; moreover, the furies of Avernus <note>the underworld</note> are driven away, vexing the limbs of men with various torments. What? Am I silent or do I speak? The vows of no one are seen to be empty, whoever asks for help with a sound heart. But why am I, exhausted, finishing everything, carried in a small boat? Long ago Phoebus <note>the sun</note> ordered me to rest, so that I would not be overwhelmed by the burden. You, divine one, be mindful of your worshippers often, and favor the slight efforts of our labor, and favor us eternally.

The ancients also used the term "leading of a funeral" in the same sense: Juvenal, *Satire* 1: *The funeral is led, to be applauded by angry friends.* On this matter, more shortly. The Romans were also called *Quirites* <gloss>Roman citizens</gloss> from *Quirinus* (Rosinus, Book II, Chapter XVII, *Roman Antiquities*; Gaius, Book I of the *Institutes*, Title 2, § 3), and likewise *Latini* <gloss>Latins</gloss> from *Latinus*, King of Italy, father-in-law of Aeneas (Rosinus, Book I, Chapter 1, *Roman Antiquities*).

## Thus was the Definition of the Name: the Definition of the Thing follows. Thesis V.

->*A funeral is the leading forth of the deceased, with customary rites, to a place designated for the honorable burial of bodies.*<-

Having completed those things which pertain to the definition of the name, we make an approach to the definition of the thing, since it explains the nature and essence of each thing (Bertius, Book IV, *Peripatetic Logic*, Chapter II). We place here, however, an essential definition, which consists of genus and difference (Horneius, Book IV, *Dialectics*, Chapter III, number 8). The genus is "leading forth," because leading belongs properly to funerals, as Servius holds on the *Georgics*, Book IV, although it also belongs to weddings; yet they have this word in common, as they have many common rites, such as the procession, torches, the bier, wreaths, ointments, and others, which Artemidorus also touched upon (Book II, Chapter LIV; Kirchmann, Book II, Chapter I, *On the Roman Funeral*). The other words of the definition contain the difference, which together constitute a causal definition: for the efficient cause of a funeral is the deceased, who also provide the material here; the formal cause are the customary rites, which are found in Rosinus (Book V, Chapter XXXIX, *Roman Antiquities*), Kirchmann, and others. The final cause is honorable burial, which is the highest happiness (Dempster on the cited passage of Rosinus), as also above in Thesis I, although there is another cause with respect to the living, namely, that bodies foul to sight and smell should be removed (Dempster, ibid.). Where one must simultaneously note the subject, the place designated for honorable burial, which for us is the cemetery (Gerhard, on the topic of death, § 90. See our Thesis XII).

## Thus conjunctively: it follows distinctly: then in the division of funerals. Thesis VI.

### And some funerals are indictive.

For although other distinctions arise from the different age, means, dignity, and last will of those to be buried: yet, with these being diligently considered, we find that funerals were of two kinds (Kirchmann, Book 1, Chapter IV, *On the Roman Funeral*), which distinction arose from games held in honor of the deceased, which they called funeral games, as witnessed by Rosinus (Book V, Chapter XXXIX, *Roman Antiquities*). The first kind is the Indictive Funeral: so called, according to Festus, because the people were called to it by a herald (Rosinus, loc. cit.). It is said to be from *indicendo* <gloss>proclaiming</gloss>, which word the ancients used in this meaning (Kirchmann, ibid.). Suetonius in *Caesar*: *The funeral being proclaimed, the pyre was built in the Field of Mars.* Cicero, in his *Oration for his House to the Pontiffs* and *On the Consular Provinces*. The illustrious Scaliger has observed the solemn words of this proclamation long ago from Terence (*Phormio*, Act V, last scene) and Varro (Book IV, *On the Latin Language*). Moreover, Indictive Funerals were most extensive, and besides other sumptuous equipment, were also celebrated with games (Cicero, Book II, *On the Laws*; Becmann, *On Origins*, p. 706; Rosinus and Kirchmann, in the cited places; Scaliger, Book I, *Ausonian Lectures*, Chapter XXVIII), with circus riders also employed (Festus Pompeius, Book XVII; Dempster on Rosinus, *Antiquities*, Book V, Chapter XXIV). The Public funeral can be referred to here, which was sometimes the same as the Indictive, as in Apuleius (Book 11, *Metamorphoses*), sometimes only a part of it, when, for instance, a cessation of business was proclaimed, or public mourning, or expenses were made from the public treasury (Kirchmann, ibid.). This honor was granted to Syphax, King of Numidia (Valerius Maximus, Book V, Chapter 1; Suetonius in *Vitellius*, Chapter III); to Sphaerus, Augustus’s freedman and tutor (Dio, Book XLVIII); to Piso, Urban Prefect (the same, Dio, Book LXIV). Illustrious women were not without a share of this (Idem, Book XLVII; Xiphilinus in *Tiberius*). There were furthermore various kinds of Public Funerals according to the diversity of honors managed by the deceased, such as Praetorian, Consular, Censorial, and Triumphal, as Polybius indicates (Book 6, *Histories*), where, however, Lipsius noted that the triumphal was confused with the censorial under the emperors. The most worthy was the Censorial, by which princes were carried out, such as Claudius (Tacitus, Book XII). Whence Spartianus in *Aelius Verus* calls it an Imperial funeral; in *Opilius Macrinus*, a Royal one. For the Censorship was the most honored among the magistracies (Plutarch in *Cato the Elder*).

Legatis ergo in Franciam remeantibus unctio Pipini Suessione à Bonifacio peracta est, moxque Pipinus Rex dictus ab omnibus, et more gentis circumlatus clypeo, solioque impositus est. The rest of the nobles, the more prompt one was in service, the more he was elevated with wealth and honors, and having been increased by new things, they preferred the decorative and present to the old and vile. Nor did they distribute sacred and profane dignities to men of their own faction with less skill; they had distributed public offices to their friends as if it were their own right, and had cunningly transferred wealth consecrated to monasteries and churches to their clients, with the intention that everyone should desire only this: that the royal name and power should reside with him who would increase benefits, not overturn them.

<margin>Pippin prepares himself to occupy the kingdom.</margin>
Pippin, therefore, into whom alone the glory and authority of his father Martel and the administration of France had passed—after his brother Gripho was killed in the crossing of the Alps and the other, Carloman, had voluntarily embraced the monastic life—was driven by ambition to seize the kingdom. He saw himself flourishing in age, blessed with offspring, and supported by the love of all. The revenues of the kingdom, the dignities, fortresses, and soldiers were, like the nerves of a body or the gears of some automaton, turned and moved at his nod. He was, in the end, master of the kingdom in all but the name alone. Against him, Childeric was destitute not only of every aid but even of his own spirit, so unworthy of the royal title that he did not even pass for a man, and would have fallen headlong if pushed even by a finger.

For we see that in this battle some famous men, strenuous leaders, excellent centurions, and brave soldiers have been missed, because Mars picks off every strenuous man for himself and wagers on the bravest. We have received with the incredible grief of all that Augustinus Barbadicus, a man of the highest nobility, of excellent greatness of spirit, and of singular love for his Fatherland, has been taken. Having attained all the grades of honor in the city that were permitted by his age, having achieved the highest praise and glory in the discharge of those duties, having governed the *Julian* Forum <note>A political or administrative center in Venice</note> prudently and sacredly, having protected the borders of the Empire with great constancy and marvelous eloquence when there was a controversy about their governance, having served in most honorable embassies, and having managed the *Paduan* Prefecture with incredible wisdom and integrity, nothing else was lacking for his immortal praise except that, after the passage of some years, he should himself recall the memory of the Principate of the best princes, Marcus and Augustinus, his kinsmen: *Behold, death has carried him off! rationem cum in nullo alio assequatur præterquam in auro, hoc naturæ metallicæ vlimum vocatur, quia solum exemplum. Non tamen ignoro etiam generationis progressu aliquos ita sentire quasi à Mercurio per plumbum & reliqua ascenderet ad aurum, alios vero hoc statim intendi, sed vitio inducto vel cohærente, alia fieri; quarum sententiarum illam vt verba sonant, repudiamus, hanc explicamus vt dictum est. Quanquam enim postea alterum in alterum transmutetur; tamen non necesse est naturam simpliciter aurum intendere sed metallum perfectum, cuius exemplar vnicum aurum esse accidit. Hanc rem declaramus per elementa quorum certe analogiam in nobilitate philosophus aperte est confessus, dum scripsit à terra sequentia esse formaliora, & sic digniora. Iam autem no intendit vnum tantum natura, licet ad dignius semper aspiret quod est in toto illo genere: fique ignis esset vnum tantum & solum exemplum dignissimi, accideret hunc solum intendi. Transmutatio vero ex materia Symbolismo est, & neutiquam hinc pendet quod à terra natura ad ignem procedat. Ita & secundo sophismati inventum remedium est. Poteramus autem etiam aliter respondere, nempe quod aliud sit <term>τὸ καθόλου</term> in docendo aliud <term>τὸ ἐπ' ἴσης</term> in euentu naturali. Autores respicere genericam absolutionem arguit quod no vnum aurum, sed aurum & argentum perfecto subiiciant, quanquam impariter. Sed satis illustris est prior explicatio.

<margin>Natura intendit metallum perfectu, quod postea accidit aurum esse, aut proximo gradu argentum.</margin>

<margin>3. Peccatum in Dialetticam.</margin>

### CHAPTER VIII.
### How one ought to respond to the objections?

We do not deny that the definition of "perfect" applies to every metal, but not that of a "perfect metal." There are also perfect vices and monsters, just as there are corruptions, as the philosopher <note>referring to Aristotle</note> says. Therefore, if brass becomes perfectly vicious, it nonetheless has a definition, just as if it were integral in its own nature. But there is another ratio regarding an absolute metal. For let us establish that mercurial matter, the form of concrete juice, ductility or extension, constancy in fire, and purity are in the definition of a metal. If all these are absolute in every metal, let us certainly say all are perfect, and equally so, if they are nonetheless equal, with each one differing from the other by its form and specific properties, just as in an animal which is defined by sense and motion. If these things are also of equal absoluteness in all, such as in an elephant, lion, ox, etc., by reason of their genus—even though they accommodate themselves to their species—all are perfect, which is, however, not the case. For in insects, shelled animals, etc., a defect is detected; and yet a fly, an oyster, a crab, etc., can be called perfect. Thus, the first objection has been sufficiently addressed.

<margin>2.</margin>
In the second, the craftsmen by no means equate the ratio of a "perfect metal" with gold, as if they judge that to be perfect which corresponds entirely to gold. For they constitute that as perfect in the metallic genus which has those things that generically inhere in all metals, although besides these, gold has both its own form and specific differences. But since that consummation is found in no other thing except in gold, it happens that only this is the exemplar of a perfect metal, and from there the authors also convert it with "perfect metal." It should therefore have been said that that is perfect which has all the absolute qualities of a metal, just as they are in gold, not that it is exactly as gold. From this, however, it also came about that they said gold is the goal of nature, not, of course, because it intends only this, but because it is the most perfect and the best.

<margin>According to the axis of Berau, the only exemplar of a perfect metal is gold, to which he nonetheless adds silver due to its proximate grade.</margin>

### CAP. VIII.
### Quomodo ad obiecta respondendum?

OMni metallo competere perfecti definitionem non abnuimus, sed non metalli perfecti. Sunt & vitia & monstra perfecta, sicut & corruptiones, vt ait, philosophus. Itaque æs si fit vitiosum perfecte, itidem habeat definitionem similiter si in sua natura fit integrum. Alia vero ratio est ad metallum absolutum. Statuamus enim in metalli definitione inesse materiam mercurialem, succi concreti forma, ductilitatem seu extensionem, constantiam in igni, puritatem. Si hæc omnia sunt in omni metallo absoluta, dicamus sane omnia perfecta, eaque pariter, si pariter nihilominus vno quolibet ab altero differente sua forma & proprietatibus specificis, sicut in animali quod definitur sensu & motu, quæ & ipsa si sunt in omnib. paris absolutionis sicut in Elephante, leone, boue &c. ratione generis, licet se accommodent ad speciem suam: omnia sunt perfecta, quod tamen non est. Nam in insectis, testatis &c. defectus deprehenditur; & tamen potest musca ostreon, cancer &c. perfectus dici. Ita satis factum est obiecto primo.

<margin>2.</margin>
In secundo neutiquam artifices rationem metalli, perfecti æquiparant auro, quasi id perfectum iudicent quod omnino auro respondet. Nam perfectum in genere metallico id constituunt, quod ea quæ generice insunt in omnibus metallis habet absoluta, quanquam præter ea aurum habeat tam suam formam, quàm differentias specificas. Quoniam vero in alio nullo inuenitur ea consummatio, præterquam in auro, euenit vt solum hoc exemplar fit metalli perfecti, atque inde etiam autores conuertant ipsum cum metallo perfecto. Dicendum itaque sic erat id perfectum esse quod omnia metalli habet absoluta, sicut sunt in auro non quod plane est vt aurum. Hinc vero etiam factum est vt dixerint aurum esse scopum naturæ, no scilicet quod hoc tantum intendat, sed quod perfectu & optimum quam ratio.

<margin>Perfecti metallitantum vnicum exemplar iuxta axei Berau est aurum, cui tamen adiungit argentum ob proximum gradum.</margin>

<margin>Cur aurum scopus naturæ in metallis dictum.</margin>

Est timor Dei in amore, fide vera, spe solida, in rebus secundis & aduersis, ac vita denique vniuersa.

### REVS HVIVS PRECEPTI.
Qui vitam conditionemque suam, in omni fortunae habitu, alij, quam deo adscribit, in se aut suis, non deo confidit.

## PRECEPTVM .II.
### NON ADSVMES NOMEN DEI TVI

Est gloriam, honorem, benedictionem, deo referre, illum solum colere, quicquid boni habeas huic vni acceptum referre, illum inuocare, te ipsum detestari. Quicquid autem boni sit, dei nomen esse ambigit nemo.

### ILLIVS PRECEPTI REVS.
Qui in aliud, dei nomine, quam ad illius gloriam vtitur. Qui suo sibi aliquo bono blanditur, virtutem laudemque aliunde quam a deo quaerit.

## PRECEPTVM .III.
### SABBATA SANCTIFICES.
Est deo intendere, atque illius gratiam & solam appetere, ac inquirere.

### REVS.
Quicunque animo non feriatur deo, sacra luce operi, instat: diuina non curat, vel frigide curat: requiem, & a vicijs, sabbatum non colit.

## PRECEPTVM IIII
### HONORA PATREM ET MATREM.
Est deo obedire, & propter deum omni potestati, etiam ad tyrannidem vsque, parentes non salutationibus tantum, & nutu, sed ipsa operum sedulitas te iuuare, beneficijs vel maxime prosequi.

### REVS.

### Preceptum. V.
## NON OCCIDES.

Est patientia, pax, humanitas, misericordia, & (vt vno dicam) vita tota sine maleuolentiae amaritudine, in hostem etiam prompta & benefica.

### REVS.

Qui consilio, ope & opera, fratrem non adiutat, a proximo malum non prohibet.

### Preceptum. VI.
## NON ADVLTERES.

Est animorum, sermonis, & operum puritas & verecundia, victus parsimonia, caelestium rerum illibatus amor, voluptatum contemptus, solius dei dilectio.

### REVS.

Quicunque voluptatibus dissoluuntur, risu & gaudio immodestius fruuntur, aut fruentes non cohibent frenantque. Quique aliarum rerum, quam dei curam animam agere permittunt.

### Preceptum. VII.
## NON FVRABERIS.

Est omnis auaritiae fuga, laeta paupertas, liberalitas, humanitas.

### REVS.

Quicunque mutuum, & absque fenore gratis, proximo dare nolint, qui animum ad mundi aliqua bona intemperantius addunt, qui inuiti, paupertatem perferunt, elemosynam negant, aut non tempestiuiter largiuntur, qui dolo & impostura proximum circumueniunt.

### Preceptum. VIII.
## NON DICAS TESTIMONIVM FALSVM.

Est dictorum factorumque nuda & simplex veritas, lingua pacem fouens, fratris commodum quaerens, discordiam componere cupiens, detrectationem refellens, diffamiam proximi expurgans & tegens.

### REVS.

it; yet with the person from whom he heard it, and with his own judgment modestly added. *Zevecot, in the cited location.* He should diligently be careful that his household staff, without his consultation, do not insert into the letters of friends those things which strictly concern the Embassy, *Marselaer, in the cited location;* he should reserve the final re-reading of the letters to be sent for himself, and necessarily require that a copy of them be presented to him.

23. With the Embassy now thoroughly completed, and an honorable dismissal obtained, *Heider, in the cited location; Vernulaeus, in the cited location, number 5,* the Ambassador rightly makes his journey back to his own people, *Paschalius, Chapter 79,* provided that his creditors have been satisfied first. *Kirchner, Book 2, Chapter 9, at length.* It is not without disgrace or suspicion that he omits to bid that final FAREWELL to the Prince he approached, and to give thanks modestly for the services received. As often as gifts are given to the Ambassador about to depart, observing first the custom of his own Republic, he should accept them in such a way that he himself is not captured. *Marselaer, Book 2, dissertation 45.* For the Ambassadors of the Venetians, it is a capital offense to have accepted gifts; *Bodin, Book 3, On the Republic, Chapter 1;* as it was also once for the Athenians. *Xenophon, Book 7, History of Greece.* The Romans, however, just as they dismissed no Ambassadors of enemies ungifted, so too did they not fear to accept gifts from non-enemies. *Livy, Book 39.* Behold the reason! Because in the gifts of enemies there is a suspicion of corruption, and it is presumed that a good end cannot be intended by them; for their mind is composed for mere fraud and corruption. *Keckermann, in the cited dissertation, problem 14.* We also believe it matters whether something is given for the sake of honor, benevolence, or corruption and seduction, *see Gentilis, Book 3, Chapter 20; Bernegger, Miscellaneous Questions from Tacitus's Germania and Agricola 16; Siebenthal, in the cited location, question 11; Koning, in the cited location, Chapter 43, number 10; Vernulaeus, in the cited location,* or whether it is worthy of the Ambassador or the Sender, or whether it was promised before the business was finished, *Heider, in the cited location,* unless his Prince, for certain reasons, wishes for such a thing to be accepted indifferently. However, the mind of the giver will teach for whom the gifts were donated, which will easily be understood from the quality of the gift. *See Kirchner, Book 2, Chapter 9; Wesenbeck, on the Pandects, on this title; Salmuth, in the notes to Pancirolli, in the cited location; Heider, in the cited location.*

25. Thus far regarding ownership joined with possession and the causes of obligations. Now we must see what the causes of obligations are when the thing has not yet been delivered, nor have we obtained possession of it, but it is in the hands of a third party, and yet it is ours. The causes of these obligations are either singular or universal. The singular are: (1) <margin>1. Singular</margin> Gift between the living, (2) Gift in contemplation of death, (3) Legacy and trust. In a gift, if the thing has been delivered, the one to whom the thing is delivered becomes the owner <note>Digest, Title: On Gifts, l. 6, 13, 25, 33, § 1, 3; Institutes, Title: On the Division of Things, § 41; Digest, Title: On Acquiring Ownership of Things, l. 9, § 3</note>. Therefore, if the thing has not yet been delivered, the gift has been made either by stipulation <note>Digest, Title: On Gifts, l. 2, § 3, 4; l. 20, § 1; Code, l. 9, 22, 35, § 5</note>, or by verbal promise <note>Code, Title: On Gifts, l. 35</note>; and for this, a condictitious action is competent <note>Code, Title: On Gifts, l. 35; Novella 162, c. 2</note>, which is a useful action *in rem* <gloss>concerning a thing</gloss> <note>Code, Title: On Gifts which are under a condition, l. 3</note>. *XXIII. Excommunicatos etiam Hereticos hoc jus mittendi Legatos habere nullum est dubium. Excommunicatio enim ad disciplinam Ecclesiasticam pertinet, Legatio autem ad res civiles et seculares. Itemque missio, quae jure gentium est, spectat et considerat homines ex gentium jure, quà homines tantùm nobiscum sunt, non ex jure et more ullius regionis aut religionis. Et pacis jura Religionis diversitate non tolluntur; multò minus Legationis mutua commercia fidei contrarietate abolentur: dicit Kirchnerus libro 1. capitulo 3. cujus verba huc apponere lubuit.*

*XXIV. Quamvis etiam sint, qui liberis Franciae, Sueviae et ad tractatum Rhenanum habitantibus Nobilibus et Hanseaticis civitatibus jus Legationum ascribant, tamen, cum status Imperii non sint, in matriculâ Imperii non reperiantur, nec ad comitia vocentur, eos illud jus habere negamus cum Kirchnero libro 1. capitulo 3. numero 56. et Heiden de Legationibus. In Hanseatica enim societate contentae liberae civitates jus suum caeteris et exteris etiam quibusdam civitatibus communicare et affricare nequeunt.*

*XXV. Reginis etiam jus Legatos mittendi denegamus, si sint maritatae et penes maritum imperium sit: tùm enim nuncios tantùm mittunt, non Legatos, cum secundum legem foemina 2. Ad exteros autem mittere possunt.

XXVIII. Hi autem qui extrema necessitate coacti vitam, existimationem, uxores, liberos, facultates, Patriae libertatem et Religionis exercitium contra Principem Tyrannum propugnant, sicque deficiunt, jure a rebellione excusantur, et hoc jus Legationis habent.

XXIX. Et cum in delectu Legatorum maxima ratio sit posita, mittens, foemineo sexu ab hoc excluso, sibi de tali Legato prospiciat, qui principaliter animi et ingenii dotibus sit instructissimus; secundario etiam bonis corporis et fortunae polleat.

XXX. Bona enim animi potissimum requirimus propter negotii gravitatem, ut Legatus exquisitissimam omnium rerum habeat scientiam, acutissimum judicium et ingenii dexteritatem: Et summatim omnibus virtutibus, sit conspicuus. Verum cum nemo hominum ita omnibus numeris absolutus sit atque perfectus, talem ex multis Princeps seligat, qui doctrina, fidelitate, Taciturnitate et diligentia caeteris praestet. XX. No one denies that the right of embassy pertains to the free cities of the empire: for they are feudal cities of the Empire, acknowledging only the Caesar as superior, and thence they are called "Free and Imperial Cities, which are subject to no one but the Emperor and the Empire" <note>original: "Freye vnd Reichs-Städte/ so niemand/ als dem Käyser vnd Reiche vnterworffen"</note>: And they are also inserted in the matricula of the Empire, Gail, *Observation 21, number 2*. They bear the same inconveniences as Electors and Princes, in the Recess of the Empire published at Augsburg in the year 1548, § "When also" <note>original: "Wann auch"</note>, Gail, *said observation 21, number 9*. When diets are convened by the Emperor, they have the right of suffrage in them, *Recess of the Empire, Public Audience published in the year 1548, § When also, Gail, said place, number 9*; indeed, they have the first instance in the Imperial Chamber, Gail, *1, observation 17*. And thus, since in this part they enjoy the same privileges and rights as Princes, Gail concludes that one must judge of those cities no differently than of the Prince himself, *2, observation 57, number 3*.

XXI. However, this distinction between the embassies of Princes and other estates of the Empire must be well attended to; that if they send Legates within the limits of the Empire, and indeed to the Emperor or public diets, they are, speaking properly, called not Legates but deputies: yet with the rights and privileges of Legates retained. For the Lord Besold says, Legates are sent to a peer; Deputies to a superior; Commissaries to an inferior. But when they are sent to other Princes of the Empire or to foreign Kings or Republics, they retain both the name and the privileges of Legates.

XXII. However, this caution must be applied, that they be sent away to foreigners in such business as concerns only their own territory. If, however, they were to send Legates to foreigners for causes of the Empire under their own auspices, without the Emperor's knowledge and consent, they would commit the crime of high treason <note>original: "crimen perduellionis"</note>, and would fall into a sin against the Caesarean Majesty, Vayer 6. 7.

XXI. Hoc tamen discrimen Legationum Principum et caterorum Imperii statuum probè attendendum est; quòd si intra Imperii limites et quidem ad Imperatorem, vel Comitia publica Legatos mittant, eos propriè loquendo non Legatos sed deputatos dici: retentis tamen juribus et privilegiis Legatorum. Legati enim, inquit, Dominus Besold. mittuntur ad parem; Deputati ad superiorem; Commissarii ad inferiorem. Cum verò ad alios Principes Imperii vel ad exteros Reges vel Respublicas mittantur, et nomen et privilegia retinent Legatorum.

XXII. Haec autem cautela adhibenda, ut in tali negotio ad exteros ablegentur, quod territorium suum tantum concernit. Si verò propter Imperii causas suis auspiciis inscio et non consentiente Imperatore ad exteros Legatos mitterent, crimen perduellionis committerent, et in Caesaream Maiestatem piaculum inciderent Vayer 6. 7.

When Judas saw this, he brings back thirty talents to the leaders, he gives such a complaint with his voice: "Woe to me now, a wretch, betraying the pure one by a crime." He went away, he weaves bonds for his neck; he ended his life while he hangs from a high tree, his bowels were hanging out with his belly burst open. The impious race of the Jews were setting Jesus before the chair of Pilate, hurting him with a false crime; they say with a lying throat: "This man is a seditionist, this man shatters peace, he boldly forces men into arms, he forbids paying tribute to the Caesarean kingdom, and he burns with a desire for the kingdom." Pilate addresses Jesus, and begins with such things: "Are you guilty of the deed that spreading rumor reports? Are you the King of the Jewish people? Born from the lineage of famous Kings? EUCHARIUS. Now tell me briefly what should be decided about the Weasel, and how it ought to be named in the common tongue. 

ANONYMOUS. The name of "weasel" is taken in a narrower sense by some writers, and in a broader sense by others. For among the ancients, there are two kinds of weasels: one domestic and common, which is called <term>galē</term> <gloss>weasel</gloss> in Greek; the other kind is wild, which is called <term>iktis</term> <gloss>marten</gloss> in Greek. But the term "weasel" began to be used by later authors not only for the *Gale* and the *Ictis*, but also for the cat, and for the fish that they call the Lamprey, and for the bird that is called <term>weicker</term> <gloss>weaver/finch</gloss> in German. 

EUCHARIUS. Now I desire to know from you how the Latins name Ermines or Hermellas, Wisellas, Mardras, Furos, Iltos, and Frettas. For we use these names commonly now. 

ANONYMOUS. I would prefer that you know this from another. For I see that men, even learned ones, have sweated much over this matter.

## On the Chapel of Saint Nicholas for the youth of Freising.

If you, little boy, are not drawn to an age similar to your own,
And do not wish to be an emulator of the divine Nicholas;
Do not refuse to approach the nearby thresholds of Nicholas,
Let him at least attract you with his golden spheres.
You ask, I see no gifts of gold there; that is true;
For the Saint sees no one who seeks those things.

## Fountain of Saint Corbinian in Weyhenstephan.

Here where the slopes of the very high mount incline,
And the fountain flows of its own accord with scarcely any murmur,
By the impulse of his staff and prayers sent to the stars,
Corbinian produced flowing Waters.
This wave does not only remove thirst from those who thirst,
But, when drawn, it also often provides help to the sick.
Stop, Traveler, and drink this wave most eagerly,
Perhaps it also has within it that which may heal you.

## On the Chapel of Saint Corbinian built above the fountain.

The Chapel which was built for you at the base of the Mount,

It is present, not a <term>Simulacrum</term> made of <term>Olive</term> wood (by which blind superstition shadowed the gentleness of its false gods), but an immense sea of <term>Mercy</term>, to be boarded by the basin of <term>Baptism</term> and the vehicle of prayers. That celebrated <term>Bōmos Elaion</term> <gloss>Altar of Oil</gloss> is that which obtains the help not of fictitious deities, but of the omnipotent Father. What equally satiates the mind of the thinker? What restores the fatigued senses so much? It strengthens virtues, invigorates good and honest morals, and nourishes chaste affections. Every dish of the Soul is arid unless this heavenly OIL is added; it is insipid if it is not seasoned with this salt. <margin>Nicephorus, Book I, Eccl. Hist., ch. 17. Suidas, Orosius, Book VI.
