That venerable LIGHT, the DAY desired and loved for so many centuries, that splendid BIRTHDAY, was believed by Antiquity to have become known to the Roman Emperor <term>Octavian</term> through a notable portent more easily than it was demonstrated. Namely, that in memory of victorious virtue, at the request of the Senate and People of <term>Rome</term>, he sought an intermission of three days to perform honors befitting a divinity, and meanwhile learned from the prophetic monuments of Antiquity of the majesty of his successor. Yet suddenly, at high noon, a golden CIRCLE was found around the Sun, and in its center a beautiful VIRGIN with a BOY, together with some golden letters expressing THE ALTAR OF THE SON OF THE LIVING GOD. Then the seer, showing the prodigy, announced that the boy born that same day was greater than <term>Augustus</term>. <term>Caesar</term>, moved by the insolent portent, consecrated an ALTAR TO THE FIRST-BORN OF GOD in the very <term>Capitol</term>. and the following because of the express command of the Apostle to Romans 13:1, 2 and the following, 1 Peter 2:18, 19, and because such subjects are forbidden by the law of the sword (Matthew 26:52). And also, by Civil Law, the use of arms is prohibited to private individuals (*Law 1, Code, On the use of arms; Novella 17, chapter the final; chapter 1, § "Who is a rustic," On keeping the peace, in Feudal uses*). Therefore, what is not allowed to these directly will also not be allowed to others indirectly under the pretext of a Cliental treaty. But if the subjects are not merely private individuals, but the magistrate sustains a person subordinated to a superior, and has been assumed into a share of the cares: then, just as they themselves [are entitled], they are rightly [protected] against unjust force by a Magistrate exceeding his bounds: 1. Because of the office of Magistrate which they hold. 2. Because of the prescription of natural law. 3. Because of the manner of mutual obligation. 4. Because of the Theological axiom that the Gospel does not abolish politics. 5. Because of the testimonies of approved Examples. 6. Because of the consequence of the absurd: to defend themselves (Gerhard, aforementioned place, n. 485; Reinking, aforementioned law, book 1, class 1, c. 5, n. 44 and following). So also, those who are in their clientage can be summoned for their defense. However, it is more humane that the protector is not obligated to defense against a parent and his own blood (*Law: "The laws of blood," Digest, On the Rule of Law; § the last, Institutes, On the succession of agnates and guardians; Law: "Of humanity," 23, Code, On excuses from guardianship*).

### XXIV.

If several persons received into protection by the same party are attacked by outsiders at the same time, the cause of those who are older in protection is stronger (*argument from Law 2, Law: "If the estate," 4, Code, Who is stronger in pledge; Law: "As often as," 98, Digest, On the Rule of Law; argument from Law 9, §4, Digest, On the Publician Action; chapter "He who," extra, On Prebends, in the Sext; chapter "He who is prior," 54, On the Rule of Law, in the Sext*). But if the strength suffices, both must be helped (*argument from Law 49, On optimal legacies*). If one fosters a better cause than the other, equity dictates that the more just cause must be assisted. If they are fighting among themselves, I believe neither should be assisted (from *chapter "Finally," 14, q. 5*).

### XXV.

Moreover, the client is bound by law to reimburse the protector for the expenses made for the defense (*Law: "The works," 21, Digest, On the works of freedmen; argument from Law 33, in the end, On the Administration of Guardians*). And this is true even if the protector has succumbed and been defeated.

Nec enim *Abrahamus*, fidelissimus DEI servus, tétricas *Aegyptiorum* naenias tantâ imbiberat cupiditate, ut ab iisdem abduci planè non potuerit, nisi DEus hujus ceremoniae indultu ipsi velificaretur, id quod de Hebraeis seqvioris aevi asserunt *Marshamus & Spencerus.* Verum cum solius DEI voluntatem & nutum diligentissimè semper sit secutus, nonnisi divino mandato induci potuit, ut circumcisionem, non ex corrupto cultus *Aegyptiaci* fonte, sed divinae sapientiae penu profluentem, in se susciperet. Conf. & hic contra *Marshamum Sam. Basnage in Exerc. Historico-Critic. p. 119.* Regerit è contrario *Marshamus p. 75.* ex hoc loco non probari, *Abrahamum* primum hominum fuisse circumcisum, proinde *Origenem* falsum dixisse existimat, qui *Celso* ita respondit. §. 24. Philosophers who set out to explain the nature of the intellect consider two things primarily in it: namely, actions and habit. The habit of the intellect, which others call intellectual memory, is nothing other, according to the mind of the Philosopher (<term>Controv. 8, Book 3, On the Soul</term>), than a certain facility born from various acts, by which the intellect perceives things. Most make its actions threefold, according to the threefold mode in which the intellect is occupied about its object. For it either represents the object simply, or it brings forth a judgment about the object represented to it, or it infers one thing from the judged object. The first action they call simple operation, the second judgment, the third discourse. Others, having excluded judgment and discourse from the intellect and left it with only simple apprehension, wish to say that judging or affirming are acts of the will—to which I would assent when I notice that, while I judge, I judge freely, so that finding freedom in my judgment, I would easily conclude that the will must also be in it, since freedom is so essential to the will that it cannot be taken from the will—to these, I say, I would assent, were I not to experience at every moment that the powers I have of judging participate in the intellect. For I cannot deny that I am conscious of those actions while they are being performed, or that I lack knowledge of the object that I am dividing, etc.; for it would be madness to judge what I do not know.

§. 25. Moved by these reasons, I posit this assertion: judgment and discourse participate in the nature of both faculties, namely, intellect and will, and therefore there is a third faculty in me arising from the two others taken jointly, such as the faculty I have of opening and communicating my concepts to others, in which is always found the perception of the mind and the will to reveal to another what we conceive.

§. 26. Simple apprehension is the first operation or thought of the mind, by which we know something without affirmation or negation, or the thought by which we contemplate an image, notion, concept, and idea, and set it before ourselves.

§. 24. Intellectus naturam explicaturi Philosophi, duo imprimis in ipso actiones scilicet et habitum considerant. Intellectus habitus, quem alii memoriam intellectualem vocant, nihil aliud est secundum mentem Philosophi *Controv. 8. lib. 3. de anima*, præter facilitatem quandam ex variis actibus ortam, quâ intellectus res percipit. Triplices verò ejus actiones plerique faciunt pro triplici modo quo intellectus circa suum objectum versatur. Vel enim objectum simpliciter repræsentat, vel judicium de objecto sibi repræsentato profert, vel aliud ex objecto judicato infert. Primam actionem, simplicem operationem, secundam judicium, tertiam discursum vocant. Alii seclusis ab intellectu, judicio et discursu, eique solâ relictâ simplici apprehensione, judicare seu affirmare volunt esse actus voluntatis, quibus assentirer, cùm animadvertam, me, dum judico, liberè judicare, ita ut libertatem in meo judicio reperiens, voluntatem ei etiam inesse debere facilè concludam, quandoquidem libertas adeò sit voluntati essentialis, ut à voluntate tolli non possit, his inquam, assentirer, ni singulis momentis potentias quas habeo judicandi de intellectu participare, experirer. Non possum namque negare me actionum illarum, dum peraguntur, conscium esse, aut objecti quod divido et cetera cognitionem non habere; dementia quippe esset id judicare quod nescirem.

Motus his rationibus hanc pono assertionem, judicium et discursum utriusque facultatis intellectus scilicet et voluntatis naturam participare, adeoqué tertiam dari in me facultatem ex duabus aliis conjunctim sumptis exsurgentem, qualis est facultas quam habeo meos conceptus aliis aperiendi et communicandi, in qua semper reperitur mentis perceptio et voluntas alteri, quod concipimus, detegendi.

§. 26. Est autem simplex apprehensio, prima mentis operatio seu cogitatio, quâ sine affirmatione aut negatione aliquid cognoscimus, sive cogitatio quâ imaginem, notionem,

§. 29. Universaliter non valere dixi: Non dubium enim quin à sensibus etiam aliquas species intellectus hauriat. Verissimum namque quod annotat Dominus la Forge omnes nostras ideas à quatuor differentibus causis excitari, actione scilicet sensuum, vestigiis memoriæ, actione spirituum animalium à corde ad cerebrum ascendentium, et denique ab ipsa mente se ad cogitandum determinante. A sensibus hoc modo excitari communis est Philosophorum opinio. Objectum nempe sensuum externorum veluti fores primò propellit. per hos introductum ingerit sese in sensum internum seu materialem phantasiam; hâc deinde crassiori objecti specie excitatus intellectus illapsum in sensum internum objectum, protinus apprehendit, ejusque expressionem in animo effingit.

§. 30. Sensuum autem, quos in me deprehendo, naturam si inspiciam, negare non possum, eos quoque aliam esse hujus quam habeo percipiendi potentiæ speciem; Nam quamvis sentire aut imaginari non possim sine corpore, actio tamen illa mentis, quâ sensationis aut imaginationis conscius sum, est planè spiritualis et incorporea. Definiuntur itaque perceptiones, quibus motus à corpore aliquo objecto fibrillis nervorum impressus et in cerebrum delatus, ac sensorio communi mediantibus spiritibus animalibus, ventriculis cerebri contentis, communicatus, à mente in sensorio communi percipitur; ita ut rectè tres hi in sentiendo gradus ponantur: motus organi, mentis cogitatio, et voluntatis determinatio. *Vide Dominum la Chambre in Characteribus passionum de natura doloris. pagina 215. et sequentes* ubi sensationem, cognitionem seu perceptionem esse evincit.

§. 31. Dividuntur vulgò in externos et internos. Quatenus externo perficitur instrumento, externus, quatenus interno, internus appellatur. Quam foedum ac triste malum sit benignissimae lucis privatio, et tenebrarum contra horribilium infusio, experimento suo probant tristissimo Aegyptii, quorum terram ad frangendum Pharaonis animum, ut ex durissima servitute Populum Israëliticum dimitteret, post octo, sed frustra immissas plagas gravissimas, tanta etiam tenebrarum caligine divina Nemesis inundavit, ut iis horribilius quicquam vix mente concipi, nedum verbis exprimi posse videatur. Historiam tenebrarum istarum exponit divinae Majestatis Secretarius Moses, Exodus X, 21, 22, 23. et Liber Sapientiae, qui Philonis esse creditur, capitulo XVII. Apud utrumque autem eas descriptas reperimus, partim ut horribiles, partim ut mirabiles. Horribiles fuisse arguit (1) earum palpatio, de qua Moses loco citato versu 21. ויהי חשך על־ארץ מצרים וימש חשך id est (juxta translationem Hieronymi) *Et sint tenebrae super terram Aegypti, tam densae, ut palpari queant.* Etsi enim quidam Interpretes istud verbum ימש forment a radice מוש quod significat, *recessit, discessit, amovit*, ut sensus esset, tam densas fuisse tenebras, ut noctis tenebras auferrent: Id autem est, ut prorsus obruerent obscuritatem noctis, et noctis tenebrae prae illis nihil esse viderentur, non secus, ac majus lumen aufert minus, id est obscurat, ut non videatur; Cui interpretationi Paraphrasis favet Chaldaica, quae istud ימש reddidit per ויעדי a Radice עדי id est *recessit*, ut sint tenebrae בתר דיעדי ליליא id est etiam postquam recesserit obscuritas noctis: Rectius tamen formatur a radice משש *palpavit, contrectavit*, ut sit Futurum in Niphal, et commode reddi possit: וימש חשך et palpabitur obtenebratio. Sic enim intellexerunt etiam Septuaginta Interpretes reddentes illud per σκότος ψηλαφητὸν (â verbo ψηλαφάω, *contrecto, palpo*) id est tenebras palpabiles, quae tactu percipi possint. Quomodo vero palpabiles? Nam palpari non potest, nisi corpus, tenebrae autem non modo corpus non sunt, sed nec ens ullum positivum, quemadmodum Philosophi loquuntur. Adde quod sensus tenebrarum, sicut etiam lucis, est visus: Sensus vero palpandi est tactus, et praecipuè qui in manibus est: Respondent nonnulli cum Jansenio et Lorino in capitulo XVII. Sapientiae istas tenebras dici palpabiles non ratione sui, sed ratione Aegyptiorum, qui oculis capti fuerint, ne videre possent, ut cogerentur more caecorum palpando parietes ingredi. Sed hoc fingitur praeter Scripturam, quae non dicit, Aegyptios fuisse percussos caecitate, sicut dictum est de Sodomitis Genesis XIX, 11. et de militibus Regis Syriae II. Regum VI, 18. Sed ait: Fuisse tenebras factas super universa terrâ Aegypti, quae palparentur. Palpatio vero excoecationi minùs congruit. Confugiunt alii cum Glossa ordinaria, quae Ambrosium Laudunensem habet autorem, ad Hyperbolen, dictas fuisse palpabiles ad declarandam obscuritatis magnitudinem. Sed enim cum per se repugnet tenebris, quae sunt mera privatio luminis, esse palpabiles: quantumvis excrescat ratio tenebrarum et privatio luminis, semper repugnabit tenebris, esse ipsas palpabiles: Siquidem illae pertinent ad sensum visus, hoc autem ad sensum tactus. Verior itaque eorum videtur sententia, (quam non Benedictus Pererius modò Disputatione 2. Quaestione 2. in Exodus, verùm etiam ex Nostratibus Dominus Försterus concione 32. super Exodus pagina 198. Dominus Rungius in Exodus pagina 356. et Dominus Dietericus in concione 1. super capitulo XVII. Libri Sapientiae amplectuntur) per tenebras significari hoc loco non ipsas per se, quatenus significant privationem luminis, sed ipsummet aërem tenebrosum, qui crassissimorum vaporum admixtione ita densus et confertus erat, ut manu palparetur. Si enim tenebrae per se et propriè tales intelligendae essent, quae luminis inferunt privationem, referendum id esset vel ad Eclipsin Solis, vel ad radiorum Solis subtractionem. Atqui neutrum est probabile. Non prius: Nam (1) eclipsis Solis in novilunio fit per diametralem corporis lunaris interpositionem inter Solem et terram: Atqui tenebrae istae triduo ante novilunium mensis primi contigerunt. (2) obscuratio totius Solis in eclipsi naturali ne unam quidem horam durare potest: Aegyptiae vero tenebrae totum triduum durârunt. Non posterius.

Nam posita radiorum Solarium subtractione, sequeretur (a) et reliqua sidera splendorem suum amisisse. Quod tamen factum non est. Sic enim legitur Sap. XVII, 5. οὔτε ἄστρων ἐκλαμπροὶ φλόγες καταιγάζειν ὑπέμενον τὴν στυγνὴν ἐκείνην νύκτα, i. e. neque stellarum nitidae flammae illuminare sustinebant tristem illam noctem. (β) Obscuritatem istam fuisse generalem: Atqui Scriptura eam propriam dicit Aegyptiorum Exod. X, 21. 22. Sap. XVII, 20. Ubi leguntur ista: μόνοις δὲ ἐκείνοις ἐπετέτατο βαρεῖα νύξ, i. e. Solis autem illis superposita erat gravis nox. Horribiles fuisse tenebras arguit (2.) earum duratio. Fuerunt enim tenebrae non trium horarum, quales tempore Passionis Christi universam terram occuparunt, durantes a meridie horis integris tribus, Matth. XXVII, 45. Marc. XV, 33. Luc. XXIII, 44. neque bidui, cujusmodi tenebras in Sicilia quondam evenisse, ob Ætnæorum ignium eruptionem solito majorem, narrat his verbis Cicero lib. 2. de natura Deorum: Nos, inquit, tenebras cogitemus tantas, quanta quondam, eruptione Ætnæorum ignium finitimas Regiones obscuravisse dicuntur, ut per biduum, nemo hominem homo agnosceret: cum autem tertia die Sol luxisset, tum ut revixisse sibi viderentur: Sed triduanae fuerunt tenebrae, ab eo tempore, quo quisque vel agriculturae, vel pecuariae vel aliis negotiis occupatus erat, tribus integris diebus durantes sine ullo interstitio alicujus luminis vel naturalis vel artificialis, quia ignis etiam, quo utimur quotidie, vel aere turbato extinguebatur, vel a crassissimis tenebris vincebatur: Quod in lib. Sap. XVII, 5. his verbis exprimitur: Καὶ πυρὸς μὲν οὐδεμία βία κατίσχυεν φωτίζειν, i. e. Et ignis quidem nulla vis poterat lucere. Horribiles fuisse tenebras arguit etiam (3) Adjuncta iis hominum vexatio. Permiserat enim Dominus diabolo, qui ab Apostolo Ephes. VI, 12. κοσμοκράτωρ τοῦ σκότους τοῦ αἰῶνος τούτου dicitur, ut diris larvis et illusionibus homines conterrèrent, et tantum non exanimarent. Quem terrorem liber Sapientiae c. v. 3. 4. 6. et 15. his verbis describit: λανθάνοντες γὰρ νομίζοντες ἐπικρυφαίοις ἁμαρτήμασιν, ἀφεγγεῖ λήθης παρακαλύμματι ἐσκορπίσθησαν, θαμβούμενοι δεινῶς καὶ ἰνδάλμασιν ἐκταρασσόμενοι. οὐδὲ γὰρ ὁ κατέχων αὐτοὺς μυχὸς ἀφόβους διεφύλασσεν. ἦχοι γὰρ καταράσσοντες αὐτοὺς περιεκόπουν, καὶ φάσματα ἀμειδήτοις κατηφῆ προσώποις ἐνεφανίζετο. διεφαίνετο δὲ αὐτοῖς μόνον αὐτομάτη πυρὰ φόβου πλήρης, ἐκδειματούμενοι δὲ τῆς μὴ θεωρουμένης ἐκείνης ὄψεως, ἡγοῦντο χείρω τὰ βλεπόμενα. τὰ μὲν τέρασιν ἠλαύνοντο Φαντασμάτων, τὰ δὲ τῆς ψυχῆς παρελύοντο προδοσίᾳ, αἰφνίδιος γὰρ αὐτοῖς καὶ ἀπροσδόκητος φόβος ἐπῆλθεν. i. e. Latere enim putantes occultis peccatis, tenebroso oblivionis velamento dispersi sunt paventes horrende et simulacris perturbati. Neque enim quae continebat illos spelunca intrepidos custodiebat: Sonitus autem perturbantes eos circumstrepebant, et visiones tristibus moesta vultibus apparebant. Apparebat autem illis solum spontanea pyra timore plena; territi autem a non visa illa visione, aestimabant deteriora quae videbantur. Aliquando quidem monstris agitabantur phantasmatum, aliquando anima dissolvebantur traditione: Subitaneus enim illis et insperatus timor supervenit. Augebant terrorem istum angor conscientiae et facinorum recordatio, de qua iterum lib. Sap. c. v. 19. εἴτε πνεῦμα συρίζον, ἢ περὶ ἀμφιλαφεῖς κλάδους ὀρνέων ἦχος εὐμελὴς, ἢ ῥυθμὸς ὑδάτων πορευομένων βίᾳ, ἢ κτύπος ἀπηνὴς καταρριπτομένων πετρῶν, ἢ σκιρτώντων ζώων δρόμος ἀθεώρητος, ἢ ὠρυομένων ἀπηνεστάτων θηρίων φωνὴ, ἢ ἀντανακλωμένη ἐκ κοιλότητος ὀρέων ἠχὼ, παρέλυεν αὐτοὺς ἐκφοβοῦντα, i. e. Sive Spiritus sibilans, aut circum densos ramos avium sonitus suavis, aut concentus aquae euntis vi, aut sonus validus precipitatarum petrarum, aut lascivientium animalium cursus invisus, aut ululantium ferarum bestiarum vox, aut repercussa de concavitate montium echo, dissolvebant illos deterrentia. Δειλὸν γὰρ ἰδίως πονηρία μάρτυρι καταδικαζομένη· ἀεὶ δὲ προσείληφε τὰ χαλεπὰ συνεχομένη τῇ συνειδήσει, i. e. Timida res enim proprio malitiae teste condemnata. Semper autem praeoccupavit saeva contenta (perturbata) conscientia, ibidem v. 11. Atque hinc dubio procul factum, ut nemo etiam moveret se de loco, in quo erat, Exod. X, 21, quod illis accidit, non quod crassities et densitas aeris impedierit motum progressivum, uti Paulus Burgensis arbitratur, quasi in eodem loco penitus fuerint immobiles, tanquam saxa vel arbores, ut nec verba proferre nec gemitus aut ejulatus edere aut exspirare, nec pedes aut manus movere possent: Nam in lib. Sap. cap. XVIII, 1. scriptum est, fuisse tunc exauditas voces Ægyptiorum ab Hebraeis; sed quia vel terrificis admodum visis pavefacti metuebant, si se moverent, ne quam primum.

Inde igitur quis non intelligat, tenebras istas Ægyptiacas fuisse maximè omnium horribiles? Ast fuerunt etiam tenebræ *mirabiles*. Mira enim sunt omnia, sive hujus plagæ principium, sive instrumentum, sive Israëlitis in mediis tenebris concessi luminis beneficium consideres. *Principium* earum <margin>22.</margin> fuit non Magicum, sicut Marcus Paulus Venetus de Regionibus Oriental. lib. 1. cap. 22. de civitate Camandu & Regione Reobarle memoriæ prodidit, esse ibi multos prædones, *qui arte diabolicâ id efficiant, ut aër interdiu per magnum temporis spatium adeò obscuretur, ut à nemine videri & caveri possint, prorogentque hujusmodi caliginem interdum quinque, & aliquando septem diebus:* Sed divinissimum. Quemadmodum enim reliquas; Ita & hanc plagam Dominus per fidelem servum suum Mosen Ægyptiis immisit Exod. X, 21. Deus enim est qui ponit tenebras, & est nox, Ps. CIV, 20. qui induit cælos tenebris & quasi saccum ponit operimentum eorum, Esa. L, 4. *Instrumentum* quo Dominus ad infligendam istam plagam uti voluit, fuit partim *vilissimum*, nempe manus & in manu gestatus baculus Moyfis, quem ille in cælum extendere jussus est, Exod. l. c. v. 21. partim *singularissimum*, videlicet non eclipsis aliqua solaris extraordinaria, nec oculorum Ægyptiorum occæcatio, sed densissima nebula & vapor crassissimus, quo aër oppletus fuit, quem nervosè M. Hartmann. Schacher conc. IX. de plagis Ægyptiac: his verbis describit: *Unser HERR GOTT hat einen schrecklichen Dampff / Dunst und Nebel darzu gebraucht / welchen Er aus dem Meer / Wasser und Erdreich sich jähling und geschwinde hat aufziehen lassen / und damit die Lufft in Egyptenland / gantz wider die Natur / dermassen erfüllet / daß weder Sonne noch Mond / noch einige Sterne mit ihren Glantz und Schein haben hindurch dringen / und den elenden Menschen leuchten können.* Quid verò dicam de miro *luminis beneficio*, quod Hebræi, Ægyptiis tantâ offusis & oppressis caligine, clarissima cæli luce usi fuerint? Sic enim Moses l. c. v. <margin>23.</margin> 23. *Ubicunque autem habitabant filii Israël, lux erat;* Et liber Sap. c. 17, 20. ὅλος γὰρ ὁ κόσμος λαμπρῷ κατελάμπετο Φωτί, καὶ ἀνεμποδίστοις συνείχετο ἔργοις i. e. *Totus enim mundus nitido illuminabatur lumine, & inpeditis continebatur operibus.* Et cap. 18. v. 1. τοῖς δὲ ὁσίοις σου μέγιστον ἦν φῶς, i. e. *At sanctis tuis maxima erat lux.* Ecce igitur lucem non post tenebras, sicut in primordio rerum omnium contigit Gen. 1, 2. 3. 4. sed in tenebris. Radios solares, luminis effectores, Deus ad Hebræos porrigebat ita, ut non modò in terra Gosen, regiæ Pharaonis sedi, urbi Zonan, quam alii Tanin vocant, vicinissimâ, verùm etiam *in sedibus suis*, i. e. (annotante Cornel. à Lap. ad l. c. Exod.) non tantùm in vicis, plateis vel domibus vicinis, sed in eadem domo, imò in suis cubiculis, ubi servire cogebantur Ægyptiis, fuo quisque perfungi labore posset. Meritò hîc quæras cum Apostolo 2. Cor. 6, 14. *quæ communio luci cum tenebris?* Sed ita placuit Divinæ Sapientiæ, ad declarandum, tantummodò populum Israëlis, i. e. eos solùm, qui maneant in vera Ecclesia Catholica, veritatis & gratiæ lucem adspicere, cæteris gentibus, densissimâ vitiorum errorumque caligine oppressis. Num & qua ratione tenebræ istæ, quibus olim *Freiberga Nostra* & in Paganismo & in Papismo involuta fuit, cum Ægyptiis comparari possint, per chartæ hujus angustiam evolvere non licet. Illa verò in hunc usque diem meritiffimò jure gratulatur sibi, gratias agens Patri Cælesti, qui idoneos incolas ejus fecit ad participandam sortem sanctorum in luce; qui liberavit eos à potestate tenebrarum ac transtulit in regnum Filii sui dilecti, Coloss. 1, 12. <margin>12. 13.</margin> 13. 14. Affections follow causes. Order requires it thus. All bodies have quantity, and therefore so do the CHRIST-APPLES. Their size is best revealed by inspection. At one moment they are equal to chickpeas, at another to peas. They agree in appearance with dried wild pears. Even the stalks correspond in quantity to the stems of pears.

15. When or in what place CHRIST-APPLES are produced became known from the above. This occurs according to the Old Style at the 12th hour, on December 24th. This place is the German town of Altenstadt <note>original: "Altenstadium"</note>. A village, namely, situated eight and two-fifths <term>stadia</term> <gloss>units of distance, approximately one mile</gloss> towards the west from Bayreuth. More could indeed be reported about this, but I will not reheat the cabbage <note>A classical idiom meaning to repeat something tedious.</note>. 16. Do you desire, without a doubt, witnesses of these CHRIST-APPLES? Behold, there are very many. The Most Serene Prince and Lord himself, LORD ERDMANN AUGUSTUS, of blessed memory, the father of our Most Serene [Prince], honored this apple with his own Presence because of these fruits, and plucked such from it: those who were following the Most Serene Prince at that time are still in part alive. They show those apples accepted on that day even today. All of Altenstadt and many of our citizens also testify to these. Whom else do you want?

17. You have, therefore, READER, these our CHRIST-APPLES. And these were the things that had to be proposed at this time. Read and re-read the *Histories of Plants*; read Pliny and Theophrastus; yet you will find no such apples. The books of ARISTOTLE on plants would certainly be silent about such things, if they were still extant. But the injury of time denies them to us. ### LXII.

Quod si uero cum eiusmodi certamen susceptum sit, qui praeter diuinam Scripturam, sanctorum Patrum quoque, et uniuersalis Ecclesiae autoritatem non recuset, nullum extat, quod eadem ratione probari non ualeat.

### LXIII.

Ceterum Theologiae munus, non id solum est, quod modo exposuimus, nempe principia sua contra negantes, aut impugnantes defendere, aliasque et alias conclusiones, quae ad rem Christianam tuendam et illustrandam faciant, rationis ui inde colligere: uerum etiam internis externisque scientiae huius praesidiis, et adminiculis adhibitis, ualide utrumque communire.

### LXIIII.

Interna et propria Theologiae praesidia eas rationes appellamus, quae petuntur ex Scriptura Canonica: ex fida Christi et Apostolorum traditione: ex Catholica et Apostolicae Ecclesiae autoritate, ex Conciliorum generalium, Romanorumque Pontificum Canonibus: ex ueterum denique et recentiorum Patrum, Theologorumque monumentis.

### LXV.

<margin>+</margin> Externa, et quasi ex alieno fundo emendicata, ea dici possunt, quae sumuntur ex naturalium Philosophorum placitis, ex Iureconsultorum responsis: nam et ipsi quoque inter uerae Philosophiae Professores censeri uolunt: ex rerum gestarum commentariis: ex ipsis demum humanae rationis opibus.

### LXVI.

Etenim cum duplex sit argumentandi genus: alterum autoritate nitens Theologo proprium, alterum ratione instructum Philosopho peculiare, si priori et proprio uti non datur, quod priori proximum est Theologus arripiens, pro autoritate, ratione se defendit: saepe tamen utrumque probandi genus simul coniungit.

### LXVII.

Hinc patet stultam eorum esse sapientiam, qui de Theologico quopiam argumento uerba facturi, Patrum, Conciliorum, et Scripturarum autoritate, ueluti parum firma repudiata, ratiunculis tantum ex naturali Philosophia emendicatis, disceptant. Non enim intelligunt μωρόσοφοι illi,

### LV.

You will say that none of these things surpasses the sense of reason, and that in such a way, even if they are sometimes false, they can nevertheless be held as true; but the mysteries of faith, from which the Theologian weaves his argumentation, exceed all sense and all thought of the mind by a great deal.

### LVI.

Let it be so; but it had to be so, especially in those matters which are believed concerning God without evidence of reason. For since God, the Best and Greatest <note>original: "Opt. Max." (Optimus Maximus)</note>, surpasses all reason and exists above all nature and thought, it was necessary that many things should pertain to Him which would exceed the grasp of the human mind; for such a great thing cannot be comprehended by the narrowness of our intellect.

### LVII.

But if the works of God could be comprehended by human reason, and if what and how great He Himself is could be understood by us, God would surely not truly be God; for everything that our intellect can grasp of God by itself is very narrow and infinitely less than the divine majesty.

### LVIII.

Yet it is not because they are of such a kind that they should therefore be held as vain or unworthy of faith. For all and each are most worthy of faith, as they have been received long ago not only by the unanimous consent of the entire Catholic and Apostolic Church, which is the pillar and foundation of truth, and approved by its long and constant use, but also often confirmed by many and great miracles.

### LIX.

Among which, certainly, one should not consider it a minor thing that twelve men of humble lot, destitute of all human wisdom and power, could persuade the wise of the age, and those given over to belly and flesh, of those things from which the common judgment of men mostly shrinks.

### LX.

For what is more alien to human sense than to worship a man who was put on a cross? And for the sake of His worship and love, to regard life, all fortunes, and all the conveniences of this world as nothing? To regard hunger, thirst, cold, and the utmost poverty of all things in place of the greatest delights? To pour forth ardent prayers for those who persecute and slander? To show oneself joyful in adversities and sad in prosperity? etc.

### LVI.

Sit ita: at ita esse debuit, in ijs praesertim, quae de Deo citra rationis euidentiam creduntur. Nam cum Deus Opt. Max. rationem omnem superet, supraque omnem naturam, et cogitationem existat, necessum fuit, ut multa ei conuenirent, quae humanae mentis captum excederent: nostri enim intellectus angustiis tanta res comprehendi non potest.

### LVII.

Quod si humana ratione Dei opera comprehendi, qualisque et quantus esset ipse, a nobis intelligi posset, Deus profecto uere Deus non esset: perangustum est enim omne illud, et diuina maiestate infinitis partibus minus, quod intellectus noster, de Deo per se capere potest.

### LVIII.

Neque tamen quia eiusmodi sunt isthaec, ideo etiam pro uanis, aut fide indignis habenda sunt: sunt enim omnia et singula fide dignissima, utpote non solum unanimi totius Catholicae et Apostolicae Ecclesiae, quae columna et firmamentum ueritatis est, consensione iam olim recepta, longoque et constanti eiusdem usu approbata, uerum etiam multis saepe, et magnis rerum miraculis confirmata.

### LIX.

Inter quae sane non pro minimo habendum est, duodecim abiectae sortis homines, omni humana sapientia, et potentia destitutos, ea saeculi sapientibus, uentrique et carni deditis hominibus persuadere potuisse, a quibus commune hominum iudicium abhorret maxime.

### LXIII.

### XLV.

<margin>Whether the sense of Scripture is obscure.</margin>
Their other objection also labours under no less futility, by which they clamour that Scripture is obscure, and therefore they do not admit just anyone to the reading of it.

### XLVI.

Although we cannot deny that CERTAIN passages in the Holy Scriptures are found to be more difficult and obscure to us, since the Lord Peter himself affirms that there are some such things in the Pauline Epistles. 2 Pet. 3:16.

### XLVII.

Nevertheless, we rightly conclude with the Lord Augustine that from these very obscurities nothing at all can be derived which has not been most plainly explained and resolved by the Holy Spirit in other, clearer passages of Scripture.

### XLVIII.

Therefore, although some obscure things are found in the Holy Code, the sense of Scripture itself is nonetheless clear and manifest, and all and singular articles of religion have open testimonies in the Scriptures.

### XLIX.

But such is the shame of the Papists, that they do not blush to accuse the mouth of divine Truth of lying, whereas Deut. 30:11 affirms that the commandment of God is not hidden, nor far off, but v. 14, very near.

### L.

Moreover, they resist David to his face, who in Ps. 19:8 affirms of the word of God that the commandment of the Lord is clear and enlightens the eyes, and in Ps. 119:105 says that it is a lamp to his feet and a light to his paths.

### LI.

And certainly, the Apostle Peter thinks far better and more honourably of it, whose successors the Roman Pontiffs falsely boast themselves to be, saying: We have a more sure prophetic word, to which you do well to pay attention, as to a lamp shining in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in our hearts. 2 Peter 1:19.

In infinitum igitur distant, ut essentia ita & persona finita & infinita: Essentia finita est individua ob unitatem & incommunicabilis ad plures personas ob finitatem: Infinita vel licet sit summe individua ob summam unitatem, tamen vere est communicabilis ad plures personas ob infinitatem. In finitis persona una distinguitur ab altera non minus essendi singularitate, quàm subsistendi incommunicabilitate: At in mysterio <term>Trinitatis</term> personae distinguuntur ab invicem subsistendi saltim incommunicabilitate, non vero essentiae singularitate, una non est altera, ejusdem tamen est cum altera essentiae numericae. Illic persona quaevis tota distincta est ab alia persona & separata, nullamque habent intrinsecam connexionem: Heic tametsi personae distinguantur realiter, non tamen possunt separari in esse, sed ejus ratione una est in altera, nec esse potest extra alteram ob essentiae identitatem. Breviter: *Personae finitae distinguuntur tempore, voluntate, virtute, operatione, loco:* At in divinis personis ob essentiae <term>ὁμοουσίαν</term> est coaeternitas, una voluntas, una virtus, una operatio, & ubi una ibi altera. And yet, properly speaking, <term>to intelligens</term> <gloss>the intelligent</gloss> is not the difference of a person, for in these things, as transcendents, genus and difference do not have a place, nor does it pertain to the formal reason of a person, but to the material, in that a person formally agrees with a subject. The formal of a person is <term>authyparxia</term> <gloss>self-existence</gloss> and the incommunicability of subsistence, that is, the ultimate reason of subsisting, and independence in subsisting, by the force of which a nature is ultimately actuated in the reason of subsisting, and cannot be united with another and communicated in such a way that it receives the reason of subsisting from it, or is actuated and completed further by it. This formal reason of a person is expressed by two terms, of which one is *positive*, <term>authyparxia</term>, because a person and a subject is <term>authyparkton</term> <gloss>self-subsisting</gloss> and <term>idiosystaton</term> <gloss>self-constituted</gloss>, terminated by a proper personality. But the law (as Varro elegantly wrote) neither disparages the innocent because of a feud, nor forgives the guilty because of friendship: but, as Cicero says, it speaks to all with one and a common voice. Which, however, some in Livy call into criticism, while saying that the King and the Law are contending with each other, they say that he is a man for whom there is room for favor and pardon; that this is a thing harsh and inexorable.

But also with sumptuary laws (which we know also existed among the Romans from Gellius and Macrobius), devised most ingeniously and skillfully, he chastised and repressed the luxury of citizens, and indeed of women most of all. For when most other legislators had imposed a pecuniary fine on those who had offended against sumptuary laws, Zaleucus did nothing of the sort; but he permitted everything to everyone only by applying disgraceful conditions. For he wanted it to be permitted for a woman to use gold in her adornment, and to be dressed in painted clothing, only if she wanted to be considered a prostitute by everyone. Honest matrons were to be clothed in simple dress and white garments. He ordered a free woman not to go out into public accompanied by more than one handmaiden, unless she wanted to appear drunk: nor did he permit her to go out at night, unless she wanted to be accused of lewdness. He forbade men, however, from wearing a gold ring and being clothed in Milesian garments, unless they wanted to be seen as followers of whores or lurkers in others' beds: just as Laertius book 1 also is the author that the Magi of the Persians forbade their people the outward cultivation and use of gold. By this method, however, Zaleucus achieved in a short time, and indeed without punishment, what others could scarcely achieve in a long time and with a heavy threatened penalty, that the citizens were dedicated to modesty and temperance. For who of an honest face would have wanted to expose himself to the laughter and mockery of all, as if the sign of his own disgrace were lifted? So also at Athens there was a law that only prostitutes should wear flowery and painted garments, as Suidas testifies: and it is certain that at Rome too, the habit of prostitutes and matrons was once different. For they used yellow clothing: so that of course, as Plautus testifies, the customs of a virgin diverge far from a "she-wolf," so also they might be distinguished from each other by their clothes themselves. Wherefore he who has attempted the chastity of a matron or virgin, when they were dressed in prostitute's clothing, is denied to be held for *iniuriarum* <gloss>damages for insults</gloss> by Ulpian in law 15, also among Labeo, section 15, *if one [violates] virgins*, <term>Digesto</term> <gloss>Digest</gloss> on insults.

Nam ita demum licere voluit mulieri aurum in mundo suo adhibere, et picta indui veste, si pro meretrice ab omnibus haberi vellet. Honestae matronae simplice cultu et veste candida amicirentur. Mulierem liberam non pluribus vna ancilla pedisequa et cognatis suis comitatam iussit in publicum prodire, nisi si ebria videri vellet: Neque noctu eam foras prodire permisit, nisi si probri insimulari vellet. Viris autem prohibuit annulum aureum gestare, et veste Milesia indui, nisi scortorum sectatores, aut alienorum subsessores cubilium videri vellent: quemadmodum et Magos Persarum exteriore cultu et vsu auri suis interdixisse, auctor est *Laertius libro 1.* Hac autem ratione *Zaleucus* id assecutus est breui, et quidem sine poena, quod alij vix longo tempore grauique interminata poena assequi potuerunt, vt ciues modestiae et temperantiae essent dediti. Quis enim integrae frontis quasi signo turpitudinis propriae sublato omnium sese risui ac ludibrio exponere voluisset? ## præstantissimorum Imperatoris Flavii IVSTINIANI, CORPO-
## RIS IVRIS (cuius pulcerrimam partem, Pandectas,
## ipse sanctissimum Templum Iustitiæ appellat)
## et TEMPLI SOPHIÆ.

<image-desc size="small" type="decorative" significance="low">An ornamental drop-cap letter 'I' at the beginning of the first line of the poem.</image-desc>

*Iustitiæ Sophiæque olim augustissima templa*
*Sunt structa auspiciis IVSTINIANE tuis.*
*Illud Iuris amor, Legum et studiosa voluntas,*
*O Astræa, Iouis filia cara, tibi;*
*Hoc tibi sacrauit, CHRISTE, ô Sapientia Patris,*
*In cultus pietas officiosa tuos.*
*Materies illi Leges ac Iura fuêre*
*Prudentum, et priscis condita Cæsaribus;*
*Materiem lapides huic et cæmenta dedêre,*
*Argentum, et gemmæ, et fulua metalla suam.*
*Hæc educta fuit fabris ad sidera moles,*
*Organa quis, ferra, malleus, atque manus;*
*Illa Triboniano erecta est structura magistro:*
*Ingenium et calamus malleus huius erat.*
*Barbara detinet hoc iam gens Mahometica captum,*
*Et spurcat miserè foeda superstitio.*
*Illud desuetumque diu, tenebrisque sepultum,*
*In lucem Saxo protulit, inque forum.*
*Temporeque ex illo rediuiui gloria Iuris*
*Romani in terris et super astra volat:*
*Muneribusque aras onerantes templa frequentant*
*Hæc, quos Sol oriens occiduusque videt.*
*Dic, vtrum melior templum fortuna sequatur,*
*Anne sacrum Sophiæ, Iustitiæ anne sacrum?*
*Scilicet ingenij monimenta perennia viuunt;*
*At quod opus manus hac condidit, illa ruit.*
*Nominis, ô bone CHRISTE, tui consurgito vindex,*
*Et populo Sophiæ redde age fana tuo.*

### §. XV.

Senis illa fuit conditio, quem inveteratâ apud Caesarem gratiâ super caeteros amicos meminimus aliàs floruisse. Qui igitur mirum sit, si Filii multum deteriore loco fuerunt? Certè Archelaum vereri Principem oportuit, cujus voluntas dignitatem ejus initiò imminuit, ira planè postea prostravit, Viennâ ad exilii acerbitatem perferendam lectâ. *Nold. p. 229.* Imperiosam Principis vocem Josephus non praetermisit, *Ant. l. 17. c. 15.* ut assentiamur facilè Spanhemio, vindici Evangelistae, qui βασιλεύειν haud ita finibus angustis circumscribit, quin inferiorem regiâ potentiam interdum significatu suo complectatur. *vol. 2. Dub. 86. conf. l. c.*

### §. XVI.

Utrum ergò succensebunt nobis Tetrarchae, Palaestinae orâ conlusi, si precarium indicemus modò imperium illos esse sortitos? Perculsi quidem haud dubiè jacuerunt, qvoties Principem adversùs apparerent esse qvicqvam moliti. Sicut Antipae contigit, ab Herodiade incitato; non Philippo composito homini, qvi sibi sapientius consulebat; etsi uterqve aliàs obseqvium multis officiis Principi testaretur. *Ant. 18. c. 9.* Mitto Lysaniae fata, & Zenodori, & aliorum, qvos gravem necesse fuit calamitatem persentiscere, si ut irascerenter Domini, flagitiis aut partium studio interdum efficiebant. *Ant. 15. c. 13.*

### §. XVIII.

Ita Tetrarchas quidem universè speculati sumus, re-
per quadrantum dynastas aptâ brevitate expressâ; nunc de
singulis quin videamus, nihil impedit aut vetat. Prior
apud Lucam verò est Antipas; potior imperio etiam, li-
cet aetate minor. Cujus incestum, foedam simulatio-
nem, invidiam, ac tyrannicam crudelitatem, cum fortu-
narum ruinâ, Josephus graviter multis locis describit, E-

historiae multa linquentes, brevi recensione officio nostro

Indeed, another believes that he ruled with such power that it was not intact for the Romans either to command anything while he lived, or to conduct a census in Judea. <note>Scal. l. c. Vales. annotations, p. 11.</note> Yet nothing could deter Casaubon from indicating that Herod was in the power of the Roman citizens <term>Quiritum</term> <gloss>Roman citizens/Quirites</gloss>, no differently than any of the provincial governors. Hence, one should not hope that more might be obtained from him beyond his fiduciary power. <note>Exercit 1. on the apparatus of the annals, no. 5.</note>

## §. XIV.

It is not my place to settle the dispute between such great men, nor to pronounce the judgment of a judge, as I see Spanheim had once intended to assume those parts with prudent counsel. Yet he believes he was under clientela, relying on the authority of Appian who made him tributary, especially since so many provocations intervened, he himself having been called more than once to plead his cause, and barely defending himself against hostile and infested court cases with the lowest obsequiousness. <note>Dub. Ev. 7. Part. 2.</note> Why then did it matter if he was occasionally greeted as a Friend of Augustus <term>Φίλον</term> <gloss>Friend</gloss>, and an ally <term>καὶ σύμμαχον</term> <gloss>and ally</gloss>, if he threatens to treat him as a subject in the future? Or what did it achieve to claim for a foul man the power of making a will and punishing his own offspring, if he did not promptly divide the family estate, and Caesar allowed him to usurp neither without permission? As is manifest from <note>Ant. b. 15. c. 13. Cf. b. 16. c. 15. and 17.</note> The case of Antony pertains here, from which it was necessary for Herod to be in peril regarding his kingdom. <note>Ant. 15. c. 9.</note>

Nunc ad aliam litem progressum facio, quam doctissimus Anglorum excitavit, γαλιλαίας voci Tetrarchia Herodis universa inclusa, cum transjordanem imperasse & sciret, & fateretur. that wounded small crows <note>original: "corniculae"</note> and those drenched in blood return, it is certain that this is a lie for three reasons. The first is because the climates from the East to the West are of the same temperament in cold and heat: and therefore there would be no remedy if they withdrew to the East. The second is that it has been discovered that they withdraw from our entire habitable world, remaining in no part of it. The third is because, since the bird is cold, using cold and viscous food, it has a necessity to hide during the time of the generation of phlegm, as was determined in the preceding sections. That it is not discovered where they hide is because they conceal themselves greatly in the deserts of marshes and caves, just as other hiding creatures do.

| That it is also said that the male of this bird senses adultery in its mate through scent unless she has first been washed in spring waters, || is false and fabricated.

25. | <term>Choretes</term> <gloss>a type of bird</gloss> are birds that fight with ravens without a treaty: yet they cease from fighting at night, but they fight at every other time and steal each other’s chicks. ||

26. | The <term>Calandris</term> <gloss>Calandra lark</gloss> is a bird in color and figure similar in all respects to the lark, but larger in size, and it modulates its voice with the same turns as the lark, but its voice is coarser and higher and is very sonorous, as if desiring nothing else but to sing, and for this reason it is enclosed in cages because of its song. ||

27. The raven is a well-known bird, larger and more perfect among those that are of the raven kind, it is entirely black and strong of beak and body, | very clamorous, || laying eggs and brooding before the spring time, and before thunder, and it sometimes ejects one of its chicks out of weariness of feeding it. ||

This bird is sometimes domesticated, speaks, and imitates the songs of domestic birds and steals much, and sometimes, when coerced by threats, it restores what it stole. | It is, however, as the fables say, a friend of the fox and an enemy of the donkey, and for this reason it sometimes blinds the donkey and renders it useless and bites its back. The <term>Achylon</term> <gloss>a type of bird</gloss>, however, is a bird that is a friend of the donkey and an enemy of the fox, and for this reason these two birds are enemies to one another. ||

I once saw a hunting raven that took a partridge and other wild ravens: but it did not take the ravens unless relying on the help of a man nearby. ¶

28. | The crow or small crow <note>original: "cornix sive cornicula"</note> is a bird of the raven kind, in which kind the male feeds the female incubating the eggs, and in this it agrees with ravens: for this is a trait of the kind rather than the species. Parents also follow their offspring even when they are already flying and feed them out of the love of piety.

### XXIII.

Another point must be made regarding someone who wishes to produce newly discovered documents after a sentence has been passed.

For it is a serious precedent that decided cases should be overturned under the guise of newly discovered documents, <note>original: "lex sub specie. 4. Codex de Re Iudicat."</note> and after a matter has been judged or decided by oath, nothing further is sought, <note>original: "lex post rem. 56. Digesta dicto titulo."</note> Although this law must be understood in relation to the second statement according to the law *Admonendi* 31, Digest, On Oaths; yet our opinion is not thereby infringed. In doubtful cases, judges are accustomed to decide in favor of him who has sworn an oath, and against such a sentence (being one passed not upon full proof, but supplemented by an oath), newly discovered documents are deservedly admitted, Bartolus on the said law *Admonendi*, number 1, Wesenbecius in his Paratitla On Oaths, number 11. But since this is permitted specifically by the constitutions of princes, the authority of a *res judicata* <gloss>a matter already judged</gloss> prohibits us from saying the same if the sentence was passed on the basis of true and ordinary proofs, <note>original: "lex si patronus. 12. paragrapho si quis cùm exhaeredatus esset. Digesta de bon. libert."</note> Hence also, in public business, emperors allow the use of newly discovered instruments for cause, <note>original: "lex Imperatores. 35. Digesta de Re Iudicat."</note> Therefore, in private cases, newly discovered documents cannot regularly be produced, argument from the law *Jus Singulare* 16, Digest, On Laws.

### XXIV.

Regarding the production <term>editio</term> <gloss>official disclosure/presentation</gloss> of documents, it must be known that the plaintiff is bound to produce them for the defendant, <note>a</note> but not the other way around. <note>b</note>

<gloss>a The law "It is not new" 5, the law "Just" 6, the final law, Code, On Disclosure.</gloss> <gloss>b Nor indeed should the origin of a claim be founded on the documents of the one who is being sued, according to the final law mentioned, Code, on this title. And the plaintiff ought to bring his own proofs of his intent, law "Too heavy" 7, Code, On Witnesses, since it is in his power when he wishes to litigate, law "He who in another's" 42, Digest, On Rules of Law. And if the plaintiff does not prove his case, the one who is sued ought to prevail, even if he presents nothing himself, law "He who accuses" 4, and Alciatus there at number 1 and 24, Code, On Disclosure.</gloss>

But are documents to be disclosed to the plaintiff at least to establish a replication by the defendant? We still deny this.

**XX V.** Ad alterum genus intellectionum pertinet enunciatio mentalis, quam, ut Recentiores distinguant à propositione, etiam ad tertiam mentis operationem spectante, et virtualem discursum includente, rectè definiunt, judicium immediatum de re aliqua: id est tale, quod praedicatum de subiecto affirmat propter connexionem inter ipsummet subiectum et praedicatum. Cùm è contrà omnis discursus sit judicium mediatum, quia mediatè approbat connexionem praedicati cum subiecto. Potissima horum actuum proprietas est veritas formalis, quae nihil est aliud, quam conformitas judicij cum obiecto, sicut econtrà falsitas est difformitas judicij cum obiecto; ut proinde judicium verum sit illud, quod enunciat obiectum ita se habere, sicut à parte rei se habet: falsum illud, si obiectum non ita se habet, sicut ipsum enunciat.

**XX VI.** Enunciatio semel vera nunquam potest transire in falsam, nec vicissim falsa in veram; cognitio enim eadem, semper idem repraesentat, ergo cognitio, quae cum veritate repraesentavit Adamum scribere, pro hoc instanti, quod copula verbalis designavit, repraesentavit in aeternum Adamum scribere hoc instanti. Sicut enim impossibile est Adamum scripsisse hoc instanti A, et non scripsisse hoc instanti A, ita impossibile est, ut cognitio quae verè repraesentat illum hoc instanti A scripsisse, aliquando repraesentet illum non scripsisse: cum propositio in aeternum tantùm de hoc, et de nullo alio instanti loquatur. De falsitate pari modo discurrendum est, quod si propositio repraesentaret aliud tempus ab illo, quod primò repraesentârat, hoc ipso non eadem, sed alia et nova esset repraesentatio, et consequenter nova cognitio.

**XX VII.** Ad tertium et primarium genus operationum humani intellectûs spectat discursus formalis, sive syllogismus; qui est oratio, in qua quibusdam positis, aliud quiddam, ab his, quae posita sunt, necessario accidit, eò quod haec sunt. Et essentialiter non tantùm conclusionem, sed ipsas etiam praemissas involuit, nec ullus censetur condidisse syllogismum formalem, qui vel aliquid infert sine ullis praemissis, vel factis praemissis nihil infert. Ut autem assensus conclusionis ab alio assensu immediatè judicativo dignosci possit, debet intrinsecè attingere obiectum praemissarum tanquam motivum, et rationem formalem assentiendi. Quod inde probatur, quia omnis actus tendens in aliquod obiectum materiale propter aliud formale, debet attingere illud obiectum formale: atqui motivum formale conclusionis quà talis est obiectum Praemissarum, sive identitas extremorum cum medio tertio, ergo debet actus conclusionis, quà talis, illud obiectum attingere. Confirmatur; quia nisi actus conclusionis attingat iterum motivum formale, in aliquibus syllogismis non poterit dari ratio, cur haec propositio potiùs sit conclusio, quàm alia ex tribus, quaelibet enim illarum potest per modum conclusionis ex alijs inferri.

**XX VIII.** Praeter objectum conclusionis, et obiectum praemissarum debet ab actu couclusionis etiam attingi bonitas illationis, quae est identitas inter obiectum praemissarum et obiectum conclusionis: nam etiam haec bonitas est partiale motivum, quod una cum obiecto praemissarum intellectum movet ad inferendam conclusionem; ablata enim hâc unicâ connexione inter obiectum praemissarum et obiectum con-

Sicuti ergo, cum medicinam amamus propter sanitatem, etiam amamus connexionem, quam habet medicina cum sanitate reparanda, quia seclusâ hac connexione medicinam non amaremus, ita etiam intellectus, vt possit moueri ad concludendum, non debet tantùm attingere obiectum præmissarum, sed etiam bonitatem illationis.

XXIX. Dubitant quidam num judicium de bonitate illationis debeat esse actus distinctus et intermedius, inter assensum præmissarum, et assensum conclusionis, per quem intellectus reflexè cognoscat hanc conclusionem ritè inferri ex his præmissis, eò quòd illa sint identificata inter se, quæ sunt identificata uni tertio. Nos probabiliùs existimamus, *judicium de bonitate illationis ab actu conclusionis distinctum non necessariò semper requiri*, maximè in hominibus exercitatis, quibus clarissimè notum est principium illud, *quæcunque sunt eadem uni tertio, etc.* Nam tales postquam in præmissis viderunt, extrema conclusionis esse identificata uni tertio, immediatè conclusionis actum inferunt, qui simul et semel et obiectum præmissarum, et bonitatem illationis, et obiectum conclusionis attingit. In iis tamen hominibus, qui in faciendis syllogismis exercitati non sunt, quique etiam, postquam viderunt, duo esse identificata uni tertio, adhuc dubitare possunt, an illa duo sint identificata inter se, omnino *sequi putamus judicium de bonitate illationis distinctum, et ipsam conclusionem præcedens*: tam imperfectus enim horum intellectus non est sufficienter determinatus per obiectum præmissarum ad conclusionem sine ulla hæsitatione inferendam.

# *Operationes Voluntatis humanæ.*

XXX. Voluntatem esse virtutem spiritualem liberam, obiecti appetitiuam, certum est apud omnes: eandem nec ab intellectu, nec ab anima distingui, supra thesi tertia insinuauimus. *Obiectum materiale*, circa quod illa versatur, est omne id, quod intellectus sub ratione boni vel mali cognoscere potest. *Obiectum formale*, siue illud, quod immediatè voluntatem mouet, est bonum et malum, prius mouet ad actus prosecutionis; posteriùs ad actus fugæ. Bonum, quod voluntatem mouet, triplex est: *honestum, delectabile, utile*. Nullum ex his voluntatem allicere potest, nisi priùs sit cognitum: ipsa tamen cognitio non est motiuum voluntatis, sed mera conditio applicans motiuum. *Malum ut malum*, siue tantùm sub ratione mali propositum, voluntas amare non potest, secùs si sub ratione boni saltem apparentis obijciatur.

XXXI. Ordinariè loquendo, vt aliquod bonum nobis ipsis amemus, et appetamus, sufficit cognoscere illud bonum esse nobis conueniens; nec opus est, vt in nobis ipsis aliquam bonitatem agnoscamus, propter quam digni simus, vt nobis tale bonum amemus. Si verò alteri personæ amamus, aut cupimus aliquod bonum, requiritur, vt in illa apprehendamus aliquam bonitatem, propter quam illam tali bono dignam æstimamus. Vt enim (ordinariè loquendo) possim me coniungere per affectum cum bono proximi mei, quatenus illi bonum est, debeo me prius coniungere per affectum

### XXII.
The human intellect, as it is distinguished from the angelic, is a spiritual cognitive virtue, requiring for some state at least to operate dependently upon a <term>phantasm</term> <gloss>sensory image</gloss>: it is not really distinguished from the soul, and in one man it is unique; yet it bears various names according to the variety of its operations. Its object is being taken in its whole breadth, as it includes uncreated and created being, natural and supernatural, positive and negative, real and rational being: for we experience that we are occupied with all these in our intellect, whether clearly or obscurely, or through proper or alien <term>species</term>. The operations of this power are those vital acts by which a man is formally and intrinsically rendered intelligent.

### XXIII.
Intellection (the same, indeed an even greater reason exists for volition) consists formally in a quality identified with the action by the soul that depends on it; and thus it is a modal entity, which is not only immediately united to the soul by itself, but also proceeds from it without an intermediate action distinct from the entity of intellection itself. The reason is that a free act, for example love, is intrinsically and in itself free; yet nothing is free formally, intrinsically, and in itself except the formal exercise itself or the free determination of the will by which it applies itself freely to this object and flees another. This determination, however, cannot be anything other than a free action producing love: therefore, so that love may be free in itself and intrinsically, it must have its production identified with itself. We feel the same about intellection; for this is not an image of an object that is just any kind or dead, as a wooden statue of Caesar is, but is a living representation and an actual attention of the soul; which seems to be able to be understood as little without the effort and action of the soul itself as the former, therefore the vital image of the object must have the productive action itself identified with itself: for intellection is also the exercise of the intellect, just as love is the exercise of the will.

### XXIV.
The intellections of man are for the most part revoked to three genera: namely, apprehension, judgment or enunciation, and discourse. Apprehension is an act of the intellect that represents an object in a simple way, affirming or denying nothing about it. Concerning this genus of acts, many difficulties occur through philosophy, and we propose one: namely, whether the human intellect can objectively prescind <gloss>abstract or separate</gloss> between formalities identified in an object, that is, attaining one while not attaining the others? We judge it more probable that it implies a contradiction in created things for acts of the intellect to objectively prescind. The reason is because if, for example, animality could be known in man without knowing rationality, then the same indivisible thing could be known and not known; these are no less contradictory than being produced and not being produced, existing and not existing; which, since they cannot be verified of one and the same created thing according to all, one and the same thing will not be able to be known and not known. More correctly, therefore, a virtue of formally prescinding is granted to the intellect, such that the act elicited through it attains all formalities identified in the object at all, yet with this distinction: that it knows one clearly, others confusedly, or in such a way that by the force of that cognition it cannot give an account of what kind they were.

<summary>This page explores the nature of the human intellect, defining its object and its operations (apprehension, judgment, and discourse), and argues that intellectual acts represent a vital, living process rather than a static image.</summary>

### XXII.
Intellectus humanus prout diſtinguitur ab angelico , eſt virtus cognoſcitiva ſpiritualis , exigens pro aliquo ſaltem ſtatu dependenter à phantaſmate operari : is realiter ab anima non diſtinguitur , & in vno homine vnicus eſt ; pro varietate tamen operationum varia nomina ſortitur. Eius obiectum eſt ens in tota ſua latitudine ſumptum , prout nimirum includit ens increatum & creatum , naturale & ſupernaturale , poſitivum & negativum , ens reale & rationis : experimur enim , nos circa hæc omnia intellectu verſari , vel clarè , vel obſcurè , vel per ſpecies proprias vel alienas. Operationes huius potentiæ ſunt illi actus vitales , per quos homo formaliter & intrinſecè redditur intelligens.

### XXIII.
Intellectio ( par , imò maior eſt ratio de volitione ) conſiſtit formaliter in qualitate per actionem ſecum identificatam ab anima dependente , adeoque eſt entitas modalis , quæ non tantùm animæ immediatè per ſe vnitur , ſed etiam ab eadem ſine actione intermedia , ab ipſa entitate intellectionis diſtincta , procedit. Ratio eſt quia actus liber , verbi gratia amor , eſt intrinſecè , & in ſe , liber , atqui nihil eſt liberum formaliter intrinſecè , & in ſe , niſi ipſum formale exercitium ſeu ipſa libera determinatio voluntatis , per quam ſe liberè huic obiecto applicat , ab alio fugit. Hæc autem determinatio non poteſt aliquid aliud eſſe , quàm libera actio productiva amoris : ergo ut amor ſit in ſe , & intrinſecè liber , debet habere ſecum identificatam ſui productionem. Quod ipſum de intellectione ſentimus ; hæc enim eſt imago obiecti non qualiscunque & emortua , vti eſt ſtatua lignea Cæſaris , ſed eſt viva repræſentatio , & actualis animæ attentio ; quod tam parùm ſine ipſius animæ conatu , & actione intelligi poſſe videtur , quàm prius , ergo imago vitalis obiecti debet ſecum habere identificatam ipſam actionem productivam : nam etiam intellectio eſt ipſum exercitium intellectûs , ſicut amor eſt exercitium voluntatis.

### XXIV.
Intellectiones hominis ferè ad tria genera revocantur : videlicet apprehenſionem , iudicium ſeu enuntiationem , & diſcurſum. Apprehenſio eſt actus intellectûs , qui ſimplici quodam modo repræſentat obiectum , nihil de eo affirmando , vel negando. Circa hoc genus actuum plures per Philoſophiam occurrunt difficultates , nos vnam proponimus : An ſcilicet intellectus humanus inter formalitates in obiecto identificatas præſcindere obiectivè poſſit , vnam ſcilicet attingendo , alias verò non attingendo ? Probabiliùs iudicamus , implicare in rebus creatis actus intellectûs obiectivè præſcindentes. Ratio eſt , quia ſi verbi gratia in homine cognoſci poſſet animalitas non cognitâ rationalitate , tum eadem indiviſibilis res poſſet cognoſci , & non cognoſci , hæc non ſunt minus contradictoria , quàm produci & non produci , exiſtere & non exiſtere ; quæ cum iuxta omnes de vna eademque re creata verificari non poſſint , non etiam poterit vna & eadem res cognoſci , & non cognoſci. Rectiùs itaque conceditur intellectui Virtus formaliter præſcindendi , ita , vt actus per illum elicitus omnes omnino formalitates in obiecto identificatas attingat , cum hoc tamen diſcrimine , quod vnam cognoſcat clarè , alias confuſè , ſive ita , vt vi illius cognitionis non poſſit rationem reddere quales fuerint.

XXXII. Actus voluntatis sunt multiplices. Primaria illorum praerogatiua est, quod soli illi possint esse formaliter, et intrinsece liberi. Est autem libertas duplex: vna in actu primo, quae potentiae, altera in actu secundo, quae operationi competit. Libertas in actu primo est potentia libera, siue talis, quae, positis omnibus ad agendum requisitis, potest agere et non agere: libertas in actu secundo est ipsa operatio, quae ita procedit a suo principio, vt positis omnibus requisitis potuerit non procedere, adeoque; cuius negatio potest coniungi cum principio proximo et adaequato, in actu primo completo. Pro utriusque definitionis ampliore declaratione; aduerto primo: nomine praerequisitorum ad actum secundum intelligi ex parte Dei concursum indifferentem paratum, ne impediatur creatura, quo minus se pro arbitratu ad quemcunque effectum extendere possit. Ex parte obiecti adesse debet repraesentatio indifferens tam sub ratione boni, quam sub ratione mali, aut saltem molesti. Ex parte creaturae, potentia expedita, et immunis ab omnibus impedimentis, et insuper absentia omnis principij, quod ita necessario secum trahit effectum, vt cum contrario, vel negatione illius effectus potentia proxima coniungi non possit. Secundum: potentiam liberam debere pro arbitratu simul (simultate potentiae) posse agere et non agere, non in sensu diuiso, sed in sensu composito, hoc est, posito quod omnia requisita ad agendum adsint, non vero in sensu diuiso tantum, hoc est ita, vt agere quidem possit, cum adsint omnia requisita ex parte actus primi, non autem possit agere, si vel vnicum ex requisitis desit. Nam etiam agentia necessaria, quando omnia adsunt, possunt agere, si vnum desit, non possunt agere: vt ergo agentia libera ab his discernantur, debent illa etiam in praesentia omnium requisitorum actionem posse omittere.

XXXIII. Libertas in actu primo subdiuiditur in libertatem contradictionis, siue quoad exercitium, et in libertatem contrarietatis, siue quoad specificationem. Prior est ad actus contradictorios, vt amare et non amare, velle et non velle. Libertas contrarietatis est ad actus contrarios <term>verbi gratia</term> amorem et odium. Rem exemplo declaramus. Deus <term>verbi gratia</term> vt summe bonus proponitur per intellectum voluntati vt amandus, cum aliqua tamen molestia in exercitio amoris subeunda. Vi huius cognitionis voluntas tantum libera est libertate contradictionis, vel ad ponendum, vel ad omittendum actum amoris. Quod si accedat alia cognitio repraesentans etiam seueritatem ipsius Dei in puniendis hominum peccatis, vel aliam rationem, mali speciem, licet falso, praeferentem, fiet voluntas libera etiam libertate contrarietatis: quia posita tali repraesentatione (modo etiam alia requisita adsint) voluntas non tantum amare potest et non amare, sed etiam actum odij amori contrarium elicere.

I will not now occupy myself with sifting through the annals of the ancients to strengthen what has been said thus far; rather, it will be pleasing to bring into the discussion the living examples of our own times, from which it will be most clearly evident that even the greatest men have not been immune from the stings of envy, with which the learned have strove to undermine each other until virtue and truth have finally triumphed. For although so many illustrious merits to the literary world fought for you, <term>Philippe de Commines</term>, you could not be untouched by this evil. But your virtues finally asserted you and snatched you from prison. They dissipated the storms and tempests of the envious, who were plotting your death for the crime of levity and perfidy falsely fabricated against you. Nor could your own most ample merits, <term>Francis Bacon of Verulam</term>, conferred upon the literary Republic, overcome the envy of other learned men, who strove to undermine your fortune with most acute weapons, the light and fame of which, however, they could not extinguish. I will now refrain from adding more prolixly the dog-like custom of certain men, who, since they can infest the fame of ingenuous men by no other means, do not deem it inhuman to attack it with slanderous barking. I will not inquire, O most distinguished <term>Budé</term>, into the goads by which you were often pierced by the mouths of the malignant, nor will I repeat the wagonloads of injuries cast upon your most skillful and eternally worthy works. It is shameful to remember the impudence that more than once desired that learned men, the lights of the century, be condemned under the guise of other crimes. Finally, may that most execrable crime, most unworthy of the memory of man, remain—by which the <term>Chinese</term>, once moved by the calumny of a certain envious philosopher <term>Lissui</term>, did not refrain from most shamefully destroying all the books of all the learned men with flames. I will add to that, with your leave, O Auditors, the vicious custom of certain people of contradicting and snarling at everyone else, which sprouts most closely from ambition and envy. For although discussions may seem truly named as such because truth was thought to be, as it were, purified through them, yet such excessive self-confidence has settled in the minds of some that, thinking nothing right unless it conforms to their own sayings, they are accustomed to move quarrels over any matter whatsoever, and to measure their outcome not so much by the investigation of truth as by the victory of the adversary. ## *Animam Rationalem in una tantum Corporis parte residere.*

I. Animam Rationalem Philo Iudaeus in corde, Parmenides & Epicurus in toto pectore, Strato Physicus in superciliorum meditullio, Erasistratus in membranulis, Herophilus in cerebri concauo siue basi. An. 1565. c. 54. p 192.* anima inquit in centro cordis posita sine sui distentione, totum corpus sibi unitum sensificat, viuificat. atque mouet, ut aranea, quae in medio telae suae residens, sentit quemlibet motum, siue exterius, siue interius in tela factum: mira sane hominis sententia.

I. Anima Rationalis non est in una tantum Corporis parte, alioqui caeteras non substantialiter informaret, sed tota est in toto continuo, & tota in qualibet eius parte, ut sentiunt omnes sani Philosophi, & Theologi, cum Aristotelis Interpretibus. *1. de Anima, t. 93.* ubi Philosophus ait ne fingi quidem posse, quam partem (scilicet determinatam ac solam) habeat in corpore intellectus, id est Anima Spiritualis.

Et quamuis Aristoteles *de respir. c. 1.* expresse dicat, animam in aliqua corporis particula existere, non tamen cum dictis veteribus sensisse censendus est, eo quod statim subiungat, quod in particulis virtutem suam habeat, id est in certis operationibus, a certis etiam ac determinatis Organis dependeat, & virtutem siue potentias suas materiales in ijs particulis seu Organis residentes, & subiectatas habeat.

<header>OF THE RATIONAL SOUL.</header>

# ERROR XIII.

## That the Rational Soul is transformed into a demon or a brute.

There was a heresy that asserted that the souls of wicked men were converted after death into demons, or into whatever brute animals were appropriate to their merits, as witness Saint Augustine in Book 9, *On the City of God*, chapter 11. Plato taught that the souls of men are demons, and that they become *Lares* <gloss>household spirits</gloss> from men if they are of good merit, but *Lemures* <gloss>restless spirits</gloss> or *Larvae* <gloss>ghosts</gloss> if they are evil. Saint Augustine, in his book *On Heresies* to Quodvultdeus, attributes this error also to Tertullian.

# CORRECTION.

I. This most foolish opinion opens the way to great crimes, for however wicked men have been, whether they imagine themselves becoming ghosts or "Divine Spirits," they become all the worse the more desirous they are of doing harm, to the point that they imagine themselves to be invited after death by certain sacrifices, as if by divine honors, so that they may do harm. And certainly, if the Rational Soul were converted into a demon or a beast, then the soul would cease to be what it was before; for whatever is naturally converted into another thing perishes in order to be turned into the other, just as when wine passes into vinegar, the wine ceases to be what it was before, whence the Rational Soul would be mortal and corruptible, which, however, Tertullian himself denied, as Saint Augustine bears witness.

II. When, however, it is said in John 8, "You are from your father the Devil," and Saint John the Baptist in Matthew 3 called the Jews "a brood of vipers," these were only metaphorical expressions, just as Scripture called Christ a "Lion" and a "Lamb," certainly not in reality, but from a certain similarity, because each had something similar: just as vipers are born devouring their mothers, so the Jews, after they had killed their fathers, namely the Prophets, now wishing to do penance, desired to be born spiritually.

III. Nor did Christ wish the Jews to be children of the devil by nature, but regarding their morals, in which children are accustomed to imitate their parents. Hence he also said to them, "If you are the Children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham." Since therefore Christ will one day say to the reprobate, "Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels," as is held in Matthew 25, a manifest difference is indicated between the souls of evil men and the demons themselves. And in Wisdom 11, it is said that God preserves souls. How would he preserve them if he converted them into demons?

### XIV.

We must not omit in this place the most difficult question of this entire treatise, as Duarenus says, which few touch upon: Of what time must account be taken when one asks about the status, condition, and quality of the testator? We shall answer with a distinction.

### XV.

The internal form of testaments is viewed in the institution of an heir, whence it is called the head and foundation of the testament, since without it nothing in it is valid, and it requires particular study.

Therefore, just as that complexion is cold and moist, it claims for itself a cause of this kind, which all natural philosophers affirm to be the star of the Moon, which has a greater convenience with that complexion than the other planets. For as astronomers write, the Moon has the power to cause humidity, because with its rising the waters increase, and with its descent they are diminished. And this water has some coldness admixed with it, just as that complexion does. This complexion occurs when a mixture is composed of the four elements or humors where the humor of water predominates over the others, and it is assimilated to water and winter. Therefore, the phlegmatic are cold and moist. And its signs, by which it ought to be known as the natural philosophers write, are these: that he is fat in the face, white, and sleepy. He has white skin because the phlegmatic is cold, having little blood. Coldness, however, is the mother of whiteness, and he has a fat body because of humidity, and he is lazy because he is heavy, on account of being moist, because every moist thing is heavy. He is fond of sleep on account of the humor ascending to the head, constricting it and individual limbs, because sleep is a binding of the senses. And he also easily receives knowledge and quickly loses it because of humidity, because the moist is fluid. And he rarely goes bald, is always timid and ignorant. And he is fleshy, having small bones in respect to the flesh in his quantity, because he lacks the heat that would wither him. And he is not quickly angered on account of coldness, and he has soft and straight hair because of humidity. And commonly he has watery eyes, and they are unstable like the Moon, having one eye larger than the other, or commonly they have a defect of the eyes. And they are very potent with women and little desiring because of coldness, but because of humidity, they emit much seed. And his manners are: when he begins to eat, he wants to have courses with a bowl, and he wants to be filled more by the eyes than by the stomach, and it seems to him that he could not be satisfied, always asking what he ought to eat. And he is not envious nor fraudulent, neither in speech nor in deed. And whenever he has drunk, he will begin to sleep, because the fumes immediately ascend to his head. Can virgins, while the flower of chastity is saved, as well as women lying in an empty bed, receive moles in the uterus? Can the said collection of flesh arise without female seed as well, but only from menstrual blood alone? And I will meet these very doubts with a plain and very brief deduction, as much as possible.

XXIIX. Some indeed think that the female alone, without the congress of a man, from herself (while they suffer nocturnal pollutions, and thus retain the emitted seed in the capacity of the uterus), can produce this crude and unfinished mass of flesh, into which, as the more significant heat of the matrix approaches, it gathers and condenses; they try to prove this with the eggs of hens that are wind-laid and unfruitful, generated without the approach of a rooster, and indeed they strive to bolster the certainty of their opinion with certain histories and observations, which we know are enumerated, but we do not place faith in them, because the guarding of the female sex is highly suspect and very difficult.

XXIX. Therefore, the decision of <term>Rodericus à Castro</term> pleases, wherein he asserts that from the white and yolk of an egg, nothing is generated unless virile sperm is sprinkled in, and thus consequently from menses and female seed, nothing can be generated unless virile sperm approaches: Therefore, he says, the more expert believe a mole is begotten from the weakness of both, namely the virile and the female seed, since a woman has nowhere been seen to have conceived a mole without a male.

XXX. But as to the fact that menses alone and intense heat are not sufficient for the progeneration of a mole, according to the opinion of others, such a reason must be brought forward: namely, that blood has no power of acting, but is destined for suffering; nor is the generation of flesh a work of heat, but primarily of the generative spirit and the formative virtue. For by the virtue and efficacy of the masculine seed, from which every principle of formation proceeds, matter is disposed so that it may take increment.

But if certain medicines promote this, they seem to do so by accident, while they either de-obstruct the pores or render the blood more turgid or even more fluid, of which there is more in the following thesis.

## VII.

**O**f the same flour are those sesquipedalian <note>i.e., long-winded, literally "foot-and-a-half-long"</note> words and vain boastings, when they brag of such a medicine by which a wound can be perfectly consolidated in the space of three days, when, however, it is not even possible to provide flesh-generating medicines. Who, I ask, ever saw flesh fashioned by a medicine or generated from a remedy? Trifles! All solid parts are from milk; if the blood abounds with this and distributes it freely through the wounded part, the wound will be healed shortly. But if it has been contaminated by an acid intemperance, or a saline one, or by a perverse mixture, healing will be a slow work. Indeed, consolidation will be awaited in vain unless first the acid is broken, or the sharp salt is tempered, or the legitimate mixture of the blood is restored. By what remedies we may achieve this, this is the task, this is the labor. For the praises of practitioners do not satisfy, as if the blood, by the help of wound-medicines adorned with some peculiar virtue for this business, were disposed in such a way that from it apt and praiseworthy flesh and every other lost substance could be promptly restored. For as long as that peculiar virtue cannot be explained, as it is in fact inexplicable to them, so long does that matter remain in an ambiguous and slippery state. And since we have noted a triple vicious state of the blood, how will it be possible to whitewash three walls with this one bucket? The most famous Craan very well chastises this error and lashes out at the perverse and irrational use of wound-decoctions. For since even the smallest

## VII.

**S**imilis farinae sunt sesquipedalia illa verba & vanae gloriationes, dum ejusmodi jactant medicamentum, quo vulnus spatio tridui perfecte consolidari possit, cum tamen ne quidem dari queant medicamenta carnem generantia : Ecquis quaeso unquam vidit carnem a medicamento fabrefactam vel ex remedio generatam ? Nugae ! Omnes partes solidae sunt ex lacte, quo si sanguis abundet idque per partem sauciatam libere dispenset, vulnus brevi sanabitur. Sin vero intemperie acida, aut salina aut perversa mixtione fuerit contaminatus, lentum opus erit sanatio. Imo frustra expectabitur consolidatio, nisi prius vel infringatur acidum : aut sal acre temperetur, aut legitima sanguinis mixtura restituatur. Quibus vero remediis id assequamur, hoc opus hic labor est. Neque enim satisfaciunt practicorum elogia, quasi sanguis ope vulnerariorum peculiari quadam virtute ad hoc negotium exornatorum ita disponatur, ut ex eo apta & laudabilis caro quaevisque alia substantia deperdita promte restitui possit : Quamdiu enim peculiaris illa virtus explicari nequit, sicut revera apud illos inexplicabilis est, tamdiu res ista versatur in ambiguo & lubrico. Et cum triplicem sanguinis statum vitiosum notaverimus, quomodo una hac fidelia tres dealbari poterunt parietes ?
