Moreover, the customs and statutes of certain places have progressed so far that they make all goods, after entering the marriage bed, so communal that they are equally masters of them while the marriage exists, just as Carpzovius testifies regarding Saxon Law in Part 3, Constitution 25, Definition 6, Number 5.

### THES. VI.

By the appellation of Paraphernal Goods, as has been adduced in some way above, both movables and immovables, and debts owed, come under Law 7, Paragraph 3 of the Digest on the "Peculium" <gloss>private fund</gloss>, however they may have reached the wife before the marriage by civil law, whether by succession or by donation made by the husband himself to the bride (Law 5, Principle; Law 27; 32, Para. "if anyone a bride"; Law penultimate, Digest on donations between husband and wife). Through which, before the constitution of Constantine in Law 15, Code on donations before marriage, even if the marriage did not follow, things became the property of the recipient in such a way that they could not be alienated by the giver through a last will (Law last, Code on the same) or revoked if the marriage were dissolved (Law 12, Code on the same), nor could they be seized by the husband's creditors, unless he could prove that they were already obligated to him (Law 13, Code on the same). Which effects, however, today obtain only if the marriage has followed, per the said Law 15; see Corvinus on the same. Moreover, donations made while the marriage exists, in those cases where there is a place for donation between spouses (some of which are enumerated in Law 15, Para. 1; Law 25, Digest on donations between husband and wife; Law 11, Code on the same), can be added to Paraphernalia. seed: ULRICUS CALIXTUS, were teaching Sacred Theology, the highest men and eternal lights of both this Academy and the Protestant Church! To hang daily from their most learned lips, and to store away for future uses what he had received, was what he willed to be the sum of his daily labors. Truly, the time was beginning to approach when the fruits of such persistent study were to be shown to the learned world. Therefore, after our subject in the year 1654 had proposed a philosophical disputation *On the Singular* and theological disputations of more than one argument—the former under the presidency of the Blessed HOMBORGIUS, the latter under those of the Doctors CALIXTUS and HILDEBRAND—and had obtained the applause of the learned in them, he modestly sought the highest honors in philosophy, which he obtained on merit on the Nones of December of the mentioned year, after preliminary exercises and examinations by the Dean of the Philosophical Order and interpreter, the Blessed JOHANNES HORNIUS, a man of most excellent and guileless heart. In order to show in fact that he had attained these not through ambition, but as a reward of erudition, after holding a preliminary disputation in the assembly of the learned, of which he himself was the moderator, with the benevolent consent of the Philosophical Order he began to teach philosophy, taking his beginning from that part of Physics which expounds the doctrine concerning the Soul. Having performed this work most happily amid the applause of the listeners, he proceeded to teach geography and history, especially that which concerns us more closely and pertains to the state of Germany, to others vigorously. Soon he instituted logical diatribes, but especially he applied himself to the philosophy of morals and civil affairs, so that he seemed to have exhausted both. From this, ten disputations began to be born for him, corresponding to the ten books of Aristotle’s Ethics to Nicomachus, in such a way that with an analysis of each instituted, the reason for demonstrating the Aristotelian conclusions from the genuine principles of this discipline can easily be noticed. ### Quæstio Sexta.

§. 11. *An si Christus post Ascensionem esset in terris, non esset noster Sacerdos?*

In Epistola ad Hebr. cap. 8. vers. 4. hæc legere est verba: *Si enim esset super terram, nec esset Sacerdos*: Ex his adversarii <unclear>furtim</unclear> colligunt, Christum corpore suo in cœlis versari et non esse in terris: Nostrum igitur est Herculi clavam extorquere et solide respondere: *primum illud*: Si Christus Sacerdos esse non posset, (si esset in terris) consequeretur, eum, cum in terris conversaretur, et in crucis ara Patri suo se offerret, et 40. diebus discipulis suis multis argumentis ostenderet, non fuisse sacerdotem. Consequens est absurdum. Ergo et antecedens. Connexi ratio in propatulo est, quia tum in terris fuit. *Secundò illud*: Si Christus, quia Sacerdos, non esset in terris, quà Deus Sacerdos non esset (quia semper ut in cœlo, ita in terra est) Posterius absurdum, ex confessione adversæ partis. Ergo et prius. *Tertium isthoc*: Si Christus quia Sacerdos, non esset in terris, secundum humanam naturam non esset Sacerdos, quia secundum eam, fatentibus illis, est in Cœlis. Posterius absurdum, quia Sacerdotium ad ipsius pertinet officium, adeoque utramque Naturam. Ergo et prius. *Denique* et *hoc*, Si in terris non esset, Sacerdos æternus non esset, quia in novissimo die de Cœlo rediturus est. Falsum hoc, Ergo et illud. Mirum ergo est adversarios huic loco, tanquam tibicini aut suggrundæ alicui ædificium suæ opinionis suffulcire: Verùm enim verò per cuniculos rem agunt. Nam 1. textui inferunt verba, *secundum humanam naturam*, 2. verba accipiunt de alterutra Christi natura, cum Epistola loquatur de toto Christo. Move jam rotam Syllogisticam, quid exibit? annon isthoc?

Moreover, they say that one ascends to the heavens through Mary, that she is the way and the gate, and that a share of the kingdom was given to her. But eternal life is given only through Christ Jesus, says Augustine in *Psalm 31, from John 10, verse 28*. "I am the way, and the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father except through me," says Christ (John 14, verse 6). "We follow you, Lord; through you, to you; we follow you because you are the way, through you because you are life, to you because you are the truth," says Bernard.

## Fifth Question.

### *§. 10. Into what kind of Heaven did Christ ascend?*

The Pontificians make the heaven a corporeal one, and believe that Christ ascended into it, whether he remains within this Heaven itself or whether he remains above and outside all the Heavens, such that he touches the convex part of the highest Heaven with his feet (Bellarmine, *Book 3 on the Incarnation of the Word, chapter 12*). If that were the case, Christ would not be said to have ascended "above all the heavens" (Ephesians 4, verse 10), to have "penetrated the heavens" (Hebrews 4, verse 14), or to have been made "higher than the heavens" (Hebrews 7, verse 26). But it would have to be said that there is some corporeal heaven outside and above the Heavens, and the same must be placed in a location, which sounder philosophy rejects. I now pass over in silence those who imagined 365 Heavens according to Irenaeus. I shall say at least something about the opinion of the adversaries of the Calvinist party: for they first fabricate some common Heaven in which Hercules, Palamedes, Numa Pompilius, or Scipio might live happily, according to that of Christ: "He who does not believe in the Son will not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him" (John 3, verses 18, 36). Secondly, they attribute to us a Ubiquistic Heaven.

### §. XV.

Indeed, whether GUSTAVUS inflicted a just punishment upon these disturbers could seem doubtful to someone. For writers testify with unanimous consent that they were seditious and looters of sacred things. It seemed better that they be removed from the midst than dismissed from the kingdom and sent away into other provinces. For most of the devil's ferments have such a nature that, even if you purge them from one region, they soon sprout up again more destructively in another. But the most religious GUSTAVUS is in no way to be reproached for the leniency of the punishment, since *hereticide* <note>original: "hæreticidium"</note> is repugnant to divine and human law alike, and supreme power over human minds is left to God alone. This dispute was once agitated between the Elector of Saxony and Philip, Landgrave of Hesse, regarding what punishment should be inflicted upon the Anabaptists. And finally, it was decided that for those who disapproved of the duties of the magistrates and incited sedition, capital punishment should be inflicted; that no one could with a clear conscience inflict the death penalty for an error in faith, but in the case of either rebellion or stubborn contumacy in propagating errors, where they either openly impugn the laws of the magistrate or hold assemblies against the so often issued and repeated edicts of princes. See Seckendorffius, *Luther. Book III, Sect. 13, §. XLII, p. 115-116.* GUSTAVUS could not deal otherwise with these superstitious men than with the papists, whose superstition, if not the same, was similar and deserved a similar punishment. He himself traveled through the provinces of the kingdom, visited the churches, inquired into the life and doctrine of the pastors, and did not wish to indulge in any vehemence of the priests or untimely rigor. Paulinus expounds this elegantly:

> *When various tumults and schisms were being stirred up here and there, King Gustavus himself [journeying through] the provinces of the kingdom*

### §. XV.

Eqvidem, an justo supplicio affecerit hos turbatores GUSTAVUS, dubium alicui videri poterat. Nam seditiosos & sacrorum expilatores fuisse, unanimi consensu testantur Scriptores. Quos e medio tolli satius videbatur quam dimitti e regno & in alias provincias ablegari. Nam pleraque diaboli fermenta eam habent naturam, ut, licet ex una regione expurges ea, tamen in alia mox iterum exitiosius repullulent. Minime vero ob lenitatem poenæ reprehendendus est Religiosissimus GUSTAVUS, quippe quod hæreticidium divino juxta & humano juri repugnat, nec nisi Deo soli in mentes humanas suprema potestas relicta est. Fuit aliqvando hæc lis inter Electorem Saxonem & Philippum Hassiæ Landgravium agitata, quæ poena Anabaptistis sit infligenda. Et demum statutum est, illis, qui Magistratus officia improbarent & seditiones concitarent, ultimum supplicium esse irrogandum, bona conscientia nemini mortis poenam inferri posse ob errorem in fide, sed in casu vel rebellionis vel obstinatæ contumaciæ in propagandis erroribus, ubi vel Magistratus jura palam impugnant, vel contra toties edita & repetita Principum edicta cœtus habent. Vid. Seckendorffius *Luther. Lib. III. Sect. 13. §. XLII. p. 115. 116.* Non poterat GUSTAVUS aliter cum his superstitiosis hominibus agere quam cum Pontificiis, qvorum similis utut non eadem superstitio erat, paremque merebatur poenam. Ipse per regni provincias proficisci, visitare Ecclesias, in Pastorum inquirere vitam & doctrinam, nec quicquam vehementiæ Sacerdotum, aut intempestivo rigori indulgere voluit. for a little while, for thirty-three continuous days, he sailed content with only sky and water. The Spanish companions began first to murmur in secret, then soon to press with open insults, to think about killing him, finally, it was suggested that he be thrown into the sea: they claimed that they had been deceived by a man from Liguria, that they were being dragged into an abyss from which it would never be permitted to return. After the thirtieth day, driven by madness, they proclaimed that he should be led back, and they goaded the man not to proceed any further: he, however, by soft words and by ample hope, delaying day after day, soothed the angry men; he preached that they should be held accountable by the kings for treason if they plotted anything adverse against him, and if he refused to obey. At length, joyful, they receive the desired sight of land. With this first voyage he revealed only six islands, and of these, two of unheard-of magnitude: one of which he called Hispaniola, and the other Joanna; but he was not certain that Joanna was an island. As they were skirting the shores of some of them, they heard the nightingale singing among the dense forests in the month of November. He discovered huge rivers of fresh water and natural harbors capable of holding great fleets. Skirting the shores of Joanna, he traveled along the northern side from the west for no less than eight hundred miles (for they say one hundred and eighty leagues), thinking it to be a continent, because neither an end nor any sign of an end appeared on the island, as far as his eyes could discern: he decided to turn back; the swells of the sea also compelled him to return, for the shores of Joanna, through various bends, were turning and curving so much toward the north that northern winds were striking the ships more sharply, since winter was prevailing. Therefore, turning the prows to the east, he reports that he had found the island of Ophir: but when the charts of cosmographers are carefully considered, those are the islands of Antilia and others adjacent; he called this one Hispaniola: wishing to test the nature of the places on its northern side, he approached the land. When the hull of the larger ship struck a flat and blind rock covered by water, it was breached and remained stuck; the level surface of the hidden rock was a help to them, so they would not be submerged; therefore, with the rest, being doubtful, they led all the men out safely. There, having first landed on the earth, they saw indigenous people; who, seeing the unheard-of race arriving, gathered in a group and fled into the dense forests like timid hares from Gallic hounds. Our men pursued the multitude and captured only a woman; when they had led her to the ships, having satisfied her well with our food and wine, and having adorned her with clothes (for that entire nation of both sexes leads a life completely naked, content with nature), they left her free. When the woman had returned to her own people (for she knew where those fleeing were retreating) and had shown how wondrous was the attire and generosity of our men, all ran together to the shores in competition, thinking that the race had been sent from heaven. They brought gold, of which they had some abundance, to the ships by swimming; they traded gold for a piece of an earthenware dish or a glass cup. If our men shared a lace, or a bell, or a fragment of a mirror, or anything else, they exhibited as much gold as it pleased them to ask, or as much as each of them could obtain. When the matter had arrived at familiar commerce, and our men investigated the customs of the nations, they learned through signs and conjectures that that nation had kings. Descending from the ships, our men were honorably received by the king and the remaining natives; <margin>The admirable kindness of the people</margin> they rose to greet our men in all the ways they could and knew. With the sun tending toward the sunset, when our men knelt according to the Christian rite to give the sign of the angelic salutation <note>the Angelus</note>, they did the same. They also adored the cross in the way they had seen the Christians worship. From the ship which we said was dashed upon the rock, that nation brought our men and everything that was carried in it to the land in their own small boats, which they call canoes, so quickly and with such a happy spirit that no relatives among us, moved by greater compassion, could help their own. It is there that the current king has fixed his residence. Although the walls are not of great height, it would be difficult to take it by assault. From antiquity until our days, no one has ever been able to make themselves master of it.

When the king had established his residence, founded his kingdom, built cities for the inhabitants, and accomplished his great designs, the elders said to one another: "Although he approaches the end of life, the king has not yet a direct heir and it is to be feared that his dynasty will die out with him." They went then to the temple of the god <term>Pi-cha-men</term> (<gloss>Vâiçravaṇa</gloss>) and begged him to give an heir to the king. All of a sudden, the head of the statue of the god opened and, from the upper part of his forehead, one saw a young child emerge. They received him and brought him to the king. The whole kingdom was filled with joy; but, as he did not drink milk, they were afraid that he would not be able to live. They went again to the temple of the god and prayed to him to provide for the nourishment of the child. All of a sudden, the earth which was found before the god offered a protrusion which rose little by little in the form of a breast. The divine child having sucked it greedily, he did not delay in acquiring the height and strength of a man. He distinguished himself by his prudence and his valor, and his laws extended far and wide. Immediately he raised a temple to the god <term>Pi-cha-men</term> in order to honor him to whom he owed his birth.

-> XXVII. <-

<margin>Why David is named first.</margin>
Moreover, as Erasmus notes, he names David first, not only because the series of the genealogy might be woven more conveniently and without repetition, which is the reason provided by the divine Jerome: but also because his memory was both more recent and more celebrated among the Hebrews, which is the reason provided by Chrysostom.

## THEOREMATA.

1. **IN DEO** datur Voluntas antecedens & consequens. An autem illa recte dicatur Misericordiae, haec justitiae, non videtur dubio carere, cum Voluntas consequens sit etiam Misericordiae & gratiae.
2. Objectum potentiae infinitae dicitur omne possibile. Et hoc innuit Angelus creatus Lucae I. versu 37. & increatus Genesis XVIII. 14. Notari hoc loco solet Hebraismus, quo verbum ponitur pro reipsa. Sed quid si quis dubium moveat an dabilis sit locus, in quo taliter capiatur?
3. Creatio recte soli & toti Sanctissimae TRINITATI tribuitur: An vero per *τὸ* dicere in Historia Creationis FILIUS DEI significetur, omnino dubitatur, nec desunt rationes dubitandi, quas publico reservabimus conflictui.
4. Non injuria Hieronymus damnatur erroris, eo quod negarit Dei Providentiam circa animalia irrationalia, cum evidenter testetur scriptura sacra, quod singula animalia & animalium subjaceant Providentiae divinae, Confer. ### §. XXIII.

It is beyond controversy that this privilege is inviolable in the place of the markets; but whether the same thing is sacred in the approach and return, or in the places through which market-goers both approach and depart, is not undeservedly doubted. For it seems that it was given for a certain place, and thus, being bound to it, cannot be extended to other places. But the rightly praised Sichard maintains the affirmative here, because he who cannot safely approach and depart does not come quietly or securely. Whence the Emperor Maximilian I, with the privilege of the markets granted to the Leipzigers, as referenced by Carpzovius in the aforementioned chapter 30, definition 28, inserted these words: Likewise the goods and properties which are driven and led to and from designated markets and storehouses shall not be stopped, hindered, or legally arrested, etc. It is required, however, that the approach and departure take place on the days of the markets, and through those places which are under the empire of the Prince granting the solemn markets; otherwise, as I would establish as undoubtedly true with the praised Carpzovius in the aforementioned definition 28, merchants in the places through which they pass either before or after the markets can not only be summoned, but their persons and things can also be detained by arrest, because the market privilege ceases when the markets have not yet begun or have already finished. And if before the markets or when they are finished it is permitted for a Creditor to summon and arrest his Debtor in the very place of the markets, how much more will it be permitted for him in the places through which the debtor prepares his approach or return?

In loco nundinarum privilegium hoc inviolabile esse extra controversiam est; num verò in accessu et reditu, seu in locis per quae nundinatores et accedunt et recedunt idipsum sacro sanctum sit haud immeritò dubitatur. Videtur enim illud loco certo datum esse, sicque eidem adstrictum ad alia extendi non posse loca. Sed rectè laudatus *Sichardus* hic affirmativam sustinet, quia quietè aut securè non venit, qui non potest securè et accedere et recedere. Unde Imperator *Maximilianus I.* privilegio nundinali *Lipsiensibus* concesso referente *Carpzovio dicto capite 30. definitione 28.* haec inseruit verba: Desgleichen die Wahren und Güter/ so zu und von bestimmten Märckten und Niederlagen getrieben und geführet werden/ nicht sollen auffgehalten/ verhindert/ oder rechtlichen arrestiret werden/ etc. Requiritur tamen, ut accessus et recessus fiat diebus nundinarum, perque illa loca, quae sub imperio sunt Principis nundinas solennes indulgentis; alias cum laudatum *Carpzovio dicto definitione 28.* indubius statuerem, mercatores in locis per quos vel ante vel post nundinas transeunt, non tantùm conveniri, sed et personas resque eorum arresto detineri posse, quia nundinis nondum coeptis, vel jam finitis privilegium nundinale cessat. Et si ante nundinas vel finitis iisdem licet Creditori Debitorem suum in ipso nundinarum loco convenire atque arrestare, quantò magis id eidem in locis, per quae debitor vel accessum vel reditum parat, licebit?

# ACT I.

## PROLOGUE.

Moses, summoned by God's command through an Angel from Limbo <note>the place reserved for the souls of the righteous before Christ</note> to the earth, denounces the crimes of King Ahab and the people of Israel. He rouses the prophet Elijah to rebuke these sins and warns him of the future persecution of the prophets.

->*Scene One.*<-

The prophets of the idol Baal conspire to kill the prophets of the true God. They approach Queen Jezebel, who is cheerfully indulging her senses, and through her, they obtain from King Ahab a decree of death against the true prophets.

->*Scene Two.*<-

Obadiah, the steward of the Royal House and, as some maintain, a secret disciple of Elijah, is aware of the death sentence passed upon the prophets. He diligently searches for those he can save and warns them of the danger and the need for flight. At the risk of his own life, he hides one hundred of them in two caves and provides them with food.

->*Scene Three.*<-

The true prophets of God are sought for execution. Some are captured. Others flee. Some remain in hiding. There are those who, through the force of threats or the hope of reward, are betrayed by informants while in hiding.

<summary>This page introduces the prologue and first three scenes of the first act, detailing the conspiracy of Baal's prophets against the servants of God, Obadiah's attempts to protect them, and the resulting persecution.</summary>

Tum Elias bovem alterum parat in holocaustum & ligna, quibus comburi debet, ter aquâ mandata aspergi, DEOque invocato statim ignis adest è Coelo & vorat holocaustum.

### *Chorus.*

Intelligentiae Coelos moventes, depulsis signis Coelorum igneis reducunt signa aquatica, & ad pluviam Coelum disponunt.

### *Scena Quarta.*

Post diuturnam trium annorum & amplius siccitatem tandem populus cum gaudio, & ferae cum tripudijs pluviam excipiunt.

### *Scena Quinta.*

Conscius minarum Iezabelis ob interfectos Baalis Prophetas Elias, dimisso puero fugit, cumque mærens & lassus obdormivisset sub Iunipero excitatur ab Angelo, & ab eodem allato cibo refectus jubetur in montem Oreb se recipere.

64. **Or legitimate [succession], proceeding from the law of the fief in cases of intestacy:** This was not always the same as itself, but born from small beginnings, it grew much later. 1, 1, 1 and 2. In this succession, the first cause is of male children to infinity, of whom some are natural and legitimate at the same time, others natural only; others legitimated, others finally legitimate only.

65. **Natural and legitimate at the same time** are either ecclesiastics, and they cannot succeed in benefits unless it has been otherwise agreed by pact, or the fief is free, or such services are required that are performed no less honorably by clerics than by laymen, or where it is expressly stated that services are to be performed by a substitute.

66. **Or seculars**, who, unless they suffer from an infirmity, such as being of unsound mind, spendthrifts, etc., or in body, such as being mute, deaf, blind, or otherwise imperfect, all succeed; without observing the distinction of whether they are posthumous or born, passed over or instituted in a testament, of the same or different marriage, constituted in parental power or emancipated: nor is it distinguished whether the fief is new or old, royal or non-royal.

67. Sons clearly do not succeed the father in a fief if they are (1) born from a marriage contracted for a <term>morganaticam</term> <gloss>morganatic union/left-handed marriage</gloss>; (2) if the father lost the fief due to a crime; (3) if the sons offended the lord during the life of the father. Obrecht 2, folio 13.

68. **Daughters or females** do not regularly succeed in a fief, because they are unable to serve; for the necessity of wars introduced fiefs, and for that reason these military benefits are usually granted. And this rule remains firm, even if the first person invested with the fief received it under the law that his descendants, male and female, could hold it. 1, 6, 1; 2, 17 m; 2, 104, 1. Because females do not succeed in this case until no males are present. Obrecht 2, folio 14, number 36. But not even in that case will females succeed, where a fief originating from a male has later come to a female by pact. Ibidem, number 9.

69. The above rule fails, however, in the following cases: (1) in a female fief when males are lacking; (2) in a free fief; (3) in a fief granted for service that can be performed equally by a female as by a male; (4) by pact; or (5) where a municipal statute provides otherwise.

70. **Natural children only.** Called <term>νόθοι</term> <gloss>illegitimate</gloss> (Novella 89), they do not succeed in any way, even if the fief was acquired by the mother; the same must be felt regarding sons legitimately begotten from bastards, also spurious and adulterous offspring, who succeed neither the mother nor the father here. At vero si imago Dei non nisi perfecta apprehenditur, absolute posita, quia perfectus Deus est, certe nec de Adamo nondum lapso dici illa potuerit, quoniam similiter propter mentionem Dei, qui infinitus est, conceperis forte infinitam. § XXIX. An autem uterqve parens, vel solus tantum pater, hunc filium rebellem adducere ad synedrium debuerit disputatur. *Theodoretus Tomus 1. operum editione Parisiis pagina 168.* existimat, & Patrem & Matrem consentire in accusatione filii hujus debuisse, anteqvam potuerit occidi. Qvæ sententia albo approbatur calculo in *Mischna de synedriis capite 8. citato § 4.* ubi dicitur: *si pater ejus velit (accusare illum) mater autem nolit, vel si pater noluerit, mater autem velit, non fit filius rebellis & contumax donec ambo voluerint.* Deinde subjungitur: *Si unus illorum (parentum) sit mutilus, vel claudus, vel mutus, vel cæcus, vel surdus, non fit filius rebellis & contumax: qvia dicitur: & prehendent illum pater & mater ejus: ergo non debent esse mutili, & educent illum, ergo non debent esse claudi, & dicent, ergo non debent esse muti, hic noster filius, ergo non debent esse cæci, non audit vocem nostram ergo non debent esse surdi.*

§ XXX. Sed nova oritur Quæstio: an Deuteronomii 21. versus 22. & 23. *Cum autem fuerit in viro peccatum qvod mereatur mortem, & occidatur, & suspendas illum in ligno, non pernoctabit cadaver ejus in ligno, sed sepeliendo sepelies illum eo die, qvoniam maledictus Dei est suspensus, & non immundabis terram tuam, qvam Jehova Deus tuus dat tibi in possessionem*, an inquam illi versus referri ad filium rebellem & contumacem debeant? Sane veteres Hebræi in ea sunt sententia, & dicunt, si parentes filio parcant, illumqve accusare nolint, qvod tum occidatur a synedrio, sive obruatur lapidibus, suspendaturqve, qvia si notorius peccator est, inquiritur in illum a senatu. *Vid. jarchii in hoc loco & Elias Misrachi, diligentissimus jarchii interpres, in hoc loco editione Cracoviensi folio 304. columna 4.*

§ XXXI. Restat ut de pernoctatione in ligno aliqva adjiciamus. Hoc certum est, suspendio post mortem fuisse punitos reos apud veteres Hebræos, ut inter alios testatur *Obadias de Saphorno in Biur al Hattora editione Venetiis folio 73. columna 1.*, ubi suspendium

Venet. fol. 93. col. 1. inf.* Poenam enim fuisse suspensionem patet, ut docet *Calovius* in *Deut. 21.* Cur autem non debuerint relinqui cadavera in ligno, inquirendum est.

§. XXXII. *Jacobus Bolducius Tom. 2. in librum job. edit. Paris. p. 132.* ex *Andrea Masio* refert rationem, cur lex supplicio crucis affectos sepeliri voluerit, esse hanc, quoniam ex diutino in cruce spectaculo facile deduci quis in extinctae animae opinionem posse videretur, minusque recte de futura corporum resurrectione cogitare.

§. XXXIII. Sed potior videtur fuisse ratio, ne tactu cadaveris immundarentur homines, inprimis cum immundities ex mortuo contracta in gente Hebraea inter omnes immundities esset maxima. Quo tendit expositio *Lucae Osiandri in Deut. 21. in fin.*

§. XXXIV. Atque sic suspendium excussum est, quomodo se apud judaeos habuerit. Licet autem lignum in quo rei suspendebantur, vocari possit patibulum, ut illud vocat *Jeckutbiel* in versione bibliorum Germanica in *Deut. 21. edit. Amstelod.* & lignum quoque sumatur pro patibulo docente *Flacio*, in *clave tit. lignum, edit. Jenensis p. 587.* tamen supplicium crucifixionis apud Hebraeos usitatum non fuit, quia non inter supplicia crucifixio tanquam peculiare supplicium recensetur, sed tantum suspensionis, tanquam alterius supplicii consequentis, mentio injicitur. Nec verbum תלה praecise significat suspendere vivum hominem, vel in crucem agere, cum etiam de illis rebus usurpetur, in quas crucifixio non cadit; v. g. suspendi dicuntur in clavo ligneo carnes vel pisces, vel panes, quae non dicuntur crucifigi. Vid. *Nathan Benjechiel in Sepher Herauch edit. Venet. fol. 162. col. 4.*

§. XXVI. With whom *Ralbag* agrees in *Perusch al Hattora, Venice edition, on blue paper, fol. 230, col. 1*, who likewise writes that this rebellious son was at the same time a thief, who squandered the goods secretly stolen from his Father so that he might indulge in food and drink, and furthermore, having been warned by the lesser Sanhedrin, and punished by it, and flogged, he did not want to return to a frugal life, so that his Parents were forced to lead him to the Sanhedrin so that more severe action would be taken against him. Compare *Jephe Mareh, Venice edition, fol. 592*.

§. XXVII. *Moses Nachmanides of Gerona* also admits, in *Biur al Hattora, Venice edition, printed without the Biblical text, fol. 146, col. 2*, that this rebellious son not only despised his Parents and opposed them, but was also a glutton and a drunkard, who shamelessly transgressed the Law of God, which mandates holiness, and that he had been afflicted with the penalty of Stoning, so that others might take an example from it and revere the divine law.

§. XXVIII. Hence also *Bechaj* writes in *Biur al Hattora, Cracow edition, fol. 127, col. 3*, that this rebellious son transgressed the divine precepts, and hence had to be led by his parents to the Sanhedrin, so that it might be shown that parents must love God and His precepts more than their son, although the love of parents for their children is most strong.

(6) A frequent locution occurs in Scripture, so that with the subject of the verb not expressed, it is gathered either from the preceding things or elsewhere (a); for example, Genesis 48:2, "and he said to Joseph," namely saying; "and he announced to Jacob," namely announcing, et cetera. "Until he avenged," namely avenging (7). In such locutions, an active verb may degenerate into the meaning of a passive, for example, with the sense by no means varied, in the cited places it can be said: "and it was said to Joseph, and it was announced to Jacob," item Genesis 16:14, "therefore he called the well," namely calling; or "therefore the well was called" (b). So that hence here too, with the same sense remaining, it can be said: "until the nation was avenged." Especially since this verb sometimes in Kal seems to signify the same as in Niphal, Exodus 21:20, Ezechiel 25:12, chapter 24:8. And it has been rendered passively by some of the most ancient Interpreters; for example, by Jonathan, who <term>עַד דְּיִתְפְּרַע עַמָּא יִשְׂרָאֵל</term>, the Syrian, who <term>ܥܕ݂ܡܐ ܕ݁ܢܸܬ݂ܦ݁ܪܲܥ ܥܲܡܐ</term> until the people was avenged. 42. Many make it a custom to stir up brawls immediately when they are a little intoxicated. Hence, many have labored over what remedy should be used to curb their impudence. It has generally prevailed that a noisy man of this kind should first be silenced; if he refuses to be silent, threats should be added; if even then the insolence of his tongue cannot be checked, he should be sent back well-thrashed at common expense to the place from whence he came. And this mode of proceeding is in accordance with the law; for evil must be removed from the people so that it does not spread further, since it is established that one scabby sheep can infect the whole flock. Nor should this beating, joined with expulsion, seem rigorous to anyone on the grounds that no one should be subjected to double punishment. <note>legal argument: Digest, Book 14, On the duties of the prefect</note> For a prior warning aggravates a second offense. <note>legal argument: Code, Book 28, Section 3, On penalties</note> And he is presumed to have already contracted the habit of offending who does not desist after being warned. <note>legal argument: Code, Book 3, On the hearing of bishops</note>

43. Many who are well-drunk take delight in the smashing of windows and the tearing apart and collision of all furnishings: Nay, we have heard of ovens being pulled down and thrown through windows. I observed all of this with pleasant admiration, having dissected perhaps two hundred crabs daily. Finally, the remaining part of the milk yields to the crab as food. Lastly, each stone is also gradually dissolved again, and bit by bit turns into nourishment. The crab eats absolutely nothing as long as those stones are in its stomach, and it lives for about 27 days, drawing sustenance both from its old stomach, which is gradually consumed, and from the use of the stones afterwards dissolved.

XIV. Indeed, these little stones <note>often called "crab's eyes"</note> provide use not only for the crab, but, thanks to the Creator’s grace, for us humans as well. It is a common saying that they are said to dissolve kidney stones, and Cardanus explains this too vulgarly: <note>kkk</note> *All stones that are generated in crabs, snails, and fish prevent the generation of stones in the kidneys and dissolve those already formed. For if the stones in these animals condense through excessive cold, they therefore cool the kidneys when ingested.* We certainly admit with Scaliger that once the heat of the kidneys is either removed or diminished, the cause of the condensation, cohesion, and hardness is also removed. But if the little stones possess coldness, it is not necessary that they have it from the generating principle; for crabs can impart their own temperament to the generated stone. We therefore debate and doubt that principle of the little stones, especially since, as Cardanus himself does not deny, <note>*</note> stones are generated in other animals by excessive heat. Furthermore, we most strongly deny that coldness alone can dissolve a mass of stone. Thus Scaliger also states: <note>lll</note> *It is clear that those things which dissolve bodies of sand that have gathered into a mass of stone by no means possess the faculty of cooling.*

about which it is concerned, insofar as reason or sense determines that this is good for oneself, for one's own, or for the whole society, according to the reason of this triple good which the will desires, there is also a triple distinction of Ethics. For Ethics, specifically so-called, governs the will privately so that it may desire what is good for itself, lest it commit anything unworthy of itself or little decent, and it hands down virtues common to all men. Economics governs the will so that it may desire what is good for one's own, and it hands down the method of increasing household affairs. Politics, however, governs the will so that it may desire what is advantageous to the whole society, lest harm be brought upon the community, and it hands down the virtues proper to those who administer the republic. I use here the term good generally for the honest, useful, and pleasant good.

For the demonstration, therefore, of such great pain, the Lord cried out with a loud voice and thus sent forth his most blessed spirit. For this cry was so great that it split the rocks, opened graves, divided the veil of the temple, darkened the sun, and shook the whole earth. Now, how much harder than stones are those who do not hear this voice, which even the senseless heard? Whence Bernard: "O hard and senseless children of Adam, whom such great kindness, such a huge flame of love, does not soften." Example of the diamond, which is divided by goat's blood when it cannot be separated by any iron. Will the blood of Christ not do in the human heart what goat's blood does in stone? Thus, therefore, it is clear what the mode of the pouring out of Christ's blood is. It follows to see what the effect and virtue of that same blood is; for if one sees what its virtue was, it will follow or resultantly become clear what its effect is. It is to be noted, therefore, that the virtue of the Lord's blood is threefold. One is the purgative [virtue] of our filth; it had the virtue of purging impure nature, because it is the blood of the most pure lamb. The second is the placative [virtue] of divine wrath; it had the virtue of placating divine wrath, because it is the blood of the most sweet spouse. The third is the perfective [virtue] of human indigence; it had the virtue of perfecting our indigence, because it is the blood of the most high God. I say that the blood of Christ poured out had the purgative virtue of our filth, because it is the blood of the most pure lamb; whence the Lord speaks in Job: "Who can make clean what is unclean?" etc. Apocalypse last: "Blessed are they who wash their robes in the blood of the lamb." And the same [author] says in his first epistle: "He loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood." For it is written in Hebrews 9 that almost all things are cleansed in blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no remission. And in chapter 10 of the same, it is added that it is impossible for the blood of bulls to take away sins. It is necessary, therefore, that sins be understood to be cleansed in the blood of the lamb, of whom John 1 says: "Behold the lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world." For who shall be made clean from the unclean? Does not he who touches the unclean necessarily become defiled? <note>Ecclesiasticus 13:1</note>. It is necessary, therefore, that the cleanser be most pure; but Christ alone was most pure, who neither contracted original sin nor ever actually sinned; nay, he could not sin. Therefore, he alone was able to wash others. Whence he says in 1 Peter 1: "You were not redeemed with corruptible things, as gold or silver, from your vain conversation, but with the precious blood of the lamb, immaculate and uncontaminated, who did not commit sin," etc. And he says notably "precious blood," because the blood of the lamb exists of such great price. Of such great price was the lamb, but the lamb existed of infinite price because he was God. Therefore, his blood was also of infinite price. Great reverence, therefore, is to be held in this blood, because those who show contempt must be struck with a great penalty. Whence Hebrews 10 <column-break/>

### 76.
But whether one has guarded or crossed the limits of necessary, just, legitimate, and guiltless defense cannot be sufficiently defined by imperial constitution, nor by the decision of interpreters, nor by any other way: and therefore we believe the entire judgment of that matter should be left to the discretion and judgment of a prudent judge. Thus far concerning the lawful defense of life or body, whether one's own or another's.

### 77.
Furthermore, as it pertains to the defense of HONOR, it is usually debated with great anxiety: if someone, affected by a very grave verbal injury, immediately inflicts a real injury and even brings about death, by what punishment should he be affected? And it is more [common] that he be subjected to a milder and extraordinary, not the ordinary, penalty of the <term>Lex Cornelia</term>.

### 78.
Indeed, if someone kills another who is inflicting rape upon himself or his children, or who is attempting to inflict it by open evidence, he is not held by any punishment at all by the rescript of the Divine Hadrian: since the fear of such an injury for good men ought to be greater than that of death.

### 79.
It is not incongruously asked in this place whether a provoked person, if he is staying in his home or another safe place, ought to appear to the challenger for a duel or contest for the sake of defending his honor? And it is proven by the authority of the law that he cannot, nor ought he, do that.

### 80.
If someone, however, inflamed by the most just anger, makes himself available to such a challenger and removes him from the midst in a heated fight, he will also have to be restrained extra-ordinarily.

### XXXIV. 

Sive capitis diminutione ejus cum quo ante quid actum vel contractum est. *lex 2. §. 1. Digestum de capitis minutione.* Est autem capitis diminutio status permutatio. *lex 1. Digestum de capitis minutione principium institutiones eodem.* sicut ergo status est triplex, libertatis, civitatis et familiæ: (hæc enim tria sunt, quæ habemus, non quidem nostro facto et contractu, sed publico beneficio, tanquam principia reliquorum jurium, quæ nobis competere possunt. *lex finalis de capitis minutione Locamerus ad principium institutiones eodem.*) ita triplex etiam ejus mutatio; maxima, per quam libertas, media per quam civitas, et minima per quam familia mutatur. *dicta lex finalis in qua et totus titulus Institutiones eodem.* quid singulæ sint, quando, et quibus modis contingant, explicatur. And among these, it is indeed denied to others, such as municipal Magistrates (Law 26, Digest on municipalities), although the *imperium* with jurisdiction, which two are always joined (Law 3, section 1, on jurisdiction; Law the last, section the end, Digest on him to whom jurisdiction is mandated), pertains to them (per Law 12, Digest on jurisdiction; joined with Law 1, Digest on judges), and this is because they do not have such jurisdiction.

XXVIII. To others it is denied only in some cases, and indeed in Canon Law, to a Legate against the sentence of the Pope (per C. *tum ex literis*, where Panorm. extra. on restitution). In Civil Law, however, to lesser Magistrates who by no means can restore against the sentence of superiors (Law 18, beginning, Digest on Minors). By the same law, only the Prince restores against the sentence of the Prince, and indeed rarely and only on account of new allegations (said Law 18, section 1). Similarly, only the Prince restores against a sentence spoken by the Procurator of Caesar or the *rationalis* (Law 1, Code on where and before whom), or spoken by another in his stead (*vice sacra*) (Law 3, Code if against a decided matter; said Law 18, section 'the same', on minors), or spoken by him whom the Prince himself gave as judge (said law 'a minor however', section 'but even if', Digest on Minors).

XXIX. Those injured and defrauded are restored, whether they be majors or minors, and these indeed both fathers of families and sons of families of whatever dignity and status they may be (provided they are free, for to slaves restitution is not given, because it cannot even benefit them, but only their masters; Law 6, Digest on restitution to the original state; Law 3, section the last, with the following law, Digest on Minors), whether male or female (Law 1, Digest on restitution to the original state); for the praetor, that is, the Magistrate who has such jurisdiction, assists men who are deceived, fallen, and defrauded (said Law 1).

XXX. Or because of fear; which must be present (Law 'fear however', beginning, Digest on that which is done because of fear), not superfluous (Law 2, section 1, Digest on from which causes a major), not vain (Law 6, Digest on that which is done because of fear); for there is no just excuse for vain fear (Law 184, Digest on the Rules of Law). But it must be of greater malice (Law 5, Digest on that which is done because of fear) and such that it might fall upon the most constant man (said Law 6, Digest on that which is done because of fear), and it must be just, such as that of death, of which in Law 7, section 1, in the same place; bodily torture, in Law 3, 'from which causes a major'; Law 4, Code on those things which are done by force or fear; chapter 'the second to last', extra. in the same place; servitude (Law 4, Digest on that which is done because of fear); defilement (Law 8, section 1, Digest in the same place). déclaré qu'en toute substance après Dieu, fût-elle purement spirituelle, l'essence est distincte de l'existence.

Cette thèse, il ne l'a jamais abandonnée. Il l'expose, avec de grands développements, dans sa *Summa contra Gentiles*, qui fut composée¹ sous le pontificat d'Urbain IV (1261-1265). Il la résume avec grande clarté dans sa *Quæstio disputata de spiritualibus creaturis*, qu'on date² du pontificat de Clément IV (1265-1268). Il la soutient encore vers la fin de sa vie, dans sa douzième et dernière discussion quodlibétique. Cette doctrine de la distinction entre l'essence et l'existence, c'est comme un sceau, imprimé dans la philosophie de Thomas d'Aquin et jamais brisé, qui affirme l'emprise des principes d'Avicenne.

Mais cette doctrine qui scellait, pour ainsi dire, l'union de sa pensée avec le Néo-platonisme arabe, Thomas d'Aquin s'en trouvait singulièrement embarrassé lorsqu'il voulait pénétrer les théories d'autres philosophes ; ni le Platonisme de saint Augustin, en effet, ni le Péripatétisme d'Aristote et d'Averroès ne s'accommodaient de cette doctrine qui leur était étrangère ; aussi, soit que Thomas d'Aquin voulût suivre le sentiment de l'Évêque d'Hippone, soit qu'il épousât l'opinion du Commentateur de Cordoue, il se voyait réduit à oublier et à faire oublier qu'il avait distingué entre l'essence et l'existence, à ne plus souffler mot de cette distinction, quand même les circonstances semblaient réclamer impérieusement qu'on en fit mention.

Parfois même, le *Doctor communis* allait jusqu'à développer des considérations qui semblaient contredire formellement celles qu'il avait exposées au *De ente et essentia*. N'est-ce pas ce qui a lieu dans ce chapitre de la *Somme contre les Gentils*³ où l'on se propose de démontrer que « Dieu est sa propre essence » ?

« Il est des formes, dit Thomas d'Aquin, que notre langage n'attribue pas à des choses subsistantes, que ces choses soient considérées, d'ailleurs, d'une manière singulière ou d'une manière universelle ; ce sont des formes qui ne subsistent pas par elles-mêmes, individualisées d'elles-mêmes. Aussi ne dit-on pas que l'animal, que l'homme, que Socrate soit la blancheur, parce que la blancheur n'est pas une chose qui subsiste par elle-même à l'état singulier ; elle reçoit son individualité du sujet subsistant [dans lequel elle réside]. »

» De même, les formes naturelles ne subsistent pas par elles-mêmes à l'état singulier ; elles sont individualisées dans des matières qui leur sont propres ; aussi ne disons-nous pas que le feu que voici soit sa propre forme.

» Les essences ou *quiddités* des genres et des espèces, en effet, sont individualisées par l'intermédiaire de la matière pourvue de dimensions déterminées (*materia signata*) qui est celle de tel ou tel individu ; il en est ainsi, bien que la *quiddité* du genre ou de l'espèce n'implique pas seulement la forme, mais encore une matière prise d'une manière générale ; voila pourquoi nous ne disons pas que Socrate ou que l'homme soit l'humanité.

» Mais l'essence divine subsiste par elle-même à l'état singulier ; elle est individualisée en elle-même ; l'essence divine doit donc être attribuée à Dieu, en sorte que l'on doit dire : Dieu est son essence. »

Examinons de près ce raisonnement ; cherchons quel axiome il suppose ; nous trouvons celui-ci : Une chose qui subsiste en elle-même est ou n'est pas identique à son essence, selon que la forme de cette chose reçoit son individuation d'une matière ou bien qu'elle est exempte de matière, subsistant en elle-même, individualisée d'elle-même.

Et de ce principe, quel est le corollaire immédiat? Le voici :

Pour une substance composée de matière et de forme, la chose réellement existante est distincte de sa forme, partant de son essence. Pour toute substance exempte de matière, qui est forme séparée, la chose subsistante est identique à son essence.

C'est la pure doctrine de Thémistius¹ ; c'est le contrepied de ce que Thomas d'Aquin, non seulement au *De ente et essentia* mais encore en cette même *Somme contre les Gentils*, a dit des créatures intellectuelles, exemptes de matière.

Mais sans insister davantage sur le principe de l'argumentation que nous venons d'emprunter à la *Somme contre les Gentils*, voyons comment cette même argumentation se précise et se développe en cet article de la *Somme théologique*² où l'on examine « Si Dieu est la même chose que son essence ou nature. »

« A cette question, écrit Saint Thomas, il faut répondre que Dieu est la même chose que son essence ou nature. Pour bien comprendre cette réponse, il faut savoir que, dans les choses composées de matière et de forme, il est nécessaire que la nature ou

founded on the axioms of Aristotle; the doctrine of the Greek philosopher and the doctrine of the Muslim philosopher are treated, in the works of the Angelic Doctor, as two allied powers that strive with common accord for the conquest of truth.

Now, this is not the case; the metaphysics of Aristotle and the metaphysics of Avicenna are not two allies of which one is disposed to second the other; they are, in spite of appearances, two irreconcilable adversaries of which each fully intends to organize according to its own principles, and without yielding anything to the other, the whole domain of philosophy. Nowhere better than in this problem of the distinction between essence and existence is the irreconcilable divergence of the two doctrines marked.

Aristotle knows only one duality, that of matter and form or, in other terms, that of existence in potency and existence in act. All existence in potency is matter. All form implies existence in act, confers actual existence. A pure form, a form exempt from matter, is an existence always actual. Every substance devoid of matter, every intelligence, therefore possesses in a necessary and, consequently, eternal manner, actual existence; it possesses it by itself, by its own nature, because it is simple form, pure act without any mixture of potency.

Avicenna admits another duality than that of matter and form, than that of existence in potency and existence in act; he admits the distinction between contingent existence and necessary existence, between the <term>possibile esse</term> <gloss>possible being</gloss> and the <term>necesse esse</term> <gloss>necessary being</gloss>. Only the first Principle has, by itself, necessary existence. All the substances that come after the first Principle, even if they were pure Intelligences, have only a contingent and created existence. By themselves, by their nature or essence, they have only the possibility to exist, the <term>possibile esse</term>; to exist or not to exist, they are indifferent. They can, it is true, exist really and actually, possess necessary existence, the <term>necesse esse</term>; but this existence, they do not hold from themselves, from their nature; they receive it from the first Principle, they are created.

This notion of creation, inconceivable to Peripateticism, and the first foundation of the Neo-platonism of Avicenna, puts between the two doctrines a dispute that refuses all conciliation.

We have seen how Saint Thomas Aquinas, from the time when he began to philosophize, from the time when he composed the treatise <term>De ente et essentia</term> <gloss>On Being and Essence</gloss>, had embraced the side of Avicenna and

Or, il n'en va pas ainsi ; la métaphysique d'Aristote et la métaphysique d'Avicenne ne sont pas deux alliées dont l'une soit disposée à seconder l'autre ; ce sont, en dépit des apparences, deux inconciliables adversaires dont chacune entend bien organiser selon ses principes propres, et sans rien céder à l'autre, tout le domaine de la philosophie. Nulle part mieux qu'en ce problème de la distinction entre l'essence et l'existence, ne se marque l'inconciliable divergence des deux doctrines.

Aristote ne connaît qu'une dualité, celle de la matière et de la forme ou, en d'autres termes, celle de l'existence en puissance et de l'existence en acte. Toute existence en puissance est une matière. Toute forme implique l'existence en acte, confère l'existence actuelle. Une forme pure, une forme exempte de matière, c'est une existence toujours actuelle. Toute substance dénuée de matière, toute intelligence possède donc d'une manière nécessaire et, partant, éternelle, l'existence actuelle ; elle la possède par elle-même, par sa propre nature, parce qu'elle est forme simple, acte pur sans aucun mélange de puissance.

Avicenne admet une autre dualité que celle de la matière et de la forme, que celle de l'existence en puissance et de l'existence en acte ; il admet la distinction entre l'existence contingente et l'existence nécessaire, entre le <term>possibile esse</term> et le <term>necesse esse</term>. Seul, le premier Principe a, par lui même, l'existence nécessaire. Toutes les substances qui viennent après le premier Principe, fussent-elles de pures Intelligences, n'ont qu'une existence contingente et créée. Par elles-mêmes, par leur nature ou essence, elles n'ont que la possibilité d'exister, le <term>possibile esse</term> ; à exister ou à ne pas exister, elles sont indifférentes. Elles peuvent, il est vrai, exister réellement et actuellement, posséder l'existence nécessaire, le <term>necesse esse</term> ; mais cette existence, elles ne la tiennent pas d'elle-même, de leur nature ; elles la reçoivent du premier Principe, elles sont créées.

Cette notion de création, inconcevable au Péripatétisme, et premier fondement du Néo-platonisme d'Avicenne, met entre les deux doctrines un différend qui se refuse à toute conciliation.

Cette conclusion, remarquons-le bien, Thomas d'Aquin ne la tire pas de quelque principe qui s'appliquerait seulement à Dieu ; il la déduit d'une proposition qu'il a établie pour toute chose non composée de matière et de forme ; cette proposition peut s'énoncer ainsi : Pour toute chose non composée de matière et de forme, le sujet individuel (*suppositum*) est la même chose que l'essence ou nature qui définit l'espèce.

Cette proposition s'applique aux anges, auxquels Thomas d'Aquin refuse toute matière, aussi bien qu'à Dieu, en sorte qu'on ne doit pas dire simplement : Chaque ange est seul en son espèce, mais : Chaque ange est sa propre nature spécifique, sa propre essence. §. 25. Tertiò dicimus: nomen principis non denotare semper per-
sonam quæ est cum imperio, sed principes etiam audire, quibus nulla in
alios competit potestas, modo præ aliis vel virtute, vel dignitate, emineant,
quales laudati illi duces omninò erant, qui nobilitate prudentiâ ac sapien-
tia alios excellebant. Quod vero legitur in libro *Judicum* nullum fuisse Re-

quemlibet, qui postea à Deo excitatus est, ipse *Bertramus loco citato Caput 9.* fate-
tur, expresseque; *Mosen, Josuam*, & *Judices*, duces tantùm fuisse, pari invi-
cem facultate præditos, agnoscit.

§. 26. Accedimus ad alteram classem, eorum scilicet qui formam Reipublicæ
Hebraeorum Aristocraticam fuisse, existimant, ut idem *Josephus, Liber IV. Antiquitatum
caput 8. Sigonius, Liber 1. caput 5. Liber VI. caput 7.* multisque alii, quos *Arnisaeus, Liber II.
re Politica caput 4. Sectio 5.* citat, quorum sententiæ suum quoque calculum addit.
Facile cum his premunt *Bertramus, caput 6. loco citato Grotius, Liber 1. citato §. 20, Schickar-
dus, de jure Regum caput 1. §. 2. Cunaeus Liber 1. caput 12.* aliique, quibus omnibus, præter
Rabbinos persuasum fuit, penes Synedrium Magnum τὸ Κύριον in Republica Hebraeorum ste-
tisse. Ut assertum hoc stabiliant, duo in primis loca ex Sacris afferunt, quo-

§. 27. Ut breviores simus quia jam §. 19. & 20. ex parte iis satisfa-

§. 28. Dein Autores citati sibi ipsis contrariantur. Josephum loco citato non aeque accurate locutum esse, ac supra, quilibet videt. Sigonius loco citato capite 5. it. Arnisaeus loco citato numero 18. propria vineta caedunt. Reliqui, quia Rabbinis nimium tribuunt, falluntur, cum in loco citato de allatis, altum plane sit silentium.

§. 29. Alter locus contra ipsos potius adversarios militat. Non urgebo jam, nec assessorum numerum, nec eorum qualitatem, nec reliqua Synedrii Magni requisita eidem respondere, sed hoc tantum regero: ne inter ipsos quidem constare, quando, vel ubi, id ipsum coeperit! Hinc plerique doctorum, missis Rabbinorum commentis, tempore Mosis, Josuae & Judicum nullum plane Synedrii Magni vestigium agnoscunt, huic ipsi loco allegato confisi, quod versu 8. Isräelitae jubentur ascendere ad locum, quem Deus illis elegerit, quod versu 10. repetitur, claro indicio, Judicium tale, occupata demum Palaestina, esse instituendum. Quo supposito, objectiones omnes in fumum abeunt. Plura non addam, sed Benevolum Lectorem ad *Johannes Vorstii Dissertatione de Synedrio Conringii disputatio laudata Sectione 24. B. D. Wendeleri Disputatio de Magno Judaico Synedrio & inprimis Johannes Seldeni, tres integros libros de Synedriis, inspecie Libro II. capitibus 15, 16. remitto*, qui intricatam hanc materiam prolixe & uberius ventilant.

§. 30. *Quare firmo adhuc talo nostra stat assertio: nimirum, DEUM Ter Optimum Maximum etsi Duces populo suo, Judicesque daret, Senatum etiam LXX. virorum sub Mose institueret; τὸ κύριον tamen in neutrum horum contulisse, ut queas vel formam aliquam Monarchicam sub Mose & Josua, vel Aristocraticam sub aliquo Synedrio; vel Regni speciem sub Judicibus statuere; sed ipsissimum Deum, sicut omnia Majestatis jura solus, ut audivimus, usurpavit; ita etiam ipsam Majestatem sibi soli reservasse: donec tandem, mutata hac sanctissima Reipublicae forma THEOCRATIA, populoque Regem hunc suum rejiciente, summam illam potestatem, volens quidem, sed magna cum indignatione, in Saulem & Successores ejus, postea transferret. Quorum ipsum quoque κύριον peculiari Disputatione Deo dante, reservabimus.*

And consequently, the <term>to Kyrion</term> <gloss>the Lordship</gloss> could reside with no one, neither a Magistrate nor a Synedrium. The minor premise is confirmed from those very Sacred passages where the adversaries sought their defense, concerning which we will speak shortly.

§. 21. Finally, in a few words against Democracy, since this does not come into controversy as much, we conclude thus:

> In any Republic where supreme power is not with the people, in that place Democracy cannot have a place. But in the Hebrew Republic, etc. The major premise is certain from the definition of Democracy. The minor premise is proven because in that Republic it was necessary to submit the people to supreme power absolutely without any limitation, and thus it behaved merely passively.

§. 22. With these premises, those arrows, already foreseen, will do less harm, and that whole weight of contrary arguments will collapse of its own accord, with which the patrons of Monocracy, such as **Josephus** in *Antiquities* Book XX, c. 8, **Tholosanus** in *De Republica* Book V, c. 3, n. 15, and **Bellarmine** in *De Romano Pontifice* Book V, c. 2, rise up against us, contending that there was either a true Monarchy under Moses and Joshua, or, according to **Bodin** in *De Republica* Book VI, c. 4, **Bertram** in *De Republica Hebraeorum* c. 5, and **Zepper** in *Politica Judaeorum* Book III, c. 5, at the very least a species of Kingdom. Hence, besides Moses, they also ascribe royal power to Joshua and certain leaders, because they are often called Kings and princes in Sacred Letters, and because it is read in the book of Judges that there was no King in Israel.

§. 23. But I respond: 1. In the same sense that Moses is called a King in the cited place, the Judges and leaders are also called Kings more than once. But it has already been said in the preceding that Scripture perhaps attributes the title itself to them not properly but improperly. For if the word of a King is taken properly, as **Aristotle** takes it in *Politics* Book III, c. 16, for one who does everything according to his own will, then certainly it cannot be ascribed to them. For it is argued thus: 2. He who does nothing by his own discretion, but does everything in the administration of the Republic by the counsel of another, is not endowed with supreme power. But Moses, Joshua, and the <term>hegemones</term> <gloss>leaders</gloss>, etc., in the Hebrew Republic did everything by the counsel of God. Therefore. And consequently, they are not to be called Kings or Monarchs. The major premise is from the philosopher in the cited place, who says: "He who is called a king according to law does not constitute a species of government," by which he himself denies that such improperly called kings constitute a proper species of royal government. The minor premise is demonstrated from the Sacred texts in the preceding §. 19. Meanwhile, it follows of its own accord that Moses, Joshua, and the Judges, speaking accurately, were Magistrates properly so-called, and with them resided whatever faculty there was, both of judging and especially of commanding.

How many days in this month are critical, how many judicial, and how many provocative, a learned physician can easily collect. These are the things which Galen hands down concerning the months.

### The Fourteenth Enunciation.

The Moon, traversing the 360 parts of the zodiac, forms 27 angles in them, in which it exercises most powerful forces. Therefore, the Sun and the other planets act by their own traversals.

<margin>On the traversals of the seven planets.</margin>
<note>A decorative floral initial S.</note>
**S**aturn traverses its orbit in 30 years; Jupiter in 12 years; Mars in two; the Sun in 365 days and approximately 6 hours; Venus and Mercury in approximately the same; the Moon in 27 days and 8 hours, in which, as we have said, it describes 16 sides in its traversals, which each one is by itself, as we have said, 27 minutes and 500 <note>units</note>, which multiplied sixteen times renders 360 parts.

<margin>16 sides, and sides, and how many are the powers of the angles.</margin>
Therefore, while the Moon is in a part chosen from the first, it is in a similar, diametric, or opposite part; therefore, situated in that part, it would exercise powers equal to the diameter. However, it exercises favorable and beneficial powers if it is constituted with good affections, but truly maleficent ones when it is vexed by more afflictive ones. Likewise, the Moon in the 90th part from the first is in the left square; therefore, situated there, it exercises powers equal to the square diameter. And these, indeed, <note>it does</note> according to the constitution and the affections or afflictions. The Moon in the 45th part exercises semi-tetragon powers, for 45 parts are half of a square, where it is said to exercise beneficial or maleficent powers according to the affections and constitutions. The Moon in the 67.5th part still exercises halved semi-tetragon powers, for 45 and 30 minutes are half of a semi-tetragon, where it imparts powers to us based on the affection or affliction. By a similar ratio, it can be collected in the other angles; for according to the ratio of the configurations and their very affections and constitutions, it exercises sometimes beneficial, sometimes maleficent powers. The other planets do not exercise their powers otherwise in their traversals, but they do so more slowly, while the Moon does so more quickly.

### The Fifteenth Enunciation.

<margin>On the cause of the crisis. And the virtue: neither the humors, nor both, are the causes of the crisis.</margin>
**T**he governing virtue of the body and the Moon in the diseases themselves, with the powers enumerated, are the first efficient, good causes of the crisis. The provocation of humors and the constitution of the Moon through the signs are the contrary; conversely, the first evil efficient causes are the provoking humor and the constitution of the Moon, while the Moon and the virtue are the instrumental ones.

<note>A decorative initial I containing a stylized human figure.</note>
**I**n illness, the virtue used to fight with the humor; therefore, when the virtue overcame, the crisis was good and pleasant for the sick person. Where, on the contrary, the harmful humor overcame, the crisis was pernicious and threatening. Therefore, neither can the virtue alone be the cause of a salutary crisis, for it would always be salutary; nor, conversely, can the threatening humor alone, for the crisis would always be ruinous, since the virtue attempts to save, and the humor attempts to kill. Wherefore, neither will both be causes and effectors at the same time, for no action arises from equal rights, as physicians testify. Therefore, it is necessary that the virtue needs the help of another; wise men conjectured this to be the Moon itself, for the reason that, more quickly than the others,

<column-break/>

<margin>Galen.</margin>
Second, because it is the first <note>influence</note> for us. Third, because it is the mover and inciter of humidity. Fourth, because it happens to the diseases themselves through the enumerated days more than others. For which reason Galen rightly and wisely deems it and the lunar causes to be the primary and especially efficient causes of a good and salutary crisis. These are either useful, constituting the cause as a whole, or auxiliary, which is enough for physicians; at that time when the virtue alone and the Moon alone, neither is sufficient, for they are too blind and general. Others are instrumental and (so to speak) *sine qua non* <gloss>without which not</gloss>, such as the provoking humor and the beneficial celestial constitution of the Moon. For unless the humor provoked, the virtue would not enter the battle; unless the Moon were placed in a good and beneficial constitution, by which it favors the virtue itself,

<margin>The lunar virtue is blind.</margin>
the crisis would not be salutary. Therefore, the two primary and first efficient causes of a salutary crisis are the virtue itself and the Moon itself; those which are instrumental are the beneficial constitution of the Moon and the provoking humor. For from these four, a salutary crisis arises, sometimes total, sometimes partial. Conversely, there are again four causes of a ruinous crisis (as we have said), one primary and especially efficient, such as the provoking humor, and the maleficent celestial constitution of the Moon; yet not these alone, for an outcome does not always arise from these alone. Therefore, there are two instrumental ones: the weakness of the virtue itself and the Moon itself. The Moon is indeed the general <note>cause</note>, without which nothing would happen; the weakness of the virtue is the special <note>cause</note>. For from these four, a ruinous or pernicious crisis arises, either in whole or in part.

But what that beneficial celestial <note>constitution</note> is, whether total or partial, or what that maleficent one is—which physicians ignorant of celestial matters said to be the opposition of a sign or a disease-specific <term>idiotropia</term> <gloss>peculiar turning/affinity</gloss>—for instance, let the disease be choleric while the Moon holds Aries, since Aries is a choleric sign, namely, hot and dry; it favors the choleric disease, yet it opposes the virtue. Conversely, when the Moon has arrived in Cancer, it opposes the disease due to the <term>idiotropia</term> <gloss>affinity</gloss> of the signs, because Cancer is cold and humid; but it contributes to the virtue. But peace to the good <note>men</note>, these things are childish.

<margin>First position.</margin>
<margin>Refutation.</margin>
First, because if a phlegmatic disease attacked us while the Moon held Aries, it would always favor the virtue at that time; and while it was in Cancer, it would favor the disease. Observation teaches the contrary of this, for often a salutary crisis has occurred where there is no agreement with the sign, neither of the virtue nor of the disease.

<margin>Beneficial and maleficent lunar constitution.</margin>
Second, it is not always the case that while the Moon runs through cold and humid signs, the air changes to cold and humid, unless other planets have arrived. Wherefore, it is worthy of reflection that a beneficial celestial constitution of the Moon always favors the virtue by hidden laws; for it changes the air to beneficial and hidden qualities, from which the virtue is strengthened and becomes superior. A maleficent constitution, however, changes the air to maleficent powers, from which the virtue itself is crushed, prostrated, and destroyed. Nor is this constitution beneficial because it is hot or cold or of any such <note>quality</note>, nor does that one <note>cause harm</note> because it is dry or humid or such; but rather they benefit or kill, which are these and that. A beneficial celestial constitution of the Moon is for it to behave well with the planets, in good places, in good limits, and with other beneficial affections, as we shall reveal later; conversely, the maleficent is when the Moon is marked by bad <note>things</note>, with bad planets, in bad limits, and is placed in other things of that kind. Archigenes .xxi. ut igitur hos summos medicine observatores conciliaret: e die ipso horam unam circiter sustulit: et inde hebdomadas edit: equam et mensem: sic namque abyciedo e die ipso horam: uterque suis dinumerationibus verum autumant. Secundo quod luna humoribus ipsis praesidet viribus duplicibus utpote communibus sibi et soli hoc est per lumen: quod commune utriusque est: et viribus et propriis bene est: per hoc quod ipsa suum peragrando circulum dum ipsa .xv. angulos (quos diximus) format: miras emittit nobis alterationes: hic mensis utriusque particeps esse debet. Quot dies hoc in mense sint decretorii: quot iudiciarii: quot ve provocatorii: doctus medicus facile colligere potest. Haec sunt quae Galenus de mensibus tradit.

### Enuntiatum decimumquartum.

luna igitur dum est in parte a prima electa: est in parte simili diametra sive opposita: idcirco illa in parte constituta / vires haequales diametrum exerceret: exercet autem vires favorabiles atque beneficas: si bonis affectibus erit constituta: maleficas vero ubi afflictioribus erit lacessita. luna itidem in parte a prima .xc. in parte prima est quadrangula sinistra: idcirco ibi constituta / vires exercet haequales diametrum quadrangulum: et has quidem pro constitutione ac affectionibus afflictioribusve: luna in parte .xlv. et pro collocata / vires exercet semitetragonas. nam .xlv. partes sunt quadranguli dimidia: ubi pro affectionibus ac constitutionibus vires beneficas maleficas ve exercere perhibet: luna in parte et pro .lxvij. et dimidia / vires exercet adhuc dimidiatas semitetragonas. nam .xlv. et minutie .xxx. sunt dimidium semitetragoni / ubi filii ratione pro affectione afflictione ve vires nobis immittit. Simili ratione caeteris in angulis colligi potest: pro ratione enim configurationum proque affectionibus ac constitutionibus ipsis: vires exercet interdum beneficas interdum maleficas: non aliter caeteri planetae suis in peragrationibus vires exercent: sed illi tardius: luna celerius re hac agant.

### Enuntiatum decimumquintum.

<margin>De causa crisis. Atque virtus: neque humorum: neque ambo causae sunt crisis.</margin>
**V**irtus corporis regitiva et luna morbis ipsis potestates enumeratis sunt primae efficiariae bonae crisis causae: humorum provocatio et lunae constitutio per signa / contrariae: contra vero malae crisis primae afficiariae causae sunt humorum provocans / ac lunae constitutio: luna hoc et virtus instirariae.

<image-desc size="small" type="decorative" significance="low">Decorative initial I with a stylized human figure or face.</image-desc>
**I**psa in aegrotatione pugnabat virtus cum humore inde cuius virtus superaverat: crisis erat bona ac aegroto iocunda: ubi contra humorum nocens / exuperabat crisis perniciosa ac minax erat: igitur nec virtus sola esse potest salutifere crisis causa: nam semper salutifera: nec contra humorum minax solus / nam semper crisis esset eritiosa: siquidem virtus servare: humor pernecare attentat. Quare nec ambo causae erunt simul atque effectrices: equis namque iuribus nulla exoritur actio / ut physici testantur: igitur oportet ut virtus alteri egeat auxilio: hoc sapientes luna ipsam coniectarunt / pro eo quod caeterorum citius

<margin>Galenus.</margin>
Secundo quod nobis prima. Tertio quod humiditatis motrix ac concitatrix. Quarto quod plus aliis morbis ipsis per dies enumeratis puenit: qua e re bene et sapide Galeno virtute ipsam et lunae causas primas et precipue effectrices autumat bonae et salutiferae crisis. sunt autem hae vel utiles causam una integra constituentes: vel sub ministrae: quod medicis sat est: tunc cum sola virtus ipsa / solasque luna neque ambe sufficiunt: sunt namque caecae nimis generales: generales aliae instrumentariae: ac (ut ita loquar) sine qua non: ut humor provocans: et celestis lune benefica constitutio: nisi enim humor provocaret: virtus praelium non adiret: nisi que luna bona ac benefica constitutione collocata esset: qua ipsi virtuti faveat.

<margin>Luna causa crisis.</margin>
<margin>Luna virtus caeca.</margin>
Crisis non esset salutifera: salutiferi igitur crisis duae precipue et primae effectrices causae sunt: virtus ipsa ac luna ipsa: quae vero instrumentarie / benefica lune constitutio et humor provocans. His enim ex quattuor / crisis salutifera interdum tota interdum partilis exoritur: eritiosae vero crisis quattuor rursus sunt causae (ut diximus) una prima ac precipue efficiarie ut humor provocans: et malefica celestis lune constitutio: non tamem solum haec. nam non semper ex his solis mox et exitum exoritur: idcirco instrumentarie sunt due virtutis ipsius imbecillitas et luna ipsa. luna quidem generalis: sine qua nihil fieret. imbecillitas virtutis specialis. bisce namque quattuor exitium seu pernitiosa exoritur crisis vel tota vel in parte. 

<margin>Concursus humorum et celi constitutorio.</margin>
<margin>Eritiosae crisis causa.</margin>
Quid autem sit ista benefica celestis vel tota vel in parte. Quid autem sit ista benefica celestis vel tota vel tio quod ve malefica: quod medici rerum celestium ignari / dixerunt esse signi adversam vel uveniente morbis idiotropiaz: verbi causa sit morbus cholericus luna tenente arietem / quoniam aries signum sit cholericum calidum videlicet siccum: favet morbo cholerico / adversat tamem virtuti. Contra quom luna pertuenerit in cancrum. nam tunc adversatur morbo ex signis idiotropia: quia cancer frigidus est et humidus: sed virtuti confert: sed pace bonum hinc puerilia sunt. 

<margin>Quid benefica celi constitutio.</margin>
<margin>Prima positio.</margin>
<margin>Impugnatio.</margin>
Primo quod si luna tenente arietem pituitosus invaserit nos morbus: semper faueret tunc virtuti: et dum in cancero esset faueret morbo huius contrarium docet obseruatio. nam sepicule crisis salutifera facta est: ubi nulla est cum signo convenientia / nec virtutis nec morbi. 

<margin>Benefica lune constitutio et malefica que.</margin>
Secundo non semper luna decurrente per frigida signa ac humida: aer mutatur ad frigidum humidumque: nisi et alii planetae uenerit. Quare est animi adversione dignum quod benefica celestis lune constitutio semper iuribus occultis virtuti favet: mutat enim aerem ad beneficas occultasque qualitates e quibus virtus pollet / ac superarior fit. Malefica vero constitutio aerem mutat ad maleficas vires / e quibus ipsa virtus eliditur / prosternitur / ac dirimitur: nec benefica. Haec constitutio prodest / qua calida sive frigida sive quovis talis: nec illa malefica hoc stat quod sicca aut humida aut talis: sed potius prosunt aut pernecant: quae haec ac ipsa. Est autem lune celestis benefica constitutio bene se cum planetis habere / bonis in locis bonis in finibus caeterisque beneficiis affectionibus / ut posterius aperiemus: malefica contra est quando luna malis insignis / malis cum planetis / malis in finibus caeteris id genus collocata sit: quae sint hae bonae malae ve affectiones / suo loco aperiet.

But lest what I, the seer, augur should vanish, may the Aeneian mother <note>Venus</note> preside over your bed.

These things for you, O GENEROUS HERO, while the hoped-for day brings the marriage torches, while your wife is led to you—royal offspring, famous, beautiful, chaste, neither rude in talent nor lacking true endowment—GENTIUS, having experienced you recently as a friend to the Muses and honoring you because of the Muses and eloquent tongues with the affection of a rejoicing mind, and wishing that love, with head veiled in laurel, might surround the bed and sustain the living fire in your hearts, and make it grow daily as much as the fresh shoots of the pine grow in the new spring. I stop: the dishes on the tables are steaming with feasts, and they leave the stomach barking with hunger near the words.

**Furthermore,** the possessor of a disputed thing is freed from the burden of providing security. <note>original: "(p) ..."</note>

### XXII.

**Thus,** faith is given to the defendant, even if he was previously seen as suspect, once he has provided a suitable surety or has provided caution in another of the aforementioned ways. <note>original: "(q) ..."</note>

### XXIII.

**In** a noxal action, the surety must present the defendant in the same case as it was when he stood surety for him. <note>original: "(r) ..."</note>

### XXIIII.

**With this** neglected, an action will be given against the surety, <note>original: "(s) ..."</note> and indeed also against him through whom it was stayed that one was not presented in court. <note>original: "(t) ..."</note>

### XXV.

**Hence,** the plaintiff, if he knows that the defendant is being hindered from being presented in court by his own slave, and, being able to prevent it, does not do so, can be repelled by an exception, <note>original: "(u) ..."</note> inasmuch as the laws prohibit anyone from taking advantage from his own deceit. <note>original: "(x) ..."</note>

**But** when both the promisor and the stipulator are weaving deceit so that the defendant is not presented in court, it is compensated in an equal manner. <note>original: "(y) ..."</note>
