Thirdly, the defender of Roman superstition brings <term>Hieronymus</term> <gloss>Jerome</gloss> into the battle line, commenting on chapter 2 of Jonah with these words: *as the heart is in the middle of a living creature, so hell is said to be in the middle of the earth.* He also praises <term>Irenaeus</term>, <term>Tertullianus</term> <gloss>Tertullian</gloss>, and <term>Nyssenus</term> <gloss>Gregory of Nyssa</gloss>, who move in this direction. But we have already warned that no protection should be sought in them, since they define and assert things that are uncertain and unknown to the Holy Scriptures. Even if we were to grant that Christ broke through to the center of the Earth; it would still burden the Roman Catholics to prove as absolute certainty that Hell is found there with those appendages, before any conclusion whatsoever can be reached about the Savior's descent according to their view. Moreover, we oppose battle line with battle line: namely, <term>Chrysostomus</term> <gloss>John Chrysostom</gloss> in Homily 44 on Matthew, and <term>Bernhardus</term> <gloss>Bernard of Clairvaux</gloss> in Sermon 1 on the Death of the Monk Humbert, who fight for our side.

*Pausanias* o) testifies that Thrace exhibits a likeness of Orpheus, in which wild beasts carved in marble and bronze surround him as he sings. And I am easily persuaded that this was his magic art, of which many accuse him; unless we prefer to oppose the more ancient usage of the word, by which, as we are taught by not a few writers p), the leaders of the Chaldaeans and Egyptians, who were in charge of directing sacrifices and ceremonies, came by the name of Magi. The same praised author reports that Orpheus q) "found the initiations of the gods, and purifications from unholy deeds, and cures for diseases, and turnings-away of divine resentments." *Herodotus* r) mentions Orphic rites, and *Caelius Rhodiginus* s) praises the oaks of Orpheus. But what does superstition not dare, the most effective mockery of human minds? The Thracians had seen a man who, although

> *remote from the region of the sky,*
> *approached the Gods with his mind, and what nature denied*
> *to human sight, he drank in with the eyes of the breast;*

therefore, they falsely judged, as did the people of Lycaonia: "the gods, having become like men, have descended to us," they decreed divine honors to the dead man, and, pressed by calamity, they do not blush to consult him about their outcome. For *Philostratus* t) left it on record that his head in Lesbos gave oracles to the Greeks, that Troy could not be taken without the arrows of Hercules; and Cyrus, consulting Orpheus about the outcome, brought back this response: "Mine, O Cyrus, are yours."

### VIII.

> A very difficult and noble question offers itself for discussion here, the decision of which has dragged the Doctors into diverse opinions. Does it hinder a stipulation if the promisor answers impersonally? And because we perceive the laws to favor the affirmative opinion more, we intrepidly decree that the negative [opinion], as being destitute of the authority of laws, must be exploded.

Let it be conceived, for example: "will it be given?" "it will be given," and so forth. And indeed, Bar., Iason, Zasius, and others think such a stipulation is not valid in *law "this stipulation" 38, §. "if anyone thus" 10, Digest on V. E.G. Among Christians, whoever has injured modesty by force, even in war, is subject to punishment everywhere. Just as the Hebrew master says of the Hebrews: *God wished that the camps of the Israelites be holy, not cast into whoredoms and other abominations, like the camps of the nations.* Among Christians, those captured in war do not become slaves: *because they had been, or ought to have been, more rightly instructed by the recommender of all charity, than that they could not be led away from the killing of miserable men, except by the concession of less cruelty.* These are the words of Grotius, explaining both of these further, J. B. 3.4, 19. and 3,7,9. By what pact Christians spare sacred places, however much they differ in their opinions, spare men on account of temples, abstain from the looting of cities, and the like, he explains the same nicely in book 3, ch. 12, n. 6 and 8.

A powerful leader and commander will be present for you,
He will give you the strength to overcome the perils of the uncertain war,
He lifted Constantine, of our British race,
To the summit of empire with great effort,
Who defeated four ill-starred tyrants in war,
Men who oppressed the worshippers of Christ with steel and flames,
While they forced them to burn incense to Idols.
You succeed Constantine in the British world;
Strive bravely, as he insisted bravely on his deeds;
Let not the praiseworthy desire for true praise grow faint,
Be certain to drive away the servile yoke from the worshippers of Christ,
Drive from your kingdom those whose only care, the wicked ones,
Is to serve Idols, and to burn incense at altars.
Nor fear the thunderer from the Capitoline rock,
Although he may cast himself into the black underworld,
He may cast mortal souls with vain effort,
With puffed-up trifles, but like bubbles of water,
Which suddenly vanish with the swift blast of the wind:
The almighty Father will cast him headlong into the underworld,
He who raises his crest to heaven with monstrous audacity,
And he will strike him with the true blow of an unfictionalized thunderbolt:
His only care is my former, now your, kingdoms,
That he may force them to serve profane Idols again,
And to pray before statues in the gentile manner,
To perfume altars with incense, and to fix kisses upon stones.
Therefore, by the lord of heaven and the parent of things,
Who gave you the vital airs and my scepters,
I adjure you, see that the foundations of true religion,
Which I placed in the kingdom, remain firm:
See that you finish the work, which I began with favorable divinity,
For whose obedience I underwent so many harsh perils,
And for whose obedience I overcame so many harsh perils:

Their office was mostly occupied with the Treasury, namely to receive and spend public money, to sell at a fair price spoils brought into the city, to open a lodging in the public house built outside the walls for legates of foreigners or allied Kings and provide them with hospitality, to preserve military standards (for they were made of gold or silver; indeed they did not use sails) in the Treasury, to register certain provincial revenues into the public accounts, to auction off uncertain ones to the publicans, and other such matters, on which <term>Rosinus</term> book VII, chapter 32; <term>Alexander ab Alexandro</term> *Genial Days* book II, chapter 2; <term>Hugo Grotius</term> book III *On the Law of War and Peace* chapter 6, section 16; and others speak more fully. However, for all other magistrates, a certain age was predetermined by the Romans, at which it was permitted for them to seek office. We find that same time observed in the Quaestorship, which we, with <term>Cicero</term> in his *Orations against Verres* and <term>Casaubon</term> on <term>Spartianus</term>'s *Hadrian*, page 7, assign to the twenty-fifth year of age. And indeed, Rome saw two Quaestors in the beginning, until later, because of so many and such great affairs, the number was doubled and in the time of <term>Julius</term> increased to four hundred in the City and the provinces; as <term>Plutarch</term> has it in the *Life of Publicola*, page 59; <term>Dio</term> in the year of the city 708, book XLIII, page 237; and <term>Alexander Neapolitanus</term> book II, chapter 2.

§. XI. We must proceed to the subject matter of the constituted Treasury, namely the revenues, which produced immense wealth when the people, the conqueror of nations, held the whole world; as <term>Julius Caesar Bulengerus</term> in his book *On Roman Revenues* and <term>Lipsius</term> in book II *On Roman Greatness* chapter 1 pursue at length. Thus, when <term>Nero</term> had decided to abolish revenues, the Senators restrained his impetus by teaching that the dissolution of the Empire would follow if the fruits by which the Republic is supported were diminished; for with the port duties removed, it was a consequence that the abolition of tributes would be demanded (<term>Tacitus</term> book XIII *Annals*). They are called <term>vectigalia</term> <gloss>revenues/taxes</gloss> from *vectura* <gloss>carrying/transport</gloss>, because, according to <term>Bodin</term>, the most ancient and common way of increasing the Treasury is to impose a tax on goods that are imported or exported.

§. XII. The word <term>vectigal</term> is sometimes taken more broadly for any emolument that flows to the Treasury, in such a way that it also includes under itself tribute and stipend, as <term>Gædd</term> on law 13 and law 49 of the Digest on the Signification of Words, and <term>Arnisaeus</term> in book III *On the Law of Majesty* chapter 7, number 5, among others, teach. Sometimes it is taken more strictly, insofar as it is a tax provided from those things that are imported or exported; in which sense it is distinguished from tribute and stipend.

Coronidis loco potiores Effectus Confraternitatis extremis saltem labris degustandi erunt. Primarius isque nobilior est, quod inducat Jus adgnationis Civilis. **XLVI.** Furthermore, the nature of the Confraternity bids one to explore the consent of the previous Confratres <gloss>fellow brothers</gloss>, if any exist, lest their right, which they have acquired in a certain hope of succession, be subverted without their knowledge and against their will, as Master Bechmann correctly warns in his *Discourse*, chapter 3, folio 1, paragraph 1.

**XLVII.** Finally, it will be advisable not to omit the consent of the subjects, *the gathered Land-Estates*, especially if a powerful province is in question, whose inhabitants, having taken up arms, are able to defend themselves against a lord unknown to them and intruded upon them against their will. Compare the Renewal of the Saxon-Hessian Confraternity of the year 1555 in Limnaeus, *Public Law* 4, 8, 162, folio 206, and Bechmann in the said place.

**XLIIX.** So much for the natural elements after the manner of the institution: let us touch upon the accidental elements of the Confraternity, that is, those which can be absent while the substance and nature of the thing are saved, and yet cannot be present unless the thing subsists. To this is referred, first, the solemnity of the Oath, which is performed either by the Confratres themselves to one another, or by their subjects to them, and is called the Homage of subjection, *Land-homage or hereditary duty*: concerning which compare George Ritter's elegant treatise. **XLVII.** Denique consultum erit, nec subditorum, der gesampten Land-Stände, consensum omittere; præsertim si de potenti provincia agitur, cujus incolæ armis correptis adversus ignotum sibique invitis obtrusum Dominum sese defendere valent. For when the infant made his first tracks with the soles of his feet,
He was seized by the love of the Clarian God <note>Apollo</note>,
Hardly mature, he strove to surpass his studies
By his own ascent of the high summits of Pindus:
And to quench his thirst with a draught of the Pegasean stream,
Which the hollow hoof of the Gorgonean horse <note>Pegasus</note> carved out.
And as soon as the learned band of the Muses saw this,
She stands, and turning to a smile, gives forth sounds from her mouth:
"The name of Hippocrene is not idly yours,
Since you drench your lips with its nectar in such a way.
Be prosperous in your virtue, boy, and do not spurn our
Divinities, for thus it is granted to travel the ethereal paths."
She had spoken: he drank the Clarian waters more with his mouth,
And performs his duties to the Muses with diligence.
Not yet did the first bloom of youth clothe his cheeks,
When he entered the famous Lycaean school of Tyrigeta:
Here, no ready opportunity was lacking for his ventures,
Here he strives to approach the Muses by the straight path.
In the study of languages he wears away the leisure of his tender life,
And rejoices to spend his days in noble art.
Hence, our new guest arrives at the learned Muses of Elitrum,
And fervently drinks the Clarian waters:
More sparing of sleep, he turns over in his hands and mind
The eloquent writings of the men whom Greece boasts.
While he seeks leisure, he is rolled into a thousand labors,
And sustains constantly new cares.
At night the weary plowman snatches light sleep,
And at night the sailor rests in the midst of the waters:
All animals on earth snatch sleep
At night; there is quiet for the winds and the Ionian sea:
But at night the soot of this black lamp is consumed,
While he renews the writings buried in decaying neglect.
Famous Aristotle, recalled from the Stygian underworld,
Often poured forth these sounds from a happy mouth:
"O Philyra, cherish the young man and hold him reverently,
He who has gained his name from the Gorgonean horse."

Movement <term>katá tópon kínēsis</term> <gloss>motion according to place</gloss> is a faculty of the sentient soul, by which any part of an animal's body may be moved from one place to another.

*Movement usually follows Appetite, which is granted even to animals. For if an animal could not move itself from place to place, Appetite would have been given to the animal in vain by nature, which nevertheless <term>mēte mēden poiei matēn mēte apoleipei tōn anangkaiōn</term> <gloss>does nothing in vain, nor does it fail in necessary things</gloss>, Aristotle, On the Soul, book 3, chapter 9, text 44. By movement here in the definition, we do not understand the movement of augmentation, by which both plants and animals grow and increase, nor of diminution, by which they decrease and diminish, nor of respiration, by which the lung draws in and expels air, nor violent movement, as when a body is propelled by force, or when the teeth of one suffering from fever chatter in the cold, but rather animal movement, by which an animal can not only move particular or peculiar limbs, but can also advance with its whole body from one place to another, which they commonly call <term>poreutikēn kínēsin</term> <gloss>progressive motion</gloss>. Hence this faculty is called not only Motive, but Locomotive, so that it may be distinguished from appetite, which is likewise a certain motive faculty. For the requirements necessary for movement, see Sennert in book 7 of the Epitome of the Science of Nature.*

At gravioribus turbis agitata ac concussa est *Hungaria*, postquam post *Andrea III.* fatum, exteros habere Reges cœpit: quales fuere *Bohemi*, *Bavari*, *Andegavenses*, *Luxenburgenses*, et tandem *Austriaci*, qui hodie regnant. Tantas enim Principum suorum mutationes quum subiret regio, multis magnisque morbis convelli eam, necessum erat: dum non solùm pro genio dominorum dispensati mores legesque, sed et novis Regibus perpetui tumultus, et indigenarum odia objectata, Rempublicam miserè affligerent. Et quanquam *Iohannes Huniades*, ejusque filius *Matthias Corvinus Rex*, quum inter exterorum imperium fluctuaret *Hungaria*, victricibus armis maximum in Europa nomen Hungarorum regnumque facerent, mox tamen tanta amplitudo collapsa est, postquam pudendô Christianis bellô Constantinopolim occupavit *Muhammedes*, et omnibus repagulis ruptis in *Hungariam* omnes impetus infudit.

Inter quos principem obtinent locum Archiepiscopi et Episcopi, quorum fortuna olim ampla, et divitiis pollens, quum nondum Turca in plurimorum profupisset exitium, aut novae religioni addicti opima eorum patrimonia carpsissent. Inde Civitates et Urbes sunt, quarum ante unum et alterum seculum magna erat potentia : nunc plerarumque vires per bellum Turcicum attritae : plurimae etiam suis consepultae ruderibus, vetustatem magis, quam vires jactare possunt.

Clearly, this allowance must be given to German writers, that while they imagine their Emperors have come into the possession of the Roman Empire, they ambitiously constrain not only the Hungarians, but also the Armenians, Cypriots, Danes, Swedes, Poles, Italians, French, and the peoples living as far as the icy Ocean within the boundaries of their Empire.

XXIX. But the falling authority of the Hungarian Kingdom was bolstered by Geza II, who had the surname of the Great: who restored with great virtue the province torn by internal discord and worn down by German arms. Thence Ladislas, his brother, takes possession of the empire, whom Roman Pontiffs later admitted into the number of the Saints, distinguished for his piety. He added Dalmatia and Croatia to the kingdom after he had restored those provinces by arms to his sister, who had married Zelomirus, King of Dalmatia, and dying, had bequeathed the ancient kingdom to her brother. Thence reigned *Coloman*, son of *Geza*: after him *Coloman, Stephen II, Bela II, Geza III, Stephen III, Ladislas II, Stephen IV, Bela III, Emeric, Ladislas III, Andrew II, Bela IV, Stephen V, Ladislas IV, Andrew III*: whom for the most part perpetual discord, the common evil of the royal family, clashed among themselves; with the Nobles aiding the insane ambition of the Princes, who, turbulent by nature and greedy for new things, were eager to change their loyalty for their own ruin. But the almost supreme destruction to the kingdom was brought by the incursion of the Tatars, who under *Bela IV* crossed into Hungary with an immense multitude, and devastated everything in a wretched manner with iron and fire. This calamity the Hungarians ascribe to their own overconfidence, too ignorant that *No one is oppressed more quickly than he who fears nothing*.

<margin>Idem decade II. libro IX.</margin>
XXX. The last of the Kings of Hungary from the family of Saint Stephen was *Andrew III*, who died in the year 1301 without male offspring. Under him the Republic underwent the greatest change and took on another form, while the King, new to reigning or weary of it, broke royal dominance and, following the example of the German Caesars, surrounded the Nobles with great privileges. From then on, the people began to raise themselves to liberty, to draw a part of the empire to themselves, to expedite the most important affairs of the kingdom in the Diets, to extend the authority of the Palatine: in short, to place such laws around the reigning King that he would bind himself by oath to hold as ratified and sacred the privileges which King *Andrew III* had granted to the people. VIII. We must think of things acting intentionally in a very different way than of those that operate physically. It penetrates everything with its subtle efficacy, and there is nothing at all that its power does not reach. It explores substances and accidents; it knows created and uncreated things; it perceives not only those things that are, but also those that are not, or indeed cannot even be. What then? Baldus, Bertachinus, Petrus Nicolaus Mozzius, and Zasius concede this only in the case where it has been initiated with a Prince. But it is of strict law according to Alvarotto, Matthaeus de Afflictis, Caccialupo, Hanneton, Curtius Junior, Clarus, Schraderus, Rosenthal, Intrighiolus, Arumaeus, and Setserus. To us, the arguments of Lord Ludwell—who departs here from the common opinion and does not acknowledge any feudal contract distinct from other contracts and businesses—do not seem entirely dismissible.

## V.

Lord Ludwell, Vulteius, Gothofredus Antonius, Borcholt, Gaeddaeus, Schneidwin, Contius, Wilhelmus Fornerius, Sonsbecius, and Niellius refer succession to the modes of acquiring a Feud. Lord Carpzovius, Suevius, Hunnius, Rittershusius, Finckelthusius, and Sculzius deny this, wishing it to pertain to the modes of constituting. Lord Struvius thinks it is a mode of neither constituting nor acquiring, as he refers those only to a new Feud. We shall defend the opinion of the former, which we are persuaded also accords with the reason of the law.

## VI.

Schraderus and Gyphanius write that a Feud is constituted by prescription. Less correctly. For prescription does not claim a place among the modes of constituting, but rather of acquiring a Feud, as Lord Ludwell and Lord Snobelius rightly warn after Vulteius and others.

### XVII.

Therefore, wisdom properly so-called is concerned with clearly divine things, and excels all other intellectual habits by far, but especially Prudence, to which others attribute the highest place, just as much as divine things excel human ones: And therefore they are not the same habits.

### XVIII.

For all would say that the wise man is the same, but the prudent man is different. If we also wished to ascribe the things with which Prudence is concerned to Wisdom, there would be many species of Wisdom, just as there are of Prudence, which is nevertheless absurd. Then, we attribute wisdom to many whom we consider lacking in Prudence. Wherefore, when they see Anaxagoras and Thales of Miletus ignorant of what is advantageous to themselves, and know things that are superfluous, wonderful, difficult, and divine, they say they are wise, but not prudent.

### XIX.

Wherefore Prudence is concerned with those things that fall under deliberation, whence the prudent man is also named deliberative. But Wisdom is concerned with the divine things we know. Then also, since Wisdom is only of universal things, Prudence is also of particular things. Hence it happens that many unskilled persons, taught by experience, are considered more prudent than those who are learned and scientific.

### LVI.

Food and drink should be moderate; food should incline toward dryness, be of good juice, easy to digest, pure, simple, and sparse; it should not be taken unless the stomach is urgent and the previous residues have been excreted. Dinner should be more frugal than lunch. Roasted things are more beneficial than boiled ones, and they should not be seasoned too much. Drink should be medicated, or thin, well-purified beer, or water for those who are thinner. It must be highly avoided if made colder by ice or saltpeter. One should not drink unless some solid food has been ingested. Not all use of wine is to be proscribed, however, for in those whose stomach is weakened, whose natural heat is dissolved, in delicate natures whose body is enervated, and in those with an excess of cold humors, the drinking of wine is necessary. Reddish, well-purified, pure, not very watery, not sulfurous, and not containing much tartar or earthy salt wines are praised; one must abstain entirely from sweet wine. Rhenish, Rhaetian, and <term>Nicrina</term> <gloss>wines from the Necker region</gloss> are praised, as are clear and year-old wines; wine of absinthe, sage wine, wine of blessed thistle, and of betony.

### LVII.

In sleep and vigils, moderation should also be maintained; although vigils dry the body, they also inflame it; midday sleep is to be avoided. If one has spent a sleepless night, one may sleep a little at midday, not immediately after food, but at least after an hour; nor should one sleep immediately after dinner, even if it is frugal. Movement should also be moderate; exercises are beneficial, but not violent, nor should one ride on horseback. Exercises should be carried out until the beginning of sweat, and they should precede food, and be performed at least twice a week. Affects of the mind, especially anger and sadness, must be restrained by the bridle of prudence, for they easily lead from a natural to a preternatural state. Galen, Book 3 of the *Art of Medicine*, text 16. Venus should be most moderate.

### LVIII.

The bowels should also perform their duty daily; if not, they must be aided by art, by means of raisins without seeds, or by dishes made from beet, spinach, cabbage, oil, and salt. Butter with sugar is the medicine of the elderly for softening the bowels. Take the root of parsley, cook it well, add fresh butter and sugar; let a draught of this broth be taken before lunch.

### §. XIII.

And indeed, as far as temples are concerned, they were generally erected in honor of Kings and Princes, as they were the ones given a greater opportunity to promote public safety. It is said that the Babylonians first built a temple to the monarch Belus, and treated him with divine honors before the gods, which temple PLINY, lib. VI, H.N., cap. 26, reports to have lasted in his own time. See PAUSANIAS in *Attica*, GYRALDUS, *Syntagma II, HISTORY OF THE GODS*, p. 180, see CHRISTOPH MATTHIAE in *Historical Theater*, p. 22. Thus, Dio records that temples were founded at Nicaea for Gaius Julius Caesar, the first of the Roman Monarchs, and also for Augustus, the successor of Julius, at Pergamon. Josephus likewise handed down to memory that a temple was built for that same Augustus by Herod. For, having received a large part of his kingdom from Augustus, Herod built a magnificent temple in honor of his benefactor <note>original: "Evergetae"</note> at the springs of the Jordan. See CALVISIUS, *CHRONOLOGICAL WORK*, p. 281, 285.

### §. XIV.

But it is clear from histories that temples were erected not only to Kings and Princes, but also to others (though by Christians, not heathens, and for a different end and manner). For those temples were built for Julius Caesar and Octavian Augustus so that they could be treated with divine worship, just as it was nothing new for the Gentiles to refer Kings or Queens into the number of the Gods. See BERNEGG, JUSTIN, lib. XIV, c. 1, & lib. XVIII, c. 6. But those temples about which we are speaking here (for we are speaking of those which have been dedicated and preserved by Christians to certain individuals; otherwise, it is known from Trogus that after the death of Pythagoras, a temple was made from his house and he was worshiped as a God) were constructed primarily in honor and glory of God, as their authors profess, and then in recollection and memory of certain pious and good men. This is evident from temples built and dedicated to Martyrs. See Calvisius, l.c., p. 479, 484.

->## SIXTH ASSERTION.<-

The form of a coin is seen in the public value, which distinguishes currency from metal and raw mass. Value, understood generally, encompasses three essential requirements: Weight, Character, and Assessment, which carry before them the goodness of the material, the truth of the weight, and the justice of the assessment. The weight of a coin forged from gold or silver must be certain and legitimate, and thus as much in the coin as in the raw mass, having deducted the costs of labor *a*. The character must express the image or insignia of the Prince and of him who by concession or privilege mints coins, so that the Insignia of Majesty and the Prince may be a witness of truth and justice in the currency *b*. The assessment is the price or public and fair estimation of a coin, not exceeding the goodness of the material and the quantity of the weight, lest otherwise the Prince offend the law of nations, to whom the coin belongs, and the communion of commerce *c*. Adjuncts of this form are the size of the coin, the round figure, the number of the value, the year, and the name of the currency *d*.

*a* For a coin, whatever it is, is entirely so by the benefit of the form impressed by public authority, by argument of the law <note>Julian, Digest on exhibiting, law 1. Digest on contracting a purchase.</note> For the form causes it to be called a coin, which was gold and silver, <note>law "who false" 19, verb "to form", Digest on the Cornelian Law on forgeries; law "elegantly" § "who rejects", Digest on the pledge action.</note> Weight, established by public faith and legitimately, excludes all fraud and imposture, and instructs the ignorant commoners regarding the truth, so that there was no need for the faith of a scale, to which we have today relapsed, <note>by argument of law 1, Digest on contracting a purchase, chapter "how much", extra on oaths; Coler. 4. on executive process, chapter 10, number 7. Duarenus 1. of disputes 6. add law 1 & 3, Code on the power of old coinage. Weight is written for gold coins and Thalers in the Monetary Ordinance of 1559. § "Ferner die gülden Müng." Imperial Recess of 1566. §.</note>

<note>Decorative red drop cap Q</note>Why have the nations raged: * & the people meditated on empty things?
The kings of the earth stood up, & the princes met together: * against the Lord, & against his Christ.
Let us break their bonds: * & let us cast away their yoke from us.
He who dwells in heaven, will laugh at them: * & the Lord will mock them.
Then he will speak to them in his anger: * & will trouble them in his fury.
But I am appointed king by him over Sion his holy mount: * preaching his commandment.
The Lord said to me: * you are my son, this day I have begotten you.
Ask of me, & I will give you the nations as your inheritance: * & the ends of the earth as your possession.
You will rule them with a rod of iron: * & you will shatter them like a potter's vessel.
And now O kings understand: * receive instruction you who judge the earth.
Serve the Lord with fear: * & exult to him with trembling.
Apprehend discipline, lest at some time the Lord be angry: * & you perish from the just way.
When his anger has enkindled in a short time: * blessed are all who trust in him.

<column-break/>

Psalm 6.
<note>Decorative red drop cap D</note>O Lord, do not argue with me in your fury: * nor in your anger chastise me.
Have mercy on me O Lord, for I am weak: * heal me O Lord, for my bones are troubled.
And my soul is troubled exceedingly: * but you O Lord how long?
Turn O Lord, & rescue my soul: * save me for the sake of your mercy.
For there is no one in death who is mindful of you: * moreover in hell who will confess to you?
I have labored in my groaning, I will wash my bed every night: * I will water my couch with my tears.
My eye is troubled by fury: * I have grown old among all my enemies.
Depart from me all you who work iniquity: * for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping.
The Lord has heard my supplication: * the Lord has received my prayer.
May all my enemies be ashamed & troubled exceedingly: * may they be turned back & be ashamed very quickly.

— V —

Phantasie allein vergegenwärtigt sich die einzelnen Akte des Dramas, welches sich in der Seele der Volksmassen abspielte, als sie zwischen Ormuzd und der Trinität hin- und herschwankten. Wir kennen nur das Ergebnis des Kampfes: der Mithriacismus wurde besiegt, und zweifellos mußte er es werden. Jedoch ist seine Niederlage nicht ausschließlich der Überlegenheit der evangelischen Moral oder der apostolischen Predigt gegenüber der Lehre der Mysterien zuzuschreiben; er ist nicht lediglich deshalb zu Grunde gegangen, weil er von der ererbten Last einer überlebten Vergangenheit zu Boden gedrückt wurde, sondern auch, weil seine Liturgie und seine Theologie zu asiatisch geblieben war, als daß der römische Geist sie ohne Widerstreben hätte acceptieren können. Umgekehrt blieb ebenderselbe Kampf, der zu gleicher Zeit in Irân zwischen den beiden Rivalen entbrannt war, für die Christen ohne Erfolg, wonicht ohne Ehre, und in den Staaten der Sassaniden ließ sich der Zoroastrismus niemals ernstlich antasten.

Aber die Niederlage Mithras bedeutete nicht das Ende seiner Macht. Er hatte die Geister für die Aufnahme eines neuen Glaubens vorbereitet, der — wie er selbst — von den Ufern des Euphrat kam und mit veränderter Taktik die Feindseligkeiten wieder eröffnete. Der Manichäismus erschien als sein Erbe und setzte sein Werk fort. Es war der letzte Ansturm, den Persien auf den Occident unternahm, und er war blutiger als die anderen — aber auch er sollte schließlich an der Widerstandsfähigkeit des christlichen Reiches scheitern.

Diese flüchtige Skizze wird, wie ich hoffe, die Wichtigkeit der Geschichte des Mithriacismus erkennen lassen. Ein Seitenschößling des alten mazdäischen Stammes, hat er in vieler Beziehung die Eigentümlichkeiten der alten Naturreligion der iranischen Stämme bewahrt und läßt uns vergleichsweise die so umstrittene Tragweite der avestischen Reformation besser verstehen. Anderseits hat er gewisse Lehren der Kirche wenn nicht inspiriert, so doch wenigstens

— VI —

präzisieren geholfen, wie die Vorstellungen von den höllischen Mächten und vom Ende der Welt. So trägt sein Aufkommen wie sein Untergang dazu bei, die Entstehungsgeschichte zweier großer Religionen aufzuhellen. In der Zeit seiner Vollkraft übte er einen nicht minder bemerkenswerten Einfluß auf die römische Gesellschaft und die römische Regierung aus. Vielleicht war Europa niemals, selbst nicht in der Epoche der mohammedanischen Invasionen, näher daran asiatisch zu werden als im 3. Jahrhundert unserer Ära; und es gab eine Zeit, in welcher der Cäsarismus anscheinend im Begriffe stand, sich in ein Khalifat zu verwandeln. Man hat oft auf die Ähnlichkeit hingewiesen, welche zwischen dem Hofe Diokletians und dem der Chosroës besteht. Der Sonnenkult und namentlich die mazdäischen Theorien machten die Ideen populär, auf welche die vergötterten Herrscher ihren monarchischen Absolutismus zu gründen suchten. Die rapide Ausbreitung der persischen Mysterien in allen Klassen der Bevölkerung diente in bewunderungswürdiger Weise dem politischen Ehrgeiz der Kaiser. Eine Sturmflut von iranischen und semitischen Gedanken brach herein, welche fast alles verschlang, was der griechische oder römische Geist in mühevoller Arbeit aufgebaut hatte; und als sich die Überschwemmung endlich verlief, da ließ sie im Volksbewußtsein einen starken Niederschlag von orientalischen Vorstellungen zurück, der niemals wieder völlig verschwand.

Ich glaube damit zur Genüge gezeigt zu haben, inwiefern der Gegenstand, den ich zu behandeln versuchte, eine eingehendere Untersuchung verdiente. Obwohl mich das Studium desselben in jeder Beziehung viel weiter geführt hat, als ich anfangs vorauszusehen vermochte, so sind mir die Arbeits- und Reisejahre doch nicht leid, welche ich ihm widmen mußte. Daß die Aufgabe, welche ich zu lösen hatte, eine schwierige war, stellte sich bald genug heraus. Einerseits wissen wir nicht, in welchem Grade das Avesta und die anderen heiligen Bücher der Parsen den Vor-

— IV —

is that the Iranian and the Greco-Latin worlds, separated as much by instinctive antipathy as by hereditary enmity, remained perpetually averse to mutual assimilation.

Nevertheless, the religion of the magi, which represents the most perfect creation of the Iranian genius, influenced Western culture three times. First, <term>Parsism</term> <gloss>Persian religion</gloss> exerted a very noticeable effect on the emergence of Judaism, and some of its main teachings spread through the mediation of Jewish colonies throughout the entire Mediterranean basin and were later adopted by Catholic orthodoxy.

<term>Mazdaism</term> acted more directly upon the European world of thought once Rome had conquered the eastern part of Asia Minor. From time immemorial, colonies of magi who had emigrated from Babylon lived there in quiet seclusion, and in these barbaric regions, by weaving their traditional beliefs with Hellenic ideas, they had in time developed a cult that was original despite its complex nature. At the beginning of our era, one saw it suddenly emerge from the darkness and advance simultaneously in the Danube and Rhine valleys and into the heart of Italy. The peoples of the Occident felt deeply that the Mazdean faith was superior to their old national religions, and the masses streamed to the altars of the foreign god. But the progress of the conqueror stalled as soon as he came into contact with Christianity. With astonishment, the two opponents perceived how similar they were in many respects, without being able to account for the causes of this similarity. And for this reason, they accused the spirit of lies of having wanted to parody their holy customs. The conflict between the two was inevitable and became a heated, irreconcilable struggle, for its stake was world domination. No one has reported to us its changing moments, and our

Dennoch hat die Religion der Magier, welche die vollendetste Schöpfung des iranischen Genius darstellt, dreimal die abendländische Kultur beeinfluſt. Zunächst übte der Parsismus eine sehr merkliche Wirkung auf die Entstehung des Judentums aus, und einige seiner Hauptlehren verbreiteten sich durch Vermittelung der jüdischen Kolonieen im ganzen Mittelmeerbecken und wurden später von der katholischen Orthodoxie übernommen.

Unmittelbarer wirkte der Mazdaismus auf die europäische Gedankenwelt, als Rom den Osten Kleinasiens erobert hatte. Seit unvordenklicher Zeit lebten dort in stiller Verborgenheit Kolonieen von Magiern, die aus Babylon ausgewandert waren und in diesen barbarischen Gegenden, indem sie ihre traditionellen Glaubensvorstellungen mit hellenischen Ideen verwoben, mit der Zeit einen trotz seiner komplexen Beschaffenheit originellen Kultus herausgebildet hatten. Am Anfang unserer Zeitrechnung sah man ihn plötzlich aus dem Dunkel auftauchen und gleichzeitig im Donau- wie im Rheintal und bis in das Herz Italiens vordringen. Die Völker des Abendlandes empfanden tief, daſs der mazdäische Glaube ihren alten Nationalreligionen überlegen war, und die Massen strömten zu den Altären des fremden Gottes. Aber die Fortschritte der Eroberers stockten, sobald er mit dem Christentum Fühlung bekam. Mit Erstaunen gewahrten die beiden Gegner, wie ähnlich sie sich in vieler Hinsicht waren, ohne sich von den Ursachen dieser Ähnlichkeit Rechenschaft geben zu können. Und darum klagten sie den Geist der Lüge an, daſs er ihre heiligen Bräuche habe parodieren wollen. Der Konflikt zwischen beiden war unvermeidlich und wurde zu einem heißen, unversöhnlichen Kampfe, denn sein Einsatz war die Weltherrschaft. Niemand hat uns seine wechselnden Momente berichtet, und unsere

Explicatis causis progredimur ad Melancholiæ *differentias*, quarum aliæ sumuntur à subjecto in quo generantur, sic alia est *Essentialis & Primaria*, quæ nimirum fit proprio vitio capitis: alia per *Consensum* seu *Accidentaria* si aliunde causatur, & hæc dividitur in *Universalem & Particularem*: *Universalis* nominatur quando causatur à toto: *Particularis* quæ in specie *Hypochondriaca* nominatur.

It is a most powerful affection, which renders lovers distracted and alters them so much that you would not recognize them as the same people. The vehemence of this is evident in <term>Medea</term>, who, due to the impotence of love and <term>zelotypia</term> <gloss>jealousy</gloss> toward <term>Jason</term>, tore her children apart; and in <term>Dido</term>, who, overcome by love for <term>Aeneas</term>, laid violent hands upon herself.

Some who suffer from insane love, however, love more impotently and consistently act less correctly by reason. Although these are led away from the right and the good by the impulse of love, they do not entirely wander in their mind, insofar as they know and acknowledge that what they are doing is less than right; nevertheless, they yield to the magnitude of the affection, see the better things, and approve of the worse. Eventually, the magnitude of the affection reaches such a point that, because of the continuous passions—by which they are vexed without any intermission—worry, sadness, cares, and anger, they finally wander entirely from reason.

From the thesis just presented, it becomes manifest that Melancholy does not arise immediately from imagination alone (as many falsely persuade themselves) but through the mediation of the generation of melancholic humor. The causes generating such a state shine forth most strongly in insane love, such as fixed and profound imaginations, worry, and especially a sudden and vehement fear, fixed sorrow, and finally, raging and horrible anger, which, if they persist for a long time, are of such power that they sap a man and lead him suddenly to extreme ruin. ### CONCERNING HETEROCLITE NOUNS

Since there are certain nouns which are declined variably, which for that reason the Greeks call <term>heteroclita</term> <gloss>irregularly inflected</gloss>, and we call them heteroclite by a Greek name, because we do not have a Latin one: it seems worthwhile in this place to write about heteroclites, if I first specify that some nouns are <term>aptota</term> <gloss>indeclinable</gloss>. Which run uniformly through all cases, such as frugi <gloss>frugal/useful</gloss>, nequam <gloss>worthless</gloss> and similar ones, and the names of numbers, from four up to one hundred. Some are <term>monoptota</term> <gloss>having one case</gloss>, which have only one case, such as sponte <gloss>by one's own will</gloss>. Some are <term>diptota</term> <gloss>having two cases</gloss>, which have only two distinct cases, such as fors <gloss>luck</gloss> forte <gloss>by chance</gloss>, tabi <gloss>decay</gloss> tabo, uerua <gloss>spits</gloss>, uerubus. For ueruum is not in use. Some are <term>triptota</term> <gloss>having three cases</gloss>, which have only three distinct cases, such as the neuters in the singular, such as templum, templi, templo: and in the plural all neuters, such as templa, templorum, templis, sidera, siderum, sideribus. Some are <term>tetraptota</term> <gloss>having four cases</gloss>, which have only four distinct cases, such as those ending in <term>r</term> of the second declension, such as puer, uir. Some are <term>pentaptota</term> <gloss>having five cases</gloss>, which have only five distinct cases, such as the masculines and feminines of the second declension, such as doctus, Priamus, populus, fagus.

And indeed, those who have believed that men initially crawled forth from the earth as a mute and base herd could scarcely have handed down anything else concerning the origin of languages. Therefore we, to whom the origin of the human race is more correctly open from the sacred codex, assert truly that the primordial language was infused into the first men, unless perhaps you wish to accept what Cratylus argues to the contrary in Plato, which is altogether vain and has already been exploded by others at greater length. Yet, although, as we mentioned above, we acknowledge the diversity of languages through a divine miracle because of the building of the Babylonian tower, nevertheless, since the mutual communication of duties among the human race must be exercised in every age, a convention could not but be entered into among diverse mortals, so that each one might use his faculty of speaking in a uniform way, and express the same things with the same words. Otherwise, there would be no use of speech, unless it were understood by both sides. Cicero points to this in the *Tusculan Disputations*, Book 5: *We are all deaf in those languages which we do not understand.* Ovid, *Tristia*, Book 5, Eclogue 7:

> *I am a barbarian here, because I am understood by no one.*

## TH. X.

Nor does it stand against this that a private individual is permitted to lose his own life for a King, Elector, or Christian prince established in danger of life, if he can save him. Which deed we read was done by Ribiscius, servant of Mauritius, D.S. Answer: This deed is not to be called <term>αὐτοχειρία</term> <gloss>suicide</gloss>; but it is founded in the dictate of right reason and love toward the public good: And it has as its primary end <term>καλόν τι</term> <gloss>a certain good/virtue</gloss>, that is, the preservation of common utility.

## TH. X. <note>sic, original repeats thesis number</note>

Nor does it stand against this that they object that it is *permitted* for a person invaded by someone to lose their own life, so that the soul of the invader might be freed. For I deny that this is permitted to the invaded, unless the aggressor is a person useful to the republic and the invaded a vile person; or if he is in danger of damnation: *as the Blessed Hülsemann once felt in the Treatise on the Law and Moderation of Correction.*

## TH. XII.

Nor does it stand against this that it is permitted for a common soldier to face inevitable danger of life for his Colonel, so that he might remain safe. For a great bond, such as a <term>Sacramentum</term> <gloss>oath of military allegiance</gloss>, obligates the soldier, by which he promised that he would promote the increase of the army and defend his safety, which in large part hangs from the safety of the Colonel.

<margin>
QUESTION
II.
</margin>

## TH. XIII.

The other QUESTION is, *whether the companions lawfully slaughtered a willing and joyous companion, so that their own lives might be preserved?* which we again deny.

## TH. XIV.

For we rightly urge the divine command on not killing, which the omnipotent legislator gave to us. And it is agreed among those who recall the acts of men to the tribunal of conscience that only that can be held for a lawful cause of killing a man which God approved in his law as just, either expressly or by evident consequence. However, that the proposed case is excepted anywhere in the command of not killing, it is scarce possible to prove with a suitable argument.

### THESIS XXIII.

Nam factum eorum tùm erat absolutè coactum à famis atrocitate et ventre auribus carente, ita, ut si extra hunc necessitatis casum fuisset, ad tale facinus non fuissent prolapsi ; tùm cum summâ quoque perturbatione animi conjunctum, qui non poterat facilè circumstantias facti perpendere, sed singulis mortem momentis anxius metuebat.

### THESIS XXIII.

Nec finis pœnarum acquiri poterat, sive emendationem lædentium spectes, qui tale quid extra necessitatis casum non ampliùs erant facturi ; sive satisfactionem pro læso, qui non ampliùs aderat ; sive præcautionem omnium, ut cautiùs mercarentur, quibus necessitatis hic casus vix timendus erat.

### THESIS XXIV.

Nec obstat, quod dicant quidam, in iis delictis, quæ pœnâ capitali coërcere Deus mandavit, quale est homicidium, non licere Majestati veniam dare. Respondeo. Circumstantiæ delicti sunt respiciendæ, ob quas Majestas civilis pœnas legibus determinatas immutare, mitigare, et exacerbare potest. Quô in casu non tam dispensatorem agit Majestas civilis, quàm interpretem, et non tam mitigat pœnam, quàm justè applicat. *Dominus Zieglerus. Dissertatio 4. de Jure Majestatis paragrapho 26.*

Neque tamen judicem in eo defenderim, quod nullô eos modô puniverit. (a) *It is an old saying that two eyes see more than one.* He who denies that this also applies to the Prince is ignorant that extreme talents are often raised to the throne: and that these, whether by age, or training, or nature, lack that first share of spirit and talent; or that the mind of one man is not capable of such a burden. Therefore, a Prince doubtful of the causes for imposing collections should take Counselors into these cares: and have their advice. *For those things which are managed by counsel are cared for better than those which are managed without counsel.* (b) We wish them to be prudent, that is, knowledgeable of the customs and spirits of the province, and of all things which Besoldus recounts at length, book 2, politics, chapter 4, page 687; furthermore, prompt in talent, and for whom advice is easy to draw from necessity, and is born under the hand. In such a case, let them first attempt everything that will help the Prince before the subsidy of the subjects. For it is not always impossible. Talent is effective when you apply it. Nor was the advice given to Claudius long ago, when he was complaining about the smallness of the treasury, absurd: *it would abound if it were received into partnership by two freedmen.* Those men were Pallas and Narcissus, the ones in charge of accounts, whom he had allowed to acquire and plunder much. *Suetonius, Claudius, chapter 28; Tacitus, 14 Annals, page 157.* (e) Although it is difficult and harsh to give counsel to a king, or to any mortal whose wealth is in the heights, it is nevertheless hardly considered by those who promise golden mountains to Princes. ### LXXX.

Nam cum constitutor simpliciter promittat se soluturum, quod
vel ipse vel alius debet: manifestum est, eum obligari citra solem-
nitatem verborum, neque iudicium eludere posse per exceptionem
viciosae stipulationis, sufficienti actori simplici pactione, quae prae-
cedenti obligationi innitatur, & hoc praetoris beneficio vestiatur.

### LXXXI.

Vnde manifeste elucet huius actionis a fideiussoria diuersitas,
cum fideiussor solemni stipulatione obligetur, & absque ea conue-
niri nequeat, vt receptior est <term>Doctorum</term> sententia per <term>legem</term> blanditus <term>Codice</term> de fi-
deiussoribus & <term>legem</term> stipulationum aliae, § satis acceptio, <term>Digestis</term> de <term>verborum obligationibus</term>
cum similibus.

### LXXXII.

Nouatione autem potior est constitutio, quod haec priorem
obligationem non tollat, quod illa facit: & cum alius pro alio con-
stituit, vterque obligatur, quod in nouationem non cadit, quo-
niam ea personam non mutat.

### LXXXIII.

Nudum autem pactum Ecclesiasticorum ex <term>capitulo primo extra de pactis</term>
huius actionis utilitatem non eleuat, quoniam id in forum ciuile,
receptiori calculo non recipitur, & denunciationes canonum mul-
tis in locis hodie contemnuntur: ubi vero earum adhuc ratio habe-
tur, ibi cum dicto pacto concurrit haec actio ciuilis, & vincit sociam
loco & modo proponendi.

### LXXXIIII.

Quemadmodum etiam prior obligatio multis de causis debi-
lior esse potest, quam ea quae oritur ex constituto, quod haec illi vel
ratione loci, vel temporis, vel alterius alicuius qualitatis & circum-
stantiae emolumenti aliquid addat. Et vt aliquando nihil fit in con-
stituto amplius, quam in praecedenti obligatione, utique tamen &
eo casu sua ipsi constat utilitas. Quod expediat actori, Reum pluri-
bus actionibus obnoxium tenere, & ex ijs vtram velit, posse eligere.

### LXXXV.

Et quamuis in formula tantum pecuniae mentio fiat, tamen ea
appellatio ad omnes res tam mobiles quam immobiles nunc perti-
net, ex receptitia iam antiquata huc transfusas, non ad eas tantum,

### LXXXVI.

Actionem de constituta pecunia sequitur apud Iustinianum: actio de peculio, quam praetor aequitate naturali motus introduxit, ne penitus ludificarentur ii, qui cum seruis aut filiis familias contrahunt, quibus domini, vel patres permittunt in rebus peculiaribus negotiari.

### LXXXVII.

Peculium autem nomen quidem habet a pecunia, quasi pusilla pecunia, id est pusillum patrimonium paragrapho ultimo Digesta eodem Sed interdum sumitur etiam pro quolibet cuiuslibet patrimonio lex cogit Digesta ad Trebellianum. Nonnunquam quoque pro pecunia praesidii causa reposita, unde dici solet, pecunia sine peculio fragilis lex si chorus paragrapho 1. Digesta de legatis 3 In hac tamen actionis forma, peculium in ea significatione accipitur, quae primo a nobis loco posita est.

### LXXXVIII.

Vt peculium sit, id quod filius familias vel seruus permissu patris vel domini, habet peculiare, separatum a rationibus paternis vel dominicis, eo deducto quod patri vel domino, vel iis qui in eorum potestate, tutela curaue sunt, debetur lex peculium, et lex sequens paragrapho ultimo Digesta de peculio.

### LXXXIX.

Non quod necesse esse putemus ut dominus vel pater semper concedant iis quos in potestate habent peculium, quoniam eo pacto filius furiosi, et seruus pupilli, vel furiosi peculium non haberent; sed quod cum Iuliano satis esse putemus, eiusmodi personas peculium iis non adimere, quibus priores domini vel patres ante concessissent lex quam Tuberonis Digesta de peculio.

### LXXXX.

Quamuis autem tam feruis quam filiis familias: peculium attribuimus non tamen eodem modo utrisque: cum seruorum peculium uniforme sit, filiorum vero quadripartitum prout a diuersis causis proficiscitur, a patre vel eius intuitu aliunde, aut simpliciter aliunde, aut ab industria militari, vel quasi.

### LXXXXI.

Neque tamen ad omnes has species accommodata est haec actio, sed ad profectitium tantum: quoniam in castrensi vel quasi filius-familias

seed:
### LXXIIII.

That seems to us to be of civil rigor rather than natural equity, that in not acquiring, the fraud of the debtor is unpunished and does not give place to this action.

### LXXV.

In which species, if an heir or co-legatee colludes with the debtor, we assert that it is consistent with equity that a Christian judge can admit the useful <term>Pauliana</term>, or at least, by disguising the name of the action, provide the same effect to the creditor, by the argument of the law 3, Digest, title *siquid in fraudem patronorum.*

### LXXVI.

Especially when we know that the fraudulent acquisition of a debtor is not usually to the fraud of creditors, as in the law 1, § *sed si emerit*, Digest, title *siquid in fraudem patronorum.*

### LXXVII.

Regarding the time and exercise of the <term>Pauliana</term>, we feel with those who establish a year from the beginning as useful, then continuous, so that however the fraudulent profit can be sought back perpetually, by the argument of the law *ait praetor*, 2 response, penultimate paragraph, Digest, title *quae in fraudem.*

### LXXVIII.

But of the <term>Pauliana</term>, enough has been said for our institute. Another example of a praetorian personal action is in <term>Iustinianus</term>: *de constituta pecunia* <gloss>concerning money promised</gloss>, which although some think is superfluous today for various reasons, and therefore useless, we nevertheless agree with others who affirm that the convenience and use of this action still remain with us in many ways.

### LXXIX.

Not indeed that the constitution does not often fall into other forms of actions, and sometimes concurs as if with a stipulation, sometimes with suretyship, sometimes with novation, sometimes even with a bare pact, often dressed in a diverse reason; and it always arises from a preceding obligation, which without a new constitution would supply its own action for demanding what is owed to each; but because the constitution always enriches and affects the prior action with a new benefit and convenience, so that it differs in something from the other already mentioned forms of actions, and has and protects its own ends and terms.

### LXXIIII.

Illud nobis rigoris civilis potius esse videtur, quam aequitatis naturalis, quod in non acquirendo debitoris fraus sit impunis, & huic actioni locum non faciat.

### LXXV.

In qua specie, si cum debitore colludat haeres vel collegatarius, Christianum iudicem utilem Paulianam admittere posse, vel saltem dissimulato nomine actionis, eundem effectum creditori praestare, aequitati consentaneum esse asserimus, argumento lex 3. Digestum siquid in fraudem patronorum.

### LXXVI.

Praesertim cum sciamus fraudulentam debitoris acquisitionem creditoribus fraudi esse non solere lex 1. § sed si emerit, Digestum siquid in fraudem patronorum.

### LXXVII.

De tempore & exercitio Paulianae, sentimus cum iis, qui annum à principio utilem statuunt, deinde continuum, ut tamen fraudulentum lucrum perpetuò repeti possit, argumento lex ait praetor, 2. responsum § penultima Digestum quae in fraudem.

### LXXVIII.

Sed de Pauliana iam, pro nostro instituto, satis multa. Alterum exemplum actionis praetoriae personalis est apud Iustinianum: de constituta pecunia, quam etsi putant quidam varijs de causis esse hodie superfluam, idcircò inutilem, nos tamen alijs astipulamur, qui huius actionis commoditatem & usum multis modis adhuc nobis constare affirmant.

### LXXIX.

Non quidem quod non saepè in alias actionum formas incidat constitutum, & modo cum stipulatione, modo cum fideiussione, modo cum novatione, etiam cum pacto aliquando nudo, saepè diversa ratione vestito, quasi concurrat: semperque ex praecedenti obligatione oriatur, quae citra novam constitutionem, suam ipsa actionem suppeditet ad exigendum quod cuique debetur; sed quod constitutio priorem actionem novo semper beneficio & commodo ita locupletet & afficiat, ut à caeteris iam nominatis actionum formis in aliquo differat, ac proprios fines & terminos habeat atque tueatur.

Much less should it be supposed that they lay alive and breathing in open tombs throughout the three days that Christ spent in the sepulcher, until they came forth after the resurrection of the Lord; rather, it is credible that the tombs remained broken open for those three days until the soul was reunited with the body.

§ 11. For after the resurrection of the Savior, the resurrected ones went out from their tombs and came into the holy city, as the text clearly asserts. For those words <term>μετὰ τὴν ἔγερσιν αὐτοῦ</term> <gloss>after his resurrection</gloss> pertain not only to the going forth, but also to the resurrection of those saints, in that those saints were both resurrected and immediately went out from the tombs after the resurrection of Christ. Nor is it an obstacle that the Evangelist does not recount this resurrection of the saints after the history of the resurrection of Christ, but rather before it. For he does this by means of <term>ὕστερον πρότερον</term> <gloss>placing the latter first</gloss>, on the occasion of the remaining miracles that occurred after the death of Christ. Divine Jerome says that these saints did not therefore rise before the Lord, even though their tombs were opened, so that the Savior might be the firstborn of the resurrection from the dead, as he is called in Colossians chapter 1, verse 18, and Revelation chapter 1, verse 5. But because some were resurrected even in the Old Testament before Christ, and indeed by Christ himself in the days of his flesh, Christ is therefore called the firstborn of the dead or from the dead, not so much in respect of time as in respect of eminence, power, and efficacy, because Christ not only rose by his own power, but also by his resurrection is not merely an example, but is also the cause of the resurrection of others to blessed life.

Therefore, he who does not know the image of God in himself, and the character of God in nature, or who does not apply the diligence to learn it, has used his time in this life uselessly, for which he will have to give a sharp account.

Now, both the Hebrew <insert>א</insert> <gloss>Aleph</gloss> and the Greek <insert>Α</insert> <gloss>Alpha</gloss> are the number <term>Unarius</term> <gloss>unity/one</gloss>, or a number, but the Latin A has no number. Through this, the Holy Spirit shows in His alphabet of nature that the end of God, or the beginning of nature, is in itself—without the <term>principium</term> <gloss>principle</gloss> of life, that is, without the **3** signs—only dark; that is, it is no number, and that without the principles of life, it should not be placed as the first fundamental number of the knowledge of God.

<margin>Job 10:22</margin>
Because within it, all colors and numbers lie hidden under the black color as a <term>hylical</term> <gloss>matter-related</gloss> mystery, and <term>Aleph Tenebroso</term> <gloss>Dark Aleph</gloss>, as in a divinely magical and unspeakable darkness, an abyss known only to God. Thus, the darkness was not the first principle of divine revelation (: for this darkness did not make God Himself manifest, but the creature :), but the life-giving <insert>Δ</insert> <gloss>triangle/fire</gloss> light and Spirit that sprang from it, as the **3** signs of the one Godhead in heaven. And for this reason, this letter has **3** little flames among the Hebrews, and **3** little strokes among the Greeks, and these **3** in one are the <term>Unarius</term>.

<margin>A</margin>De natura Pythagoras scribere adorsus esset, ita in principio dixerit, Non per aerem quem spiro, non per aquam quam bibo, non admittam huius sermonis vituperationem. Scripsit autẽ Pythagoras tria volumina, De institutione, De ciuilitate, De natura. Quod autem nomine Pythagoræ legitur, Lysidis Tarentini Pythagorici est, qui quum Thebas profugisset, Epaminondæ præceptor fuit. Refert Heraclides Serapionis filius in Sotionis Epitome, scripsisse & illum versibus De toto. Secundum item Sacrum sermonem, cuius est initium,

<margin>B</margin>> *O iuuenes tacita colite hæc pia sacra quiete.*

Tertium De anima: quartum De pietate: quintum Helothalem Epicharmi comici patrem: sextum Crotonem & alios. Porrò mysticum sermonem aiunt Hippasi fuisse, qui in iniuriam Pythagoræ scripserit, plura item ab Astone Crotoniate scripta Pythagoræ inscripta esse. Ait autem Aristoxenus complura moralium dogmatum accepisse Pythagoram à Themistoclea sorore. Ion autẽ Chius in Triaginis ait ipsum, quũ poema quoddam scripsisset, Orphei titulum adnotauisse. <margin>C</margin> Scopiadas itidem ipsius esse aiunt, cuius operis initium est, Nullius rex egens esto. Sosicrates autem in Successionibus ait, ipsum rogatum à Leonte Phliasiorum tyranno quisnam esset, dixisse, Philosophus. Præsentémque vitam dicebat celebritati simillimam. Quemadmodum enim ad hanc alii certaturi, alii negotiaturi, alii optimi futuri spectatores veniunt, ita & in vitam alios quidem gloriæ mancipia nasci, & cupiditatis aucupes, <margin>312</margin> alios verò veritatis studiosos. Et ista quidem sic se habent. Verùm in tribus illis Pythagoræ opusculis quæ diximus, feruntur ista in vniuersum. Non permittit <margin>D</margin> quenquam pro se orare, quòd ignoret quid sibi expediat. Ebrietatem seorsum perniciem vocat, omnéque nimium reprobat dicens, non debere quempiam neque laborum, neque ciborum transgredi modum. Ac de Venereis sic ait, Venerea hyeme, nõ æstate faciẽda, in autumno ac vere leuius. Omni autem tempore esse grauia & ad sanitatem minimè idonea. Rogatus quan-

<margin>A</margin>He descended into the Cave of Ida. In Egypt, he entered the inner sanctuaries, then returned to Samos, and finding his fatherland under the control of the tyrant <term>Polycrates</term>, he sought Croton in Italy. There he gave laws to the Italians and became famous along with his disciples, who numbered nearly three hundred and managed the republic in an outstanding manner, so prudently that it was deservedly seen as an <term>aristocratia</term> <gloss>republic of the best men</gloss>. <term>Heraclides Ponticus</term> reports that he was accustomed to say of himself that he had once been <term>Æthalides</term> and was considered the son of <term>Mercurius</term> <gloss>Mercury</gloss>, and that Mercury had advised him to ask for anything he wanted, except for immortality. Therefore, he asked that, both while living and after life had ended, he might retain the memory of everything that had happened. Thus, in life, he remembered all things. He also preserved the same memory after death, and some time later he entered into <term>Euphorbus</term> and was wounded by <term>Menelaus</term>. Now, <term>Euphorbus</term> said that he had once been <term>Æthalides</term> and had received from Mercury as a gift that his soul should wander in perpetual migration and pass into whatever trees or living creatures it wished, and that it should remember everything the soul had suffered in the underworld, and what the other souls suffered.

<margin>B</margin>

<margin>C</margin>After <term>Euphorbus</term> died, his soul entered <term>Hermotimus</term>, who himself, wishing to provide proof, went to the <term>Branchidae</term> <gloss>a priestly clan at Didyma</gloss> and, entering the temple of <term>Apollo</term>, pointed out the shield which <term>Menelaus</term> had affixed there. He says that when <term>Menelaus</term> had returned from Troy, he had dedicated to <term>Apollo</term> the shield, which was already rotting, and only the ivory face remained. When <term>Hermotimus</term> had finished his life, it migrated again into <term>Pyrrhus</term>, the Delian fisherman, and he remembered everything: that he had first been <term>Æthalides</term>, afterwards <term>Euphorbus</term>, then <term>Hermotimus</term>, and finally <term>Pyrrhus</term> was made, and then after <term>Pyrrhus</term> it became <term>Pythagoras</term>, and he remembered everything we have previously mentioned. Most say that <term>Pythagoras</term> wrote nothing, but they think this foolishly. For <term>Heraclitus</term> the physicist speaks about him most clearly: <term>Pythagoras</term>, son of <term>Mnesarchus</term>, practiced the study of history more than all other men, and selecting these writings, he created his own wisdom, much knowledge, and the study of the arts. <margin>A</margin>Phauorinus in octauo Omnimodæ historiæ. Alij verò Pythagoram, alium quendam aliptem athletas ita solitum enutrire dicunt, nō hunc. But this is not perpetual, for guardians appointed by testament, or by inquiry, are not burdened with the provision of security.

<margin>LI.</margin>
But if two or more are appointed by testament or inquiry, one may offer security for the indemnity of the minors, so that he alone may administer.

<margin>LII.</margin>
Unless a co-guardian or co-curator also offering security is preferred over him.

<margin>LIII.</margin>
Otherwise, if out of several no one offers security, if indeed the testator has written down who should act, he must act.

<margin>LIIII.</margin>
But if it has not been written, the one whom the majority elects shall administer.

<margin>LV.</margin>
But if the guardians themselves disagree regarding the election, the <term>Praetor</term> <gloss>a high-ranking Roman magistrate</gloss> is bound to intervene.

<margin>LVI.</margin>
Which we shall show, with the Emperor's authority, also holds true for several appointed by inquiry.

<margin>LVII.</margin>
Moreover, so that it might be better provided for minors and other persons, a <term>actio subsidiaria</term> <gloss>a subsidiary action</gloss> was invented against those who either failed to ensure that security was provided by the guardians or curators at all, or who allowed it to be provided inadequately. This, according to the Constitutions, is also extended to their heirs, by which it is also expressed that unless guardians and curators provide security, they should be restrained by the seizure of pledges.

<margin>LVIII.</margin>
Guardians and curators are, however, excused for various reasons.

<margin>LIX.</margin>
For instance, on account of the number of three, four, or five children.

Porphyry writes that when he had given diligent effort to astrology, and had finally seen through the vanity of the art and the falsity of its predictions, he revoked all faith in the astrologers. Therefore, in the book dedicated to him, titled *On the Efficiency of the Stars*, he laughed at and refuted the dogmas of the astrologers. Maternus, bearing this with difficulty, lies much about his death, as if he paid the penalty for his labor. For that it is most false is easily understood from Porphyry himself, the disciple of Plotinus, who faithfully describes the manner of his disease and death, and why and for what reason he left Rome. Diogenes Adamantius, in the philosophical sect, as in all disciplines most eminent, has often and many times refuted astrological vanity, unless perhaps his testimony is worth less because he is a Christian—but he was not a Christian. Eudorus, who also heard Plato and lived in Egypt and was considered the prince of astronomers in his time, left behind writing that nothing should be believed of the astrologers who predict the fates of men from their horoscopes. Alexander of Aphrodisias, a supreme authority in Aristotelian philosophy, in his book *On Fate* addressed to the Emperors Severus and Antoninus, rejected the necessity of fate and refuted astrological arguments. Perhaps he was drawn to mention fate only to correct the mind of Severus Caesar from such philosophical superstition. Averroes, a celebrated philosopher in the same family and a serious estimator of natural things, lacerates and attacks astrology everywhere. For in his first philosophy, he calls the astrological opinion about celestial images, under which earthly figures are thought to be subject to animals, fabulous, and with its removal, the greater part of astrological superstition falls. Similarly, explaining the *Cantica* of Avicenna, he says elsewhere that it is contrary to philosophy, and elsewhere that almost all the dogmas of the astrologers are false, and the art itself is entirely vain and weak. In his books against Algazel, he asserted that the artificial images, from which astrologers think they can derive the influence of the heavens, are inefficient. Avicenna, a great man in all disciplines, in the final book of his first philosophy, proved with many arguments that future things cannot be foreseen by astrologers. Therefore, no faith should be placed in their predictions. I omit Hericus from Asia and many other illustrious moderns who, in the Parisian academy, pursued this vanity in their dedicated works, and the greatest part of philosophers, who rather than refuting it, preferred to treat it like other deceitful arts, old wives' tales, and the ravings of illusionists. But it is worthy of note that even those who called themselves astronomers rejected this profession, which they could not do entirely without conscience and fear of falsity, since otherwise, they would have gained as much science, glory, and profit from the faith and authority of astrology as those who exercise themselves in the motions of the heavens. ### XXVI.

Cùm autem viuentis partes rarescunt, non nouam aliquam quantitatem, sed vbi duntaxat nouum vetere abiecto acquirunt, excrementitium vaporem exhalant, poros laxant, & largiùs alimentum imbibunt. Vacuum, vt naturæ viribus vniuersè dari nequit, ita nec rarescentibus viuentis partibus importatur.

Thus we will know what generates from two elements mutually destroying each other, or something else that is different, or some living thing; in this way we will easily recognize the producing causes of lightning, thunderbolts, flashes, springs, metals, herbs, plants, and trees.

### XV.

Like can usually generate like, but sometimes it cannot; therefore, a living thing is sometimes produced from a dissimilar living thing, but never from a non-living thing. Angels can produce only local motion, and perhaps also impetus, which is sometimes the main cause of the same motion; it is so far from the case that they create a living thing or any other substance. The same thing in number cannot be produced naturally again, or twice; it can be produced divinely.

### XVI.

Now it is certainly clear that generation is an action entirely different from alteration, and that generation is said to be the limit of alteration very improperly. For how, since it is an action, can it terminate alteration? And how is it not different from alteration, when it has a different limit? The formal limit of generation, in man, is indeed the union of the individual and spiritual rational soul with the divisible and material, and in all others, besides union, also divisible forms: but the ultimate and adequate limit is the whole composite.

### XVII.

Whence it is rightly defined by the Philosopher as the change of the whole into the whole, with no sensible subject remaining the same. For the whole composite is truly generated, and since prime matter can naturally support only a single substantial form—and that of some lowest species—the whole substantial composite that was before, or the sensible subject, must perish. From which it is plain that every generation which is comprehended by this definition is a certain conversion, although not every generation is absolutely a conversion, nor is every conversion a generation. For the former cannot be given outside a subject, and the latter cannot be given from a privative or negative limit.

### XVIII.

But the subject of generation is prime matter alone, endowed with quantity and other accidents, which it is not necessary to perish at the very moment of generation, since they are neither stripped of their subject, nor abandoned by their preserving cause, nor are they judged to perish by the entire and uncorrupted judgment of the senses. §. 3. I come to the celebrants themselves of this Pseudo-Jubilee, some of whom are living in Rome, or are merely present there at that time, while others are absent. Those who travel to Rome themselves are received with a great display of honor; graces are provided for them for their arrival, because they did not hesitate to celebrate this Festival, having left their native Churches for that City in which (if it is permitted to believe) the keys of the Kingdom of Heaven are, and that inexhaustible Treasury of the Church, whose Guardian and Dispenser is the Roman Pontiff, as Marchantius describes Rome in his *Hortus Pastorum* <gloss>Garden of Pastors</gloss>. Furthermore, the most plenary indulgence, remission, and pardon of all sins is promised to them, with this condition added: if they are to visit the Basilicas of the Blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, St. John Lateran, and St. Mary Major, as the Bulls of the Pontiffs expressly hold. Before Boniface VIII, indeed, as Prosius notes, those who came to Rome for the sake of the Jubilee were held to visit only the Church of St. Peter; but with the passage of time, they were bound to the others as well. For in addition to the Church of St. Peter, which had to be approached, Boniface VIII later added that of St. Paul, Clement VI that of St. John Lateran, and Gregory XI that of St. Mary Major: as if, in truth, divine Grace were to be sought in these temples in particular, when nevertheless our Savior, making no respect for this or that place, says: *Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them, Matth. 18:20.* These Churches must be visited repeatedly according to the number of days prescribed by the Roman Pontiff, which, unless it is fulfilled by those blind celebrants, there is no reason, as they say, for anyone to promise oneself the most plenary pardon of one's transgressions. Thus, the Bull of Urban VIII holds:

> *To those who devoutly visit the Lateran Church, the Basilicas of the Blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, and also St. Mary Major of the City, at least once a day for thirty continuous or interrupted days if they are Romans or Inhabitants of the City, or if they are pilgrims or otherwise foreigners, for at least fifteen days, and who pour out pious prayers to GOD for the salvation of those faithful and the whole Christian people, we mercifully in the Lord grant and impart the most plenary Indulgence, remission, and pardon of all their sins.*

To follow the examples of this man and of similar ones—Scaevola, Crassus, Sulpicius, who avoided no labor of teaching even when established in the highest dignities—is also honorable and distinguished for our Jurists, and let them know that this duty of interpreting laws and assiduity in judgments is not only full of dignity, but also pleasing to God.

### Regarding the character and life of Papinian, it shall be judged from his writings.

For speech is the index of the mind, and we willingly and frequently speak of those things which settle in our hearts: as the Poet says:

> The sailor speaks of winds, the plowman of bulls
> The soldier counts his wounds, the shepherd his sheep.

So also our Jurists have written the best precepts of life and rules for living honestly, for harming no one, and for giving each his own, to which we ought to refer and derive all our actions of life as if to a norm. Their character and life were consistent with these precepts. For they themselves wished to invite other men to the reverence of laws and the love of justice by their own example.

Such was Neratius Priscus, whose life was equal to his precepts. Such was his probity, such his loyalty, candor, integrity of character, such his wisdom and moderation in judging, and his love of justice and equity, that he was even to the most lauded Emperor Trajan

(x) Furthermore, since it is evident that <term>Bellarmine</term> was forced to build up the authority of the <term>Vulgate</term> by fear of anathema, it is certainly not a surprise that he, even if he were undoubtedly better informed about this controversy, in the hope of a future Pontificate, did not want to abandon the <term>Council of Trent</term>. Indeed, the genius of <term>Bellarmine</term>, shining most clearly, removes the Cardinal from the number of witnesses. For he took upon himself so much labor, with others, that by various readings, or omissions, or corruptions, he makes doubtful not only the letter of Scripture, but also the sense; so that he might either fish more easily in troubled waters, or even, against the will of the Holy Scriptures, extort some visible interpreter and judge of controversies, who might define and decide the genuine sense and the true reading. For this reason <term>Bellarmine</term> also prefers the <term>Vulgate</term> to the <term>Greek text</term> in this place; to show the infallible judgment of <term>Pope Damasus</term>, by whose command, it is said, <term>Jerome</term> corrected the Latin Version; and that by this reason he might also strengthen the confirmed Canons of the <term>Council of Trent</term>. Since, therefore, in court a witness who is addicted to the zeal of parties is not admitted to give testimony, especially if an antagonistic mind toward one or the other party is known, and the will to suppress the other is evident; much less here in a sacred cause, where the question is agitated concerning the principle of our faith, do we listen to such a one, who, for all that he is (while he is consistent with himself), said what he said, occupied by a perverse opinion for the favor of his own.

§. XIIX. Furthermore, it must be explained what authority two <term>Greek Codices</term> obtain against our sentiment. <term>Glassius</term> reports (z) that <term>Robertus Stephanus</term> found the reading of the <term>Vulgate</term> in two <term>Codices</term>, and indeed with truth, as is plain to one inspecting the copy of <term>Robertus Stephanus</term> printed at Frankfurt in the year 1601, in the reading of 1 Corinthians, chapter 7. Truly, if it is permitted for us to take as help the weapons of those against whom we fight, it will be an easy conjecture that this happened by the fault of the typographers. This is a frequent remedy which <term>Bellarmine</term> invokes for himself, both in the defense of the <term>Vulgate</term> against the <term>Greek text</term>, and also in the response itself to the arguments of the adversaries.

Et si judicio nostro etiam sententia aperienda est, Hieronymi opinio à genuino sensu verborum et reipsa minus abesse videtur, quando de iisdem dici existimat, mulier innupta et virgo. Etenim Praedicatum *ἁγία* de corpore intellectum, non excludit uxorem, ut quae majori cura intenta est, ne sanctitatis studio posthabito, et illecebris mundanis illaqueata, corporis castitatem exuat; quod quanto majus peccatum, tanto majore diligentia et ardore cavendum est. Jam verò si sanctitatem utrique, et uxori communem et viduae intelligat, nulla ratio adferri potest, cur de vidua intelligendus locus, adeoque incertum relinquitur, num Apostolica sententia Viduas et Virgines copulaverit; quod vult Ambrosius loco citato quae rem intente spectanti apertè sententiam nostram probabunt. Cum igitur in reipsa autoritas vacillet, quidni de testimonio etiam dubitari possit?
