Which Legislator, as he thinks it to be for the benefit of the Republic, is in no way prevented from interpreting the laid-down law in this or that way, from abrogating it entirely, or from dispensing with the same by the force of his own power, indeed even from introducing the contrary to an abrogated law, provided it is not contrary to the <term>Law of Nature</term>, even if at times <term>Civil Law</term> may seem to have constituted something beyond nature.

§. XIV. The way in which <term>Civil Law</term> is said to be changed in our section is twofold: Tacit consent and a newly enacted law. By tacit consent, if I am not mistaken, custom is understood, regarding which it will not be a burden to set down here some things that declare the matter more fully. Namely, custom can be referred both to the law of nature and to positive law. This might perhaps seem strange to someone. But to explain this, these things must be noted. The rule of the <term>Law of Nature</term> is: It is just that each one in indifferent matters should conform himself and his actions to the actions of the others who live in the Republic. By which it is manifest that custom pertains to <term>Natural Law</term>. Now, in order that it may also be referred to <term>Civil Law</term>, in aid must be summoned the laws mentioned in Digest 1.3.32, 33, 35, and 37, On Laws and Senate Consults and long-standing custom. Since those laws wish customs to be valid, and princes have subsequently approved those laws as positive law, it appears they have brought it about that customs were a part of positive law. And indeed very rightly so. Because all reason for enacting law should tend toward the peace of the Republic and the convenience of the subjects, and since institutions which the people themselves introduce tacitly and gradually without doubt fit the genius of the people best and are held by the people themselves as most convenient, it was most equitable that honorable customs prevail even without the approval of the Magistrate. seed: towards men. Do not, I beseech you, object to me here that these plagues are because of the crimes of the heretics. We are not speaking now of crimes in general; but only of the cruelty and savagery which does not exist in the heretics, but in the Roman Pontiff. Although even if it existed in the heretics, what is the wonder? If it thrives so much in the Roman Pontiff, whom you consider most absolute, does it not exist in heretics who are so imperfect and of no value? Heretics ought to have that along with other vices, just as the Roman Pontiff ought to have clemency as a practice, along with other virtues. The same must be said about the wars that have been ignited everywhere. What good is to be expected from the wicked? From the perfect and holy, good is to be expected. But O immortal God, how confused everything is! I do not say that it is not about crimes; but let us descend even to the crimes; let us enter this vast ocean. I do not deny, and many crimes exist among heretics as well—would that it were false!—but I ask you by God to tell me, are there none among you at all? Alas, how I fear that for ten crimes of heretics, a thousand may be found among you. Let us act sincerely and truly, as if God himself hears us, to whom all things are naked and open, with nothing hidden or concealed; and if you dissemble your own crimes and attenuate them, you exaggerate and amplify those of the heretics, and in this manner of rhetoricians and dialecticians, or finally of sophists. But, as I was saying, let us consider ourselves to be in the trembling presence of the living God; will you be able to deny that the wrath of God has been stirred up by your outrages and indecencies? Let us omit the cruelty and savagery, which you contend is done rightly and correctly; let us omit your doctrine, worship, and ceremonies, which you decide were handed down from the ancestors, and came down through the hands to the Roman Pontiff; let us omit other things. Let us now speak only of vices and crimes. Will you deny that greater and more nefarious crimes and sins are found anywhere than where the Roman Pontiff reigns, indeed in Rome itself before his own eyes? I will not torture myself too much here; for if you dare to deny this, you will deny equally that the Sun shines. Wherefore it would be in vain to say another word from now on; and you would prove yourselves not only sophists, but worse even than those. But if we act truly and simply, the matter would be finished in a few words. For, as I was saying, beginning from that very Rome, and surveying the whole empire of the Roman Pontiff, you will find nothing but what is foul and filthy. What shall I say about the temples themselves? Where is greater impunity and license for sinning perceived? They should indeed be called brothels rather than temples and shrines.

Here, I cannot wonder enough that so many and such great men, who are most famous for the glory of their knowledge, have labored so much not only in previous centuries, but even in this our own age, concerning the Quadrature of the Circle, and have tortured themselves gravely in describing it with no, or at least (that their good reputation may be consulted) with very meager benefit to readers. Truly, if anyone already possessed the books of Archimedes—who wrote most accurately about this matter—which were snatched from us by the envy of time, he (if I am not mistaken) would go along with our opinion, and would declare that the Quadrature of the Circle itself (if anything is to be attributed to the authority of plausible conjectures) must be completed in this way. Moreover, it is helpful to employ a medical manner of speaking in declaring these mysteries. On a wide and clean tablet, let NOTHING be placed expertly by a mathematician, and with the use of those little hatchets recently devised divinely by the coryphaeus of the Critics, let whatever hinders the Quadrature of the Circle be cut away from all sides. When, however, the things to be cut are cut, and the things to be done are done, and the things to be finished are finished, you will thus have the Quadrature of the Circle itself, perfect in all its parts. Do you not see (kind reader) what an expeditious Quadrature of the Circle an excellent knowledge of NOTHING provides you? ### X.

Quintò, pactum est vel in rem vel in personam. Pactum in rem nominatur, quando generaliter paciscor, ne petam, et illud etiam alteri prodesse potest. In personam, quando paciscor, ne à certa persona veluti à Titio petam, et hoc pactum, cùm sit personale, à persona in aliam non porrigitur *l.7.§.8.D.h.tit.* quia personalia cum persona extinguuntur. Tamen omne pactum esse in personam censetur, quia spectatur semper commodum personæ, quæ paciscitur. *R.* Etiamsi persona pacto inseratur, non inde tamen efficitur, quòd personale sit pactum, sed ut constet, cum quo pactum sit, *d.l.7. §. 8. D.h.tit.* At in dubio in rem pactum esse omninò non dubitatur, quia persona tantùm adjicitur demonstrandi causâ, et hoc colligitur ex voce (*plerumque*) in *d.l.7.§.8.eod.* nam personale pactum semper est restrictum ad certam personam. Igitur quando quæstio est an omne pactum sit personale, observandum est, an persona consideretur ut circumstantia, et ita omne pactum est inter personas; vel ut subjectum inhæsionis, et ita non omne pactum est personale. And therefore, after this constitution, Bachovius confirms that there is no longer any utility and necessity in Law 6, Code, on dowry promised.

### VIII.

A <term>nudum pactum</term> <gloss>naked pact/bare agreement</gloss> is defined as nothing other than a convention of two or more persons, which consists in the pure and mere terms or limits of the convention alone, and does not pass into a proper name of a contract, nor does it have form, solemnity, or cause from which it could assume strength and efficacy to produce an action. Nevertheless, some wish for every pact to be "naked," because a pact does not generate an action. It is true, indeed, that every pact is naked in relation to the cause which contracts have within themselves, or in relation to the name by which a contract is distinguished from a contract; but not every pact is naked in relation to the action, by which some pact generates an action, some pact forms an action; or every pact is naked while the naked and simple form of the convention remains: not every pact is naked from the special confirmation of some law; or it is naked insofar as it contains no just cause, for just as a confession of debt made without cause is naked and does not prejudice according to Law 25, at the end, Digest, on proofs. Likewise, a transfer <term>traditio</term> <gloss>delivery</gloss> without cause is called naked and does not transfer ownership, Law 31, Digest, on acquiring ownership of things; so if something is promised by pact without cause, it is called a naked pact, and does not provide the efficacy of suing.

Who will be this judge? Perhaps the one who alleges the necessity? But what if he has not appraised the matter correctly, as often happens, and is not in such straits as he imagines?
<term>The dove is terrified by the slightest rustle of a feather,</term>

But what if he in turn alleges his own needs, and explains the magnitude of the damages by which he is affected, though he has deserved no such thing? Or perhaps some third party, free from partisanship? But there is danger that such a one, by pronouncing for one side, may incur little favor with the other, and be implicated in another's hatred and even war, whether he governs his judgment as law or justice persuades, or as humanity and justice have impelled <note>x</note>. If reprisals have been simply permitted and declared, it is appropriate to seize the former; but the latter may only be distrained by way of example of a just war, when the power to seize assets does not exist or when a heinous crime has not been punished by the magistrate with the due penalty. Therefore, although it is lawful through reprisals to seize the property of even an innocent person, or even to capture his person, it would never be lawful to punish the innocent with corporal punishment. For it is diametrically opposed to the letters of Holy Scripture for the innocent to pay the penalty for another who is guilty, *Deuteronomy 24:16, Exodus 23:7, there: "You shall not kill the innocent and the just."* It should also be observed here that a creditor who has begun to hold the person or goods of another, subjected to the laws of reprisal by his actions, may not retain them, but must lead them into public custody and present the captured goods to the judge of the place where they were captured. The judge will register them in an inventory and, by public authority, will order them sold and satisfied for those for whom the said reprisals were declared. If anything remains above the debt, it must be returned to the owners, after judicial expenses have been deducted. Hence, when they are requested and granted only for the reparation of damage and the restitution of property unjustly taken, once that reparation has been made and his own things acquired, the root and foundation of the reprisals cease. Therefore, whatever is acquired further is unjust and subject to restitution, according to *Law 206 of the Rules of Law, Law 14 on the recovery of undue payments: "No one ought to be enriched at the cost of another's loss and sacrifice without cause."* How, however, one should advise someone who has been harmed and despoiled by the force of reprisals is a matter on which the interpreters do not agree. iron bars, nothing, nothing is rendered safe from plunder, even if preserved by a hundred keys. Workshops are squalid, commerce lies still, negotiations are at a standstill, markets are dissipated, fairs are taken away. The rich are emaciated to the marrow, the poor are driven to the rope, both are driven to desperation. The palaces of Princes are usurped as receptacles, the citadels of nobles as hideouts. With what ferocity mills are destroyed, villas by plunder, villages by pillaging, hamlets by devastation—it does not attain belief, even if it is told in good faith. Truly, it is more than what even barbarism itself would endure that vines are cut down, that fruit-bearing trees are uprooted, that the shoots of hops are torn out, that by the plow being sent in, crops are extinguished while in the very flower. But to whom has all the divine power of the eloquent so indulged itself that, I do not say by explaining, but by narrating, one can express the atrocity and speak of the cruelty with which there is raging against everyone without distinction of sex and age, without measure, without number? No butchery, no wickedness, no crime, no misdeed is omitted. It is little to kill a man unless a punishment unheard of among Christians and most exquisite is applied. Nothing of the clubbing, nothing of decimation, nothing of the rack, nothing of exposure to the soldiers' swords, nothing of whatever in the old age, in the old manner, was heaviest: New and unusual things are devised. Some are suspended by their feet, as they are men. Into others, torches are inserted through obscene parts; those included in sacks are deprived of breath and fumigation. Some are raised onto a cross by one foot with the head turned to the ground and hands bound behind their backs. ## XVI. Quod igitur *Aristotelis* autoritatem attinet, non arbitror his verbis evinci primarium auditus organum esse aerem τὸν συμφυῆ: quid enim per αἰσθάνηται τὰς διαφορὰς τῆς κινήσεως intelligat, ex praecedentibus apparet, ubi dicit, moto aëre exteriori, eum, qui intra est, moveri. Nimirùm haec mens est *Philosophi*, ut auditio fiat, necesse esse, ut sonus ad auditum usque extendatur, qui sonus, ut percipiatur, movere debet aerem internum in eoque omnis generis motus excitare, qui vero auditus organo communicentur. Quod si quis exinde ad primarium organum argumentabitur, non minùs <term>myringa</term> pro eo etiam agnoscere necessum habebit, quàm aerem istum connatum; impossibile cum sit, moveri aerem insitum à sono immoto <term>tympano</term>, quod à sono allabente concitatur, concitatumque speciem motus aeri interno impertit. Alii illis *Philosophi* verbis, quando dicit aerem esse connaturalem aeri, idem probare conantur, sed irrito conatu: nam si legitima esset illatio, sequeretur visus organum principale esse humorem aqueum, quoniam *Philosophus* visum aqueae naturae esse scribit, quod tamen neque cum veritate neque cum mente *Aristotelis* consentit. Aerem itaque, implantatum ut vocant, ad sonos concipiendos necessarium esse affirmo constanter: primarium organum esse nego pertinaciter.

Sequitur fenestra ovalis, per quam aditus patet ad cochleam & ad Labyrinthum, qui in interioribus ossis petrosi recessibus delitescunt; cochlea quidem in antica, Labyrinthum in postica parte. Nomina fortiti sunt hi meatus a modo progrediendi: Cochlea enim ob flexuosam circumgyrationem ita appellatur, quoniam aliquot gyris in se intorquetur. Labyrinthus autem ab anfractibus hanc appellationem obtinuit, nam ex aliquot osseis circulis, integris ferme, constituitur, initio & fine conjunctis, sed progressu separatis. XIV. After the eardrum, a certain cavity is formed in the petrous bone, in which the little bones of hearing are seen to be located, which nevertheless do not fill this place entirely; but they leave some empty space, in which, besides air, according to nature, nothing is contained. This they commonly call congenital or connate or innate air, and they hold it to be innate airy heat, which nature placed in the ears for the sake of hearing, inasmuch as it is of an airy nature according to the Philosopher <note>referring to Aristotle</note>; no differently than in the heart, igneous heat mixed with radical moisture: which truly appears unlikely to me. For I do not see the cause why the air enclosed in this cavity should be sold more as innate airy heat than that which is contained in that cavity under the sternum, or perhaps is found in the empty little caverns of the bones. Furthermore, the air contained therein can be changed from hour to hour, and it is changed. For it is false what they imagine to themselves, that this air is so confined that it cannot exhale, since the paths are sufficiently patent by which it can rush; for what forbids it from penetrating into the brain, when thick pus flows down from there into the ears: or what obstacle is there by which it might be less able to burst into the palate through the aqueduct of Fallopius, through which the excrements of the ear are purged into the mouth. Indeed, if anyone attempts, he will be able to drive air from the throat to the eardrum; but what will prevent the old guest from being expelled and the newcomer retained. And so, this air will deserve to be called congenital or innate airy heat least of all.

XIV. Post Myringa cavitas quaedam in osse petroso efformata est, in quâ auditus officula locata cernuntur, quae tamen locum istum non penitus opplent; sed aliquod vacuum spacium relinquunt, in quo praeter aerem secundùm naturam nil continetur. Hunc aerem congenitum vel connatum vel innatum communiter appellant, atque pro calido innato aereo habent, quod natura in aures Auditus gratia, quippe qui aereae est naturae secundum Philosophum locavit; non secus ac in corde calidum igneum humido radicali permixtum: quod mihi vero simile vix apparet. Non enim causam video, cur aer huic cavitati inclusus magis pro calido innato aereo venditandus sit, quam is, qui in cavitate illa sub sterno continetur, aut fortasse in ossium vacuis cavernulis reperitur. Deinde aer inibi contentus in horas mutari potest, et mutatur. Falsum etenim est quod sibi imaginantur, ita coerceri hunc aerem, ut exhalare nequeat, cùm viae sint patentes satis, qua ruere possit; quid enim vetat, ut in cerebrum non penetret, cum inde crassum pus in aures defluat: vel quod obstaculum est, quo minus in palatum erumpat per aquaeductum Fallopii, per quem excrementa auris in os expurgantur. Imò si quis attentet, è faucibus aerem ad tympanum impellere poterit; quid verò prohibebit, quin antiquus hospes expellatur et adventitius retineatur. Itaque nihil minus quàm congenitus aut calidum innatum aëreum hic aër dici merebitur.

### XIX. Ultimum in Auditus Organo considerandum est nervus auditorius, qui prope anteriora spiralis medullae crura e cerebro progressus per peculiare foramen in osse petroso fabricatum ad Cochleam et Labyrinthum transit ibique terminatur. Hic primarium et principale Auditus Organum est, ad quod si pertingit sonus percipitur; non enim absque immediato hujus nervi contactu ullus sonus cognosci potis est. Idcirco Velcurio Auditum dicit esse potentiam ordinatam in nervo expanso ad aures a cerebro apprehendens formam soni advenientis sibi. Per hunc deinde nervum soni species cerebro communicatur ac sensui communi, tanquam specierum omnium judici atque diribitori, qui postea de ea sententiam pronunciat.

### XX. Organon debito ordine insequitur Objectum, quod causae materialis locum obtinet. Duplicia autem Sensuum Objecta vulgo cum Philosopho statuuntur: communia quae a pluribus sensibus percipiuntur, propria, quae ab uno duntaxat: De illis, quoniam per accidens solum in sensus incurrunt, parum solliciti erimus, et hoc saltem, quod auditui proprium est speculabimur.

Aeterna mundi possibilitas siue potentia: deus est, vel si mauis diuina mens, quae ab eterno in semetipsa praeconcepit mundum: & potuit ab eterno creare mundum. Quae tamen non ab eterno sed in tempore compleuit & ad reale essendi actum perduxit. Hoc pacto exploditur eorum error: qui voluerunt nihil fieri posse de nouo: sed omnia praefuisse antequam fierent. Hi enim respicientes ad solam & eternam praeexistentiam causarum: actus pro potentiis: res pro rationibus: & substantias mentalium conceptionum loco sumendo: in eum errorem merito inciderunt: ut et mundum eternum esse dicerent: & naturales omnes formas, statuisse in potentia materiae: easque de gremio & visceribus materiae foras per generationem perduci: non autem eas nouiter gigni aut recreari. Aliter enim est & subsistit effectus in eminentia sue cause: & aliter in seipso. Est utique in causa, secundum potentiam, secundum rationem, & per mentalem conceptum. In seipso vero subsistit secundum actum & per reale veraque essentiam. Etenim mundus eternus quidem est potentia & conceptione diuine mentis: quae ab eterno mundum in seipsa praeuidit praeconcepitque. tempori autem est mundus actu proprio: & reali suipsius essentia: quae secundum tempus ex arcano & eterno diuine mentis nutu in esse processit.

Yet I would deny that this contrariety exerts a natural fight in the motions of the celestial orbs themselves in such a way as to induce any vicissitude or change of celestial qualities within them. For the fighting and contrariety of causes shines forth more evidently in the effects themselves than in the causes, and its vigor and efficacy is revealed not in the change of stable and permanent causes, but in the vicissitude and permutation of the effects.

<margin>Fifth question.</margin>
Your fifth petition is: Since evil spirits have lost nothing of their natural powers, why do they not now delight with that natural and real delight which they had before their fall? To this I say, according to the divine Dionysius, that all the natural gifts of demons remain lucid and entire in them to this day, but that the judgment of good and evil is corrupted in them, and consequently their will has been rendered unstable. For if you inquire of the divine Dionysius in the book <term>De Divinis Nominibus</term> <gloss>On the Divine Names</gloss>, what evil resides in demons, he says that imagination in them is headlong, their fury unreasonable, their desire demented. These things, assuredly, ensure that they no longer delight with that natural and real delight toward the desire for the highest good which they had before the fall. They possess, indeed, to this day the integrity of all their natural potencies, but these are so closed and barred in them by the wickedness of their aversion and the seal of their malice that they can never be revived toward the desire for the good.

<margin>Sixth question.</margin>

### Quaestio IV.

Praetereà operosior fortassis quaestio: Unde Magi isti accesserint, consideranda veniret, si omnia quae hic moveri soleant, adducere deberemus? Sed nos breviter certum esse dicimus & extra controversiam positum, illos ἀπὸ ἀνατολῶν ab Oriente venisse. Notum autem est, quod Oriens duplex sit: Altera simpliciter & respectu Solis sic dicta, altera γενικῶς relatè, respectu urbis sanctae sive Judaeae uti Ezechiel XI. 23. Zacharias XIV. 4. Oriens Solis & Urbis conjungitur. Jam verò à partibus mundi illos venisse credibile est, quae erant Judaeae ad orientem sitae. Sed ex qua regione praecipuè venerint, & quem locum Evangelista intenderit multum diuque studiosè quaesitum est, quia multae gentes viciniores & remotiores Judaeis ab Oriente fuerunt, sicuti nec uno in loco Magi fuisse commemorantur. Because α) these Magi of ours are not Egyptian, Aramaic-Balaamic, or of other nations, but Persian Magi, whom Suidas <note>23) In his histories, column 316.</note> distinguishes from other conjurers. Consult Peucerus <note>24) On Divination, page 176 and 194a.</note>, who, after having previously stated the noble praises of Persian magic on page 174b, says that the magic of others was the worship of evil demons, an argument which the Blessed Chemnitius also uses, saying: "Matthew therefore calls them 'Magi from the East' to signify the distinction; that they were not such magi as were in Egypt, whose profession was capital under the law of Moses, but such as the East, that is, Persia, has." Consult Casaubon <note>25) Exercit. Anti-Baron. II, number 10, page 135.</note>. β) Because it is highly probable that those men were well-versed in the book not only of nature but also of scripture, which is clearly evident from their sincere faith in Christ (which comes from hearing; here, however, through the word) and their constancy (which neither the length of the journey nor the poverty of the little Jesus nor the apathy of the Jews had broken). γ) Because, finally, it is commonly believed that they were remnants of the school of Daniel, whose doctrine Melanchthon believed these magi retained. Hence, they were made certain of the new event by the appearance of the star as most accurate physicists, and they learned from the writings of Daniel (regarding the 70 weeks), through the internal working of the Holy Spirit via the word, that the new King of the Jews had been born, not from any diabolical magic. Moreover, whatever the case may be, everyone seems to speak of them according to their own bias, says D. Libavius <note>26) Exam. Philos. Section 19, page 35.</note>, and he ingenuously adds:

> *The magi of the Old Testament do not hear well: why should God not have converted idolaters and those devoted to the usual studies in the East to the Son, when Isaiah 60:5 says that the multitude of the sea and the strength of the nations shall be converted to the Church, and since He called Abraham out of the midst of idolatry?* Yet it is consistent that, just as *Abraham* did not approve of the worship of pagan gods at all, so too these Magi were more upright; these are his words.

### §. IX.

Hoc quidem loquendi modo isti liberari possunt, aliàs facile nunquam se expedituri, utut hoc ipsis patrocinari videntur Bubulum caput ex auro effictum ab Aegyptiis pro DEO cultum fuisse, nullo modo id tamen praegnanti ratione accipiendum; Negandum equidem non est, hunc religionis modum apud Aegyptios floruisse, quippe quod ex Asse demonstrarunt Petrus Daniel, Huetius, 16. Octavius 17. quin & Bos Graecorum colendi Deum sub hac formâ, qui ex Aegpto in Graeciam penetrasse dicitur, in testimonium absque pallore vocari potest: Narrant enim peregrinatores, in Medio Insula extare ingentem aram marmoream bubulis capitibus exornatam. Nec non Indi, qui bovis cultum acceperunt ab Aegyptiis, & ad hunc diem retinuerunt, capita bubula vexillis suis appingunt; Testatur & hoc Johannes Baptista Cassalius 1) qui ex professo de veteribus Aegyptiorum ritibus scripsit, duplex depingens caput, alterum ex antiquo metallo confectum & carne nudatum, eâ additâ ratione, quòd voluissent laborem accuratè demonstrare, cùm laboriosi homines plerumque mocilenti sint: 2) Alterum ex aere similiter antiquissimo, sed carne circumdatum, quod Apin 3) repraesentasse creditur, & ab Aegyptiis pro DEO habitum 4) Ast, quamvis id nedum in dubium vocare, multò minùs negare volumus, quia ab Autoribus, quibus multa fides habenda, approbatum est 5) non tamen impetramus à nobis, ut credamus istius cultus aemulationem Israelitas imitatos esse, satis enim probatum dedimus, cultum Bovis apud Aegyptios in usum fuisse, nec non demonstratù à nobis per hunc cultus modum Israelitas à Deo defecisse confirmante ipsâ Scripturâ sacrâ.

### Thesis I.

**Quamvis** praescriptio primo aspectu cum injustitia quadam conjuncta esse videatur, cum contra naturam sit aliquem cum alterius damno fieri locupletiorem lege Jure naturae 206. Digestum de Regulis Juris, capite locupletari 4. de Regulis Juris in Ultimo, neque id quod nostrum est sine facto nostro, hoc est sine traditione nostra, argumentum paragraphus 40. Institutiones de Rerum Divisione lege 20. Codex de pactis ad alium transire possit: re tamen paulo accuratius considerata, ea non solum summe utilis ac necessaria, sed et summe justa dici potest.

Th. II. Probant hoc ea, quae docte hac de re differit Albertus Bolognetus liber de Legibus et Jure et aequitate capite 27. numero 6. et 7. Multa ejusmodi in Jure Civili reperies, inquit, quae rationi naturali videntur adversari, veluti Macedonianum, quod pecuniae mutuo filiusfamilias datae denegat repetitionem; item Vellejanum, quod mulieri quae pro alio intercesserit fidem datam frangere permittit. Nihiloque justior videtur praescriptio biennii quae facit, ut quam vere mihi non numeraveris pecuniam, perinde ac si numerasses restituere tibi compellar, id quod saepe etiam judicati facit autoritas. Haec omnia, pergit, si per se illa consideres ab omni justitia videntur esse alienissima: sed quia ideo sunt instituta, ut gravius quiddam et injustius declinetur, propterea vere justissima dici debent.

Th. III. Scilicet introducta est praescriptio ut litium aliquis sit finis, neque dominia rerum sint in incerto, principium 1. lege 1. ### Th. IV.
Neque obicem huic meo ponit asserto id quod dicitur in Numero 9. esse scilicet praescriptionem iniquum & impium aliquod praesidium: Variis enim dubium hoc resolvi potest modis. Et primo quidem resolvit illud Harprecht *ad principium 1. de usucapione numero 52. hoc modo.* Dici scilicet praescriptionem iniquum & impium praesidium non simpliciter, sed secundum quid, nimirum respectu Ecclesiae Romanae, si nimirum ea breviori tempore deberet excludi quam Constantinopolitana, vel habito respectu ad regulam quae habetur in *lege 14. Digestorum de condictione indebiti.* Secundò aliter dubium hoc diluit Manz *ad dictum principium numero 104.* dicendo, intelligendam hic esse illam praescriptionem, quae cum mala procedit fide, non verò quae cum bonâ fide, ita ut prior non verò posterior impium dici mereatur praesidium. Et haec solutio fundamentum habere videtur in verbis *textus ibi, iniquis hominibus.*

### Th. V.
Ad id verò ut justa dici possit, praescriptio requiritur, ut omnia praescriptionis observentur requisita: his enim neglectis ea nulla est atque invalida, id quod & sequentes volunt versus memoriales.

> ->Non usucapies nisi sint tibi talia quinque;<-
> ->Bona fides, justus titulus, res non vitiosa;<-
> ->Ut res tradatur, & tempus continuetur.<-

Imprimis verò ad usucapionem requiritur, ut res quae praescribitur sit habilis, & ut cum Doctoribus loquar usucapibilis seu praescriptibilis: aliàs enim reliqua requisita non prosunt, licet res bonâ fide ex justa causa accepta, & per tempus legitimum hoc est à legibus definitum, possessa sit.

### Th. VI.
Ex quibus evidenter liquet objectum praescriptionis habile non esse res furtivas vitio quippe laborantes, id quod & docet jureconsultissimus noster Imperator *§. 2. Institutionum de titulo* nec non Jurisconsultus Paulus in *lege 4. §. 6. Digestorum eodem.*

In conchyliata scopus est pallor laudatus, de quo ante. Præstantior hic est si respondet violæ serotinæ quam ile prounciat esse conchyliorú vetetissimam, modo nobis constaret, quæ nam esset hæc absque dubio. Putare licet interim violaceum colorem notari multo albo mistum, qualis est in floribus cichorii cæruleis, aut in caudæ panonis ambitu oculi á latere spectato, qui tamen est virore perfusus & aliqua flauitie aut viola canina dicta.

Next, the prepositions are to be noted, the number of which is very small in individual languages: but their use, both separate and in composition, is far most abundant and most widely diffused. Thirdly, it will be fitting to add a distinct knowledge of conjunctions for enunciation, reasoning, and order. For by these, both diverse sentences and sometimes also parts of the same enunciation and syllogistic complexions, and often also, especially in compounds, assumptions are accustomed to be convinced and gathered. Fourthly, interjections are added to these: about which it is hardly necessary or worthy to touch upon anything here, so easy is that matter and of narrow rule. Fifthly, we judge that one must pass on to the discipline of verbs: where above all the simplest verb, which grammarians call substantive, must be known: which no period can lack, even if at times it is clearly expressed, [and] at other times it lies hidden, suppressed in other verbs. Wherefore, logicians teach that it is, in simple or categorical propositions, a copula and a kind of glue of the terms to be arranged. Although the saltiness is not the same at every time of the year, but is sometimes greater and sometimes smaller, it is not significantly intensified. Then also, nature does what is best, namely the best human, the best dog, the best fly; see Sperling, *Synops. Phys.*, p. 31. Now, it is not always "best" that is "greatest"; neither the greatest man nor the greatest dog is therefore the "best." But the name of God, added to other names, declares that which is the highest and most excellent in every kind, whether of great or small things. Indeed, even in the smallest things, the wisdom and power of God shine forth no less than in the greatest things. *“In a fly,”* says the Blessed Sperling in his *Instit. Phys.*, p. 143, *“there is as much of God’s power as in a lion, the sun, or a human.”* In that place, he explains at length the wonderful construction of this little animal. But I pass over these things now, and return to the names of God. Thus also the word <term>El</term> is used in Psalm 36, ch. 7: "הרי אל" "mountains of God," that is, great and lofty. Similarly also the name <term>Yah</term> in Song of Solomon 8, ch. 6: "His coals are coals of fire, a flame of God" (שלהבתיה), that is, the greatest and most vehement. For so Aben Ezra, who prefers to be two words against the Masoretes (who, according to Ben Asher, note the word to be unique), and thinks the name <term>Yah</term> is subjoined in a similar sense to how <term>El</term> and <term>Elohim</term> are used elsewhere; see Buxtorf in his *Lexicon* under the root <term>lahav</term>, p. 387.

Whence Drusius suspects in *Praeterit. Lib. VI* on this passage, p. 235, that the "language of angels" here is what the Hebrews call <term>lashon Elohim</term>, "the language of God," that is, divine and excellent. And in this way among the Greeks, those who excel most in any kind are called <term>dioi</term> <gloss>divine</gloss>, such as Achilles, divine for the sake of bravery; Odysseus, for the sake of prudence; Alexander and Clytemnestra, divine for beauty; Eumaeus, for loyalty and benevolence; the Sea and Charybdis, for magnitude and depth; as Eustathius teaches on the *Iliad* Alpha, v. 7, p. 21, who says a little before: *“It is said of excellent humans in imitation of Jupiter; from which comes <term>dios</term>, and contractedly <term>dios</term>.”* Hence, as Aristotle observes in *Book VII of the Nicomachean Ethics*, ch. 1, *“From men arise Gods (others read 'divine') because of an excess of virtue.”* For which reason the Lacedaemonians, as the Philosopher notes in the same place, were accustomed to call and greet him divine, whom they greatly addressed

Omnia esse amicorum inter se omnia veteri prouerbio dicunt: Si quid est igitur in noua dignitate nostra, quod quidem sit expetibile, habes vnde læteris: nam et tu pariter nobiscum bonorum nostrorum es particeps, quem verum esse amicum nunquam dubitauimus. At quod nos merito id honoris consecutos arbitraris, longe falleris sententia nostra: nam qui multo inferiores sumus, quàm quibus episcopatus cura committi debuerit, plane intelligimus haudquaquam nos tales esse, quales sacro cardinalium coetui ascribi debent: cumque non ignoraremus qua doctrina, qua probitate, qua nobilitate præditos esse oporteat, qui summis de rebus acturi in senatum Apostolicum accersuntur: horrescimus sane et contremiscimus ineptitudinis nostræ memores; cum inter columnas Ecclesiæ, inter orbis cardines, inter lumina mundi collocatos nos esse videmus: scimus quantum ascendimus; sed quonam pacto, quave de causa tantum euecti supra merita nostra simus, prorsus ignoramus. Inscrutabilia sunt (vt nosti) consilia magni Dei, et arcanæ quamplures causæ, ad quas nulla potuit hominum curiositas peruenire. Nos promotionem nostram diuini Pontificis maximæque vrbis Romæ Præsulis Calisti tertij beneficentiae, summæque eius in nos charitati atque affectioni ascribimus; cui tanto magis obnoxij sumus, quanto dignitas ab eo recepta maior est, quàm nostra virtus: nec dubitamus ita placuisse rectori omnium Deo, sine cuius nutu nihil est quod in terris quidem valeat explicari. Cognoscimus tamen in quanto periculo versamur, quàm fragilis est status noster, quàm lubricus, quem ascendimus locu: cum inter doctissimos, indocti: inter expertissimos, rudes: inter probissimos, improbi, vitam agamus. Itaque protegat nos, oramus sanctissima manus Dei: et qui dedit ascendere, auferat cadere. Quod vt nobiscum rogites, obsecramus. Nec plura de cardinalatu.

<note>A decorative initial letter C contains floral motifs.</note>I learned from the letters of friends that you have been created a cardinal. I congratulate you, who for your virtue have attained worthy rewards, and myself, whose friend has been placed in a dignity where he may one day be able to help me and my kin. It is troublesome to me that you have fallen upon times which seem destined to afflict the Apostolic See. For frequent complaints are brought to my lord the Archbishop regarding the Roman Pontiff, who keeps neither the decrees of the Council of Constance nor those of the Council of Basel, nor does he think himself bound by the agreements of his predecessor, and he seems to wish to despise and utterly drain our nation. It is clear that the elections of prelates are rejected everywhere; that benefices and dignities of any quality are reserved for both cardinals and protonotaries. And you yourself, under a formula that is hitherto unusual and unheard of, have requested a reservation for three provinces of the German name. Expectative graces are granted without number; annates, or first-fruits, are exacted without any delay of time; and it is plain that even more than what is owed is extorted. The governance of churches is committed not to the deserving, but to the one who offers more. New indulgences are granted day by day to scrape up money. Exactions of tithes are ordered to be made for the sake of the Turks without consulting our prelates. Causes that were to be treated and determined in the regions are indiscriminately dragged to a convenient tribunal. A thousand ways are devised by which the Roman See may extract gold from us as if we were barbarians, with subtle ingenuity. Perluſtratis iis, quæ ad Theoriam affectûs noſtri pertinent, reſtat, ut nunc etiam, quâ methodô debeat curari, inveſtigemus atque proponamus. (3) Pleuritic persons breathe with difficulty, because the membrane adheres to the ribs and especially to the vertebrae, as *Vesling* notes, *syntag. anatom. cap. 10*, and if these are simultaneously drawn in respiration, and beset by the tumor, the respiration is made frequent and small, and it presses all the more quickly if the diaphragm is affected. (4) A hard, swift, unequal, and large pulse is perceived, sometimes also small, both by reason of the fever, arising from the warmer and boiling blood, and by reason of the affected part, from the nervous, tense, and inflamed membrane. (5) A cough is also referred to among the principal pathognomonic signs by Galen, *lib. de difficult. respirand. cap. 2*. It is dry in the beginning because, as we have said, the matter is still raw and serous, transuding the pleura, and is imbibed by the spongy lung, as it were from the part contiguous to the pleura, whence nature is afterwards irritated to expel it; but it becomes moist in the succeeding time, when the matter, through concoction, acquires a consistency fit for expectoration; for then, stirred by coughing, the matter is ejected through the rough artery <note>original: trachea</note>.

The signs of the causes provide us with this knowledge: If pure blood has been the cause of pleurisy, the sputum is red and bloody, the pain is tensive along with a pricking; fullness and tension of the veins appear around the forehead, and other signs of a plethoric constitution concur. But if this affection should depend on bilious blood, the sputum will be yellow, the fever will be more ardent, the thirst will urge more vehemently, and the pain will prick more sharply. In a phlegmatic pleurisy, however, everything will be more remiss; if an abundance of serum is joined to the blood, it will also be manifested by domestic signs. ### X I I.

## *Argumentum quod intorquent primum sit hoc.*

Insistunt: Quod alterum ab altero distinguit non est commune. Quia causa discrepantiae non est causa convenientiae. Atqui Proprium distinguit subjectum à subjecto. Ergò non potest esse Commune.

Resp. Majorem simpliciter veram nego, vita enim Animae propria distinguit corpus Animatum ab Inanimato, tamen est Communis Corpori & Animae. Quî autem hoc fit? Notandum; Proprium Communicatum distinguit etiam subjectum à subjecto, distinguit autem unumquodque ut unicuique competit, subjectum A QUOD distinguit & ei competit per inhaerentiam, originaliter, per se, primariò: AD QUOD & cui communicatur, per associationem & secundariò. Sic Commune etiam aliquid ab aliquo distinguere potest, diverso tamen modo, non simpliciter, ut accipiunt qui ista movent.

## *Exemplum sit hoc:*

Calor est Communis Igni & Aquae, duo haec subjecta distinguit ita, ut sciamus Ignem per se & primariò esse calidum, Aquam verò calidam esse non per se & primariò sed per aliud & secundariò, nimirum per unionem Ignis.

Nor does he rest solely on his own views here, but furthermore appeals to the authority of Lord <term>Carpzovius</term> <note>Benedikt Carpzov (1595–1666), a highly influential German jurist</note>, a most celebrated jurist and most expert in practical law. His words on page 2, Chapter 12, Distinction 26, numbers 1 and 2, are these: "The donation of all present and future goods is therefore invalid, since it takes away the free power of making a will." For although inheritance is a legal term, and nothing prevents the testator from having nothing in his goods according to Law 3 of the Digest on the <term>Lex Falcidia</term> <gloss>a Roman law restricting legacies to ensure the heir received one-fourth of the estate</gloss>, yet one who neither has nor can have anything, such as that person who has donated even his future goods, certainly cannot possess the power of testing, and so forth; see the cited passage, which he further confirms later from number 10 to the end. But these things and similar ones do not sway me, as I have occupied myself thus far within the bounds of civil law, within which I judge that I must still persist, since neither of these jurists is alien to me on this reasoning: the former in the words "whatever is argued in the schools," and the latter in numbers 4, 5, and so forth up to 8 inclusive, in express terms. Except that he asserts the contrary is accepted by the usage of the court, which I easily grant him, and thus a donation of universal goods, present and future, will not be unjust insofar as it is forbidden by laws, but insofar as custom has introduced the contrary, and thus has made what was previously permitted—as frequently happens in indifferent matters—illicit. Nor does the reason sought from the power of testing have any effect in Civil Law. For that was introduced in Civil Law in favor of private persons, to which, according to the rule of law, we may easily renounce; indeed, everyone who donates all their goods is believed by this very act of donating to have renounced this freedom. Likewise, it is found to be provided by no law that anyone must precisely make a testament, but this very thing is left to the judgment of each person, as the subject of legitimate successions and <term>ab intestato</term> <gloss>concerning someone who dies without a will</gloss> abundantly testifies.

Bona verò fortuna, sicut & mala, dicitur, cùm bonum, malúmve contingit: ευτυχία & δυστυχία, cùm vtrumque, bonum & malum, ingens est: estque ευτυχία, quæ à fortuna nomen habet, instabilis & dubia: quia fortuna, seu quod à fortuna est dubium est & incertum: quia neque perpetuum, neque frequens.

### XXXVII.

Conuenit fortunæ cum casu, quòd vtrumque per accidens causa est eorum, quæ rarò fiunt, & finis rationem habent.

### XXXVIII.

Differunt, quòd Casus latius fortuna patet: quia quod à fortuna est id à Casu est, non contrà: & quòd Casus, propriè sumtus, in illis est, quæ à rebus tum ratione, tum anima destitutis, sine consilio, solo naturæ instinctu, fiunt, fortuna verò in illis, quæ consilio suscipiuntur.

less nature, but a certain hidden and divine cause which, as we have said, concurs with our action beyond all our expectation and produces its own effect, of which we had not even dreamed. The Stoics called this hidden cause Fate; the Christian Lyceum calls it the providence of God.

### XXXI.

Speaking physically, however, it is rightly said that fortune is unknown to man and is not defined, because its effect is uncertain and dubious, and this is because there can be countless occasions for which a fortuitous event might follow.

### XXXII.

It is also rightly said both that nothing is done by fortune and that some things are done by fortune.

### XXXIII.

For as it is a cause by accident, certain things are done by it; but as a cause through itself, nothing at all is done by it, since it is a cause only by accident.

### XXXIV.

But also that is well said, that a reason for fortune cannot be given.

### XXXV.

For since a reason can be given only for those things which either always behave in the same way or behave so for the most part, and fortune behaves in neither of these two ways but in another and different way, it is clear that its reason cannot be given.

§. 10. This passage of Josephus must be examined a little more accurately, since it fixes another epoch of the years of Herod's reign. For it is known that the years of the reign of Herod are deduced either from the first announcement made at Rome, or from the capture of Jerusalem. Note, therefore: that the consular character supplied by Josephus indicates the year of the City 716, Varronian 717, as can be seen in the consular records in Sigonius, to which corresponds the Julian year 9, J.P. 4677. Nor does Dio Cassius indicate another year, while in Book 49 of *Roman History*, he records that the capture of Jerusalem and the execution of Antigonus occurred under the consuls Claudius and Norbanus, who held the consulship before Agrippa and Caninius Gallus, who were named by Josephus. For the consulship of these men also reaches the beginnings of the year of the J.P. 4677. However, this must be observed concerning Dio: that he makes mention of this matter at least in passing, and thus does not note the entire history, but at least the beginning of the siege with a chronological character, which we also concede fell in the consulship of Claudius and Norbanus. 2. Note: that the Olympiad, named absolutely and indefinitely, designates the first year of that Olympiad according to the usage of writers, from which, however, Josephus very often departs. Hence, 3. we restrict the indefinite Olympic character from the consular character to the beginnings of the fourth year of the 185th Olympiad. So that we refer the beginning of the siege to the end of the third year, and the capture itself to the beginnings of the fourth year of the 185th Olympiad. 4. COOPERS HILL.

Sometimes an improvident mother crushes her offspring:
It does not carry away the wealth it had bestowed with the violence 
Of a wave, like a prodigal King; nor does it ruin the gifts 
Of the green meadow, or the happy fates, and the labors of men and oxen.
But it goes good and happy, and with a constant spring; and like to God
With a rejoicing mind it rolls back its own gifts.
Nor does it have enough to enrich the fields near to itself,
But more common than the wind and the sea, it visits all things;
And it shows off the richest usury of an ungrateful bank,
And generous, it scatters itself into all shores,
And brings back the riches lying under the twin Sun
In a winged carriage, and makes our India both of them.
It seeks wealth where they are, where they are lacking It provides them;
And it bestows woods upon cities, and cities upon woods.
To such an extent that there is no Region unknown to Us,
When the whole World comes into its bosom.
O if I could flow like this, and could run down
Equal to the Subject, transparent to the very bottom,

### X.

Now, however, I approach the full burden of the labor, when a judgment must be formed regarding this miracle. For however much the appearance of the asserted miracle may exist, it is utterly overwhelmed by others and cast down by strong arguments. Indeed, it is defended by some in such a way that its falsehood makes the palm of truth doubtful. Hornius, in his notes on Sulpitius Severus, declares this to be one of those fables that a later age either invented or adopted against the faith of previous centuries. And he confirms this solely by the silence of Eusebius, of which more later. Others, however, start the matter as if from the beginning, refuting each and every testimony brought forth. First, it is argued that the book *On Hebrew Places* is not by Jerome, partly by authority and partly by the argument of the writing itself. Sixtus Senensis, a Papist, (from whom Rivetus compiled his own censure of this writing, *Critic. S. lib. 4, c. 5*) ascribes this booklet to a certain scholar who collected it from Jerome; and he finds it credible that the collector was Bede, in whose works this same booklet still exists, *lib. 4, Biblioth. Sanct. on Jerome*. Philip Labbe holds the same opinion in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Vol. 1, p. 439, Paris edition. Compare the censure of certain writers by Robert Cocus, and among them Jerome by name. Regarding Marianus Victorio and Scultingus, it is manifest that they have utterly rejected this book in the censure prefixed to the works of Jerome. For the writing itself gave cause for suspicion, since Jerome himself is cited in it near the end with these words: *Jerome in his books on Hebrew names sets down Smyrna and interprets it as Amara.* Furthermore, under the word *Damascus*, mention is made of Maavia, King of the Arabs, who only began to reign in the year of our Lord 651,

Nonnullis verò ita defenditur, ut dubiam veritati faciat palmam falsitas. Idque solùm Eusebii silentio confirmat, de quo inferius. Alii autem ab ovo quasi rem ordiuntur, singulaque et omnia adducta refellunt testimonia. Primò probatur librum de Locis Hebraicis non esse Hieronymi, partim autoritate, partim argumento ipsius scripti. Biblioth. Sanct. de Hieron. Ejusdem sententiae est Philippus Labbe de script. Eccles. Tom. 1. p. 439. ed. Paris. Conf. Roberti Coci censura quorundam Scriptorum, et in iis nominatim Hieronymi. O nimium felices illos! qui mature intelligunt, tales magistros sibi exuendos, postquam sat amplis Doctoribus, majoribus nempe suis, sese instructos esse, prudenter conjectant; quorum exemplo et gloria ad veram solidamque virtutem firmari queant et accendi. Mirifice admodum Agasicles, Lacedæmoniorum Regis, juvenile sed senilis prudentiæ effatum, quoties recordor, me delectat. Hic quippe, cur Sophistarum scholas dedignaretur? quondam interrogatus mascula indole respondit; se eorum discipulum esse malle, quorum esset filius, utpote qui virtutem ipsis factis præstarent, non illorum, qui compositis arte verbis de virtute nugarentur. Quin magni alicujus Principis, hodie rerum potentis, callidus informator (si nupera forsan magis afficiunt) à Serenissimo Patre ejus, tunc Imperii Septemviro, compellatus, feliciterne literarum studia tractaret filius? satis apposite respondit, principaliter, id est sicut paulo post ipse interpretabatur, qui ex sapientia modum teneret. # Additions, added for the sake of avoiding a vacuum.

->I.<-

<note>A decorative initial 'T' begins the paragraph.</note>
The Talmudic saying is well-worn: *Whatever is written in the Bible obscenely must be read decently: so that a man may not utter an obscene word from his mouth.* Most people take this to mean that the words placed in the Hebrew text were sufficiently honest at the time of the Scribes, and did not offend the simpler ears of that age; but in a later age, with all wickedness and filthiness growing in that people, they were so profaned by common usage that the pious could scarcely hear or pronounce them without blushing. Therefore, they think the Masoretes substituted other vowels for those words and exhibited their proper consonants in the margin. Thus the celebrated Glassius, *Phil. S., book 1, tract 3, section 8, p. 280*; Amama, *Antib. Bibl., book 3, p. 739*. But this does not please the most learned Englishman, Nicholas Fuller, in *Miscell. S., book V, c. 3 & book VI, c. 11*, who thinks the marginal <term>Qeri</term> <gloss>read</gloss> was added only for the sake of clarification. We do not simply reject either of these opinions, holding both in a sound sense, which we will explain more fully in the very debate, given the opportunity.

->II.<-

Elias Levita has somewhere: *Everything that is written in the margin is a KERI, by which it is meant that that word is read; but what is written inside (in the text) is not read at all.*

### XXII.

Finally, we have already indicated above that non-natural things bring no light moment to producing this annoying affliction; for excessively cold air can easily condense the serous-nutritive particles, and thus it will be able to be the matter of stagnation, and by means of this, of the rupture of the vessels. Food and drink take on the roles of procatarctic <note>predisposing or initial</note> causes insofar as they are consumed, erring in quality and quantity; especially, the abuse of acids fosters this disease if it does not most manifestly increase it; likewise, more vehement motion, such as running, dancing, the carrying or lifting of heavy things; the same must be said of sleep and vigils that are excessive or deficient. Things to be excreted that are retained also contribute their symbol to this, e.g., menstrual blood approaching more slowly or appearing more sparingly, or completely suppressed: retained excreta; for sometimes our uterine flow is accompanied by an immoderate flow of menses or lochia, nor rarely by the excessive veneration of <term>Veneris medullisorbae</term> <gloss>the marrow-robbing Venus/excessive sexual indulgence</gloss>. That the <term>pathemata</term> <gloss>passions/disturbances</gloss> of the mind exercise the greatest force on our disease is testified primarily by grave and long-protracted grief of the mind, great and unexpected terror, etc.

### XXIII.

The causes having been perceived, we shall also consider how this *White* discharge differs both among itself and from other diseases. Ast Anabaptistae negant hoc praesuppositum longe certissimum, sub praetextu, ac si inter Christianos omnia velint mitissima, cum tamen revera vel ex Ratione status, tanquam coetus minus potentes sic contra Magistratum rebus suis prospicere cupiant, vel superstitionem loco pietatis exosculentur; vel pestiferam αναρχιαν introducere studeant; vid. modo laudatus D. Alberti l. c. & Danaeus Opusc. t. 444. Imo iudicat Stanisl. Hosius Lib. 1. de haeresibus nostri temporis p. 428. nullam sectam tam impiam, pernitiosam & seditiosam esse, quam secta Anabaptistarum sit. Proh! quantum enim delirium est, statuere, Magistratus officium non alia ratione esse ordinationem Dei, quam Diabolus est minister Dei, cum exequitur ejus iram, aut Tamerlanes sese vocavit flagellum Dei. Vide ipsorum Confessionem Harlemi editam Anno 1618. Artic. XXXVII. Ponderanda nunc erunt ipsorum argumenta, quibus blasphemam hanc sententiam palliare potissimum conantur.

Quicquid autem (*argumentantur*) est ordinatio humana (Didymus enim & Oecumenius Graecum κτίσις, i. e. Creatura sumit pro τάξει & ordinatione) id non potest dici ordinatio divina. Atque Majestas, juxta hunc locum, &c. Respondeo. Quando Majestas a Petro ἀνθρωπίνη κτίσις vocatur, id observante Gerhardo l. c. *tres* potissimum ob causas fieri solet, nempe (1) *ratione subjecti*, quia ex hominibus, adeoque ex vulgari hominum forte divinitus ad dignitatem & potestatem Magistratus eliguntur ac evehuntur. (2.) ratione causae instrumentalis, quia plerunque per homines ad eum, quem gerunt principatum evehuntur, praesertim si sint Magistratûs inferiores. (3.) *ratione Termini ad quem*, quia in commodum humanae societatis potestas Magistratus est instituta, & eodem fine adhuc conservatur. E quibus tamen *ultimam primariam* esse existimat D. Seb.
